00073 [PDF p.6] Preface


00074 [PDF p.6] 


00075 [PDF p.6] 


00076 [PDF p.6] 


00077 [PDF p.6] 


00078 [PDF p.6] Through the past 20 years, the framework of Linear Parameter-Varying


00079 [PDF p.6] (LPV) systems has become a promising system theoretical approach to han-


00080 [PDF p.6] dle the control of mildly nonlinear and especially position dependent systems


00081 [PDF p.6] which are common in mechatronic applications and in the process indus-


00082 [PDF p.6] try. The birth of this system class was initiated by the need of engineers to


00083 [PDF p.6] achieve better performance for nonlinear and time-varying dynamics, com-


00084 [PDF p.6] mon in many industrial applications, than what the classical framework of


00085 [PDF p.6] Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) control can provide. However, it was also a pri-


00086 [PDF p.6] mary goal to preserve simplicity and “re-use” the powerful LTI results by


00087 [PDF p.6] extending them to the LPV case. The progress continued according to this


00088 [PDF p.6] philosophy and LPV control has become a well established ﬁeld with many


00089 [PDF p.6] promising applications.


00090 [PDF p.6]    Unfortunately, modeling of LPV systems, especially based on measured


00091 [PDF p.6] data (which is called system identiﬁcation) has seen a limited development


00092 [PDF p.6] since the birth of the framework. Currently this bottleneck of the LPV frame-


00093 [PDF p.6] work is halting the transfer of the LPV theory into industrial use. Without


00094 [PDF p.6] good models that fulﬁll the expectations of the users and without the under-


00095 [PDF p.6] standing how these models correspond to the dynamics of the application,


00096 [PDF p.6] it is diﬃcult to design high performance LPV control solutions. This book


00097 [PDF p.6] aims to bridge the gap between modeling and control by investigating the


00098 [PDF p.6] fundamental questions of LPV modeling and identiﬁcation. It explores the


00099 [PDF p.6] missing details of the LPV system theory that have hindered the formula-


00100 [PDF p.6] tion of a well established identiﬁcation framework. By proposing an uniﬁed


00101 [PDF p.6] LPV system theory that is based on a behavioral approach, the concepts of


00102 [PDF p.6] representations, equivalence transformations, and means to compare model


00103 [PDF p.6] structures are re-established, giving a solid basis for an identiﬁcation theory.


00104 [PDF p.6] It is also explored when and how ﬁrst-principle nonlinear models can be eﬃ-


00105 [PDF p.6] ciently converted to LPV descriptions and what are the pitfalls that must be


00106 [PDF p.6] avoided. Building on well founded system theoretical concepts, the classical


00107 [PDF p.6] LTI prediction-error framework is extended to the LPV case via the use of


00108 [PDF p.6] series-expansion representations.


00109 [PDF p.6] 


00110 [PDF p.7] VIII                                                                    Preface


00111 [PDF p.7] 


00112 [PDF p.7]    Beside completing the system theoretical aspects and founding of an LPV


00113 [PDF p.7] prediction-error framework, the book proposes a novel identiﬁcation approach


00114 [PDF p.7] based on orthonormal basis functions, which provides an eﬃcient and easy to


00115 [PDF p.7] use approach of LPV identiﬁcation. It has been shown in the LTI case that


00116 [PDF p.7] decomposing dynamical systems in terms of orthogonal expansions enables


00117 [PDF p.7] the accurate approximation of the system with a ﬁnite length expansion. By


00118 [PDF p.7] tuning the basis functions to the underlying system characteristics, the rate


00119 [PDF p.7] of convergence can be drastically decreased. This leads to highly accurate


00120 [PDF p.7] models (small bias) being represented by a few parameters (small variance),


00121 [PDF p.7] which in fact can be estimated eﬃciently via simple linear regression. This


00122 [PDF p.7] philosophy gives the basic concept of the proposed identiﬁcation approach,


00123 [PDF p.7] for which the applicability in practical scenarios is investigated and powerful


00124 [PDF p.7] algorithms are provided and analyzed.


00125 [PDF p.7]    The work presented here is the result of 5 years of research at the Delft


00126 [PDF p.7] University of Technology under the supervision of Prof. Paul M.J. Van den


00127 [PDF p.7] Hof and Peter S.C. Heuberger. Starting with the initial intention to apply


00128 [PDF p.7] simplicity of orthonormal basis function models to overcome the challenges


00129 [PDF p.7] of LPV system identiﬁcation, a long road has led to the theory which is


00130 [PDF p.7] presented in this book. Walking on this road, many excellent people have


00131 [PDF p.7] contributed to this work. Especially Prof. Jan C. Willems, at the Catholic


00132 [PDF p.7] University of Leuven, whose advice and vision about mathematical modeling


00133 [PDF p.7] helped me to ﬁnd the right track that lead to the LPV behavioral theory,


00134 [PDF p.7] that forms the basis of many concepts of this book. Prof. Carsten Scherer,


00135 [PDF p.7] at the Delft University of Technology, whose advice and extensive knowledge


00136 [PDF p.7] on LPV systems and control has always helped me to ﬁnd the missing wheel.


00137 [PDF p.7] Federico Felici, whose earth-moving questions and discussions made me aware


00138 [PDF p.7] of missing key points of the LPV system theory. But the main thanks goes to


00139 [PDF p.7] Prof. Paul M.J. Van den Hof and Peter S.C. Heuberger whose excellent guid-


00140 [PDF p.7] ance led me through these years, culminating in my Ph.D. thesis [188], which


00141 [PDF p.7] served as the basis of this book. As co-editors, they also had a signiﬁcant role


00142 [PDF p.7] in establishing this book in its current from.


00143 [PDF p.7]    The book is written as a research monograph with a broad scope, trying


00144 [PDF p.7] to cover the key issues from system theory to modeling and identiﬁcation.


00145 [PDF p.7] It is meant to be interesting for both researchers and engineers but also for


00146 [PDF p.7] graduate students in systems and control who would like to learn about the


00147 [PDF p.7] LPV framework. It also oﬀers an easy to use guide for engineers about the


00148 [PDF p.7] oﬀ-shelf solutions in LPV modeling and identiﬁcation.


00149 [PDF p.7]    I hope that you as a reader will enjoy reading it as much as it was fun to


00150 [PDF p.7] write it.

00804 [PDF p.23] Chapter 1


00805 [PDF p.23] Introduction


00806 [PDF p.23] 


00807 [PDF p.23] 


00808 [PDF p.23] 


00809 [PDF p.23] 


00810 [PDF p.23] Abstract. In this introductory chapter we give an overview on the origin of linear


00811 [PDF p.23] parameter-varying (LPV) systems and their role in the control of today’s indus-


00812 [PDF p.23] trial applications. Beside the history of this framework it is investigated what the


00813 [PDF p.23] state-of-the-art of LPV systems offers engineers to meet with the increasing expec-


00814 [PDF p.23] tations towards modern control solutions. We will see that the main bottleneck of


00815 [PDF p.23] this promising framework is the lack of a well established LPV modeling and iden-


00816 [PDF p.23] tification theory. To overcome this, the current book sets the goal to explore the


00817 [PDF p.23] lacking details of the LPV system theory and to establish a solid framework for the


00818 [PDF p.23] modeling and identification of such systems.


00819 [PDF p.23] 


00820 [PDF p.23] 


00821 [PDF p.23] 1.1     New Challenges for System Identification


00822 [PDF p.23] 


00823 [PDF p.23] Today, the need to optimize efficiency of plants in terms of performance or energy


00824 [PDF p.23] consumption and to improve reliability of automatization results in increasing ex-


00825 [PDF p.23] pectations towards automatic control applications. Engineers working in the control


00826 [PDF p.23] field have to face challenges in terms of operating industrial process in a more accu-


00827 [PDF p.23] rate way but at the same time with a lower cost in terms of used energy. For exam-


00828 [PDF p.23] ple in lithography, moving stages of wafer scanners today require fast and accurate


00829 [PDF p.23] position tracking with servo error specified in the nanometer scale. In the emerg-


00830 [PDF p.23] ing alternative energy field, the coupled nonlinear nature of wind turbines and the


00831 [PDF p.23] rapidly changing conditions of wind and grid load require more efficient and also


00832 [PDF p.23] easily reconfigurable control solutions. On the other hand, economical efficiency


00833 [PDF p.23] also drives the control field to replace existing control designs with solutions that


00834 [PDF p.23] require less sensors or actuators, but still provide the same performance. Like in


00835 [PDF p.23] the case of induction motors, high performance control based on less built-in sen-


00836 [PDF p.23] sors, like speed-sensorless drives, has great economical importance. To cope with


00837 [PDF p.23] these challenges, well applicable theoretical solutions have been developed like op-


00838 [PDF p.23] timal, robust, and nonlinear (NL) control approaches, trying to refine and extend


00839 [PDF p.23] the results of linear time-invariant (LTI) control theory, widely used in automatiza-


00840 [PDF p.23] tion. However to achieve the aimed objectives by these approaches, it is vital that

00846 [PDF p.24] 2                                                                        1 Introduction


00847 [PDF p.24] 


00848 [PDF p.24] an accurate, compact, and reliable mathematical description of the actual physical


00849 [PDF p.24] phenomenon is available.


00850 [PDF p.24]     First principle laws of physics, chemistry, biology etc. are commonly used to


00851 [PDF p.24] construct a dynamic model of the system of interest. However, such a procedure re-


00852 [PDF p.24] quires detailed process knowledge from specialists. Often it is a challenge to assem-


00853 [PDF p.24] ble the existing knowledge into a coherent and compact mathematical description.


00854 [PDF p.24] Usually, this results in a very complex model of the system dynamics, as it is hard


00855 [PDF p.24] to decide which effects are relevant and must be included in the final model and


00856 [PDF p.24] which are negligible. Such an approach is also often found to be very laborious and


00857 [PDF p.24] expensive. If the specialist’s knowledge is lacking, like in case of poorly understood


00858 [PDF p.24] systems, the derivation of a model from first principles is even impossible. More-


00859 [PDF p.24] over, certain quantities, like coefficients, rates, etc. required to build the model are


00860 [PDF p.24] often unknown, and have to be estimated by performing dedicated experiments.


00861 [PDF p.24]     Descriptions of systems can alternatively be derived by system identification,


00862 [PDF p.24] where the estimation of a dynamical model is accomplished directly from mea-


00863 [PDF p.24] sured input-output data. The expert’s knowledge still has a major role, as it gives the


00864 [PDF p.24] basic source of information that is used in the decision on parametrization, model-


00865 [PDF p.24] structure selection, experiment design, and the actual way of deriving the estimate.


00866 [PDF p.24] This knowledge also helps in judging the quality and applicability of the obtained


00867 [PDF p.24] models. Even if system identification requires human intervention and expert knowl-


00868 [PDF p.24] edge to arrive at appropriate models, it also gives a general framework in which most


00869 [PDF p.24] of the steps can be automated, providing a less laborious and cost intensive modeling


00870 [PDF p.24] process.


00871 [PDF p.24]     Starting from frequency domain approaches in the early 1940s, over the years


00872 [PDF p.24] considerable attention has been given to the identification of LTI systems, which


00873 [PDF p.24] have proven their usefulness in many engineering applications. Today LTI system


00874 [PDF p.24] identification has become a strongly founded framework considering issues of un-


00875 [PDF p.24] certainty and closed-loop identification with a vast theory on experiment design


00876 [PDF p.24] (for an overview see [144]). But the need to operate processes with higher ac-


00877 [PDF p.24] curacy/efficiency, has soon resulted in the realization that the commonly NL and


00878 [PDF p.24] time-varying (TV) nature of many physical systems must be handled by the control


00879 [PDF p.24] designs. This required better models, which initiated a significant research effort


00880 [PDF p.24] spent on identification and modeling of NL and linear time-varying (LTV) systems


00881 [PDF p.24] (see [59, 126] about the developed approaches). Despite many theoretical solutions,


00882 [PDF p.24] dealing with NL models without any structure has been found infeasible in practice


00883 [PDF p.24] both in terms of identification and control.


00884 [PDF p.24]     Today, engineers working in the industry still prefer the application of LTI


00885 [PDF p.24] control-designs, due to the attractive approaches of optimal and robust control.


00886 [PDF p.24] These approaches are preferred as they guarantee high performance and reliabil-


00887 [PDF p.24] ity, have easy and quick design schemes, and engineers have a vast experience in


00888 [PDF p.24] their application. Additionally, it has also been observed in practice that many NL


00889 [PDF p.24] systems can be well approximated by multiple LTI models that describe the behavior


00890 [PDF p.24] of the plant around some operation points. The recognition manifested in the 1980s,


00891 [PDF p.24] that instead jumping into the deep-space of NL and TV systems, a model class is


00892 [PDF p.24] needed which can serve as an extension of the existing LTI control approaches, but

00913 [PDF p.25] is still able to incorporate NL and TV dynamical aspects. This has led to the birth of


00914 [PDF p.25] linear parameter-varying (LPV) systems through the idea of gain-scheduling [166].


00915 [PDF p.25] 


00916 [PDF p.25] 


00917 [PDF p.25] 1.2    The Birth of LPV Systems


00918 [PDF p.25] In gain-scheduling, the basic concept is to linearize the NL system model at dif-


00919 [PDF p.25] ferent operating points resulting in a collection of local LTI descriptions of the


00920 [PDF p.25] plant (see Fig. 1.1). Then, subsequently, LTI controllers are designed for each lo-


00921 [PDF p.25] cal aspect. These controllers are interpolated to give a global control solution to


00922 [PDF p.25] the entire operation regime [157]. The used interpolation function is called the


00923 [PDF p.25] scheduling function in this framework and it is dependent on the current operat-


00924 [PDF p.25] ing point of the plant. To describe the changes of the operating point, a signal is


00925 [PDF p.25] introduced, which is called the scheduling signal and often denoted by p. In this


00926 [PDF p.25] way, the parameters of the resulting controller are dependent on the varying sig-


00927 [PDF p.25] nal p, hence the name parameter-varying, while the dynamic relation between the


00928 [PDF p.25] system signals is still linear. Due to many successful applications of this design


00929 [PDF p.25] methodology [177, 228, 179], gain-scheduling has become popular in industrial ap-


00930 [PDF p.25] plications, even if guarantees for overall stability of the designed LPV controllers


00931 [PDF p.25] have not been available and the possibility of malfunction has existed. After 20


00932 [PDF p.25] years, this was resolved by the introduction of interpolation based methods that


00933 [PDF p.25] guarantee global stability [182, 87]. In the mean time it was realized that in gen-


00934 [PDF p.25] eral many NL systems can be converted into an LPV form. Approaches have ap-


00935 [PDF p.25] peared that provided direct LPV models for gain-scheduling without the laborious


00936 [PDF p.25] process of NL system modeling or identification [120, 124, 36, 185]. LPV control


00937 [PDF p.25] has gained momentum during the 1990s, when the first results about the exten-


00938 [PDF p.25] sion of H∞ and H2 optimal control through linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) based


00939 [PDF p.25] optimization appeared (see [160, 6, 133]) together with μ -synthesis approaches,


00940 [PDF p.25] originating from robust LTI control [240]. Contrary to the former gain-scheduling


00941 [PDF p.25] methods, these approaches guarantee stability, optimal performance, and robust-


00942 [PDF p.25] ness over the entire operating regime of LPV models. Since then, the LPV field


00943 [PDF p.25] has evolved rapidly in the last 15 years and has become a promising framework


00944 [PDF p.25] for modern industrial control with a growing number of applications like aircrafts


00945 [PDF p.25] [112, 216], re-entry vehicles [212], automobiles [15], wind turbines [23, 103], in-


00946 [PDF p.25] duction motors [191, 147, 203], servo systems [229], wafer steppers [224, 180],


00947 [PDF p.25] 


00948 [PDF p.26] 4                                                                       1 Introduction


00949 [PDF p.26] 


00950 [PDF p.26] internet web servers [152, 187], CD-players [45] and environmental modeling [18].


00951 [PDF p.26] Unfortunately, LPV system identification and modeling could barely keep up with


00952 [PDF p.26] the advances of the control field. Only very recently, initiatives have been taken to


00953 [PDF p.26] explore many open problems and questions in this area.


00954 [PDF p.26] 


00955 [PDF p.26] 


00956 [PDF p.26] 1.3     The Present State of LPV Identification


00957 [PDF p.26] In the following, a general picture about the state-of-the-art in LPV system identifi-


00958 [PDF p.26] cation is presented. Before going into details, we establish the key steps of the clas-


00959 [PDF p.26] sical identification framework where the specifics of the LPV identification methods


00960 [PDF p.26] can be positioned and categorized.


00961 [PDF p.26] 


00962 [PDF p.26] 


00963 [PDF p.26] 1.3.1     The Identification Cycle


00964 [PDF p.26] Identification of dynamical systems on the basis of experimentally measured data


00965 [PDF p.26] consists of several design steps, which need careful treatment in order to produce


00966 [PDF p.26] an acceptable model of the system. These steps are summarized in the so-called


00967 [PDF p.26] identification cycle presented in Table 1.1. This set of steps is referred as a cycle,


00968 [PDF p.26] due to the fact that several iterations might take place, using the knowledge gathered


00969 [PDF p.26] in the previous attempts, till the desired model is delivered. In the following a brief


00970 [PDF p.26] overview of each step is given, based on [105].


00971 [PDF p.26] 


00972 [PDF p.26] 1.3.1.1   Experiment Design and Data Preprocessing


00973 [PDF p.26] 


00974 [PDF p.26] Experiment design focuses on the choice of the excitation of the system to be iden-


00975 [PDF p.26] tified in order to maximize the information content in the measured signals. The de-


00976 [PDF p.26] sign procedure is commonly accomplished with respect to a selected model class to


00977 [PDF p.26] minimize the variance, i.e. the estimation error, of the resulting model estimate. One


00978 [PDF p.26] of the most important problems is how to choose input signals that are persistently


00979 [PDF p.26] exciting (PE), i.e. they result in output signals which have enough information con-


00980 [PDF p.26] tent to describe the relevant dynamical relations of the system for estimation with a


00981 [PDF p.26] given model structure. An equally important notion is the use of adequately exciting


00982 [PDF p.26] inputs that result in informative data sets which have enough information content


00983 [PDF p.26] to distinguish between different models in the considered model class. White noise


00984 [PDF p.26] inputs are in general considered to be optimal, as they excite all frequencies of an


00985 [PDF p.26] LTI system. As physical actuation by such signals is often infeasible, in practice


00986 [PDF p.26] random binary noises, frequency sweeps, and multisines are considered. Often it is


00987 [PDF p.26] also desirable to design excitation signals for a given frequency range related to the


00988 [PDF p.26] intended application of the identified model. Beside experiment design, data prepro-


00989 [PDF p.26] cessing is focusing on the attenuation of disturbances, aliasing or other defects in


00990 [PDF p.26] the measured data.


00991 [PDF p.26] 


00992 [PDF p.27] 1.3 The Present State of LPV Identification                                         5


00993 [PDF p.27] 


00994 [PDF p.27] Table 1.1 The identification cycle


00995 [PDF p.27] 


00996 [PDF p.27] Step 1.     Experiment design, data collection and data manipulation.


00997 [PDF p.27] Step 2.     Selection of model structure (including parametrization).


00998 [PDF p.27] Step 3.     Choice of the identification criterion.


00999 [PDF p.27] Step 4.     Estimation of a model that is optimal with respect to the criterion.


01000 [PDF p.27] Step 5.     Validation of the resulting model estimate.


01001 [PDF p.27] 


01002 [PDF p.27] 


01003 [PDF p.27] 


01004 [PDF p.27] 1.3.1.2   Choice of the Model Structure


01005 [PDF p.27] 


01006 [PDF p.27] The choice of an appropriate model structure is the most crucial part of the iden-


01007 [PDF p.27] tification cycle. It determines the set in which a suitable description of the system


01008 [PDF p.27] is searched for. General questions considered in this step are the selection of the


01009 [PDF p.27] model structure in terms of the representation form (state-space (SS), input-output


01010 [PDF p.27] (IO), series expansion, etc.), parametrization, and the type of noise modeling. In


01011 [PDF p.27] terms of the well known bias/variance trade-off, the size of the model set is also


01012 [PDF p.27] important, like the number of parameters or order of the model structure. To obtain


01013 [PDF p.27] an adequate choice, the complexity of the algorithm delivering the model estimate


01014 [PDF p.27] or undesired local solutions of the estimation, non-uniqueness of the optimum, etc.,


01015 [PDF p.27] also have to be considered.


01016 [PDF p.27] 


01017 [PDF p.27] 1.3.1.3   Choice of the Identification Criterion


01018 [PDF p.27] 


01019 [PDF p.27] Selection of the identification criterion, the mathematical formulation of the perfor-


01020 [PDF p.27] mance measure of the model estimates, defines the user’s purpose or expectation


01021 [PDF p.27] towards the model of the plant. In the literature, many identification criteria are


01022 [PDF p.27] presented, but the most commonly applied is the mean-squared error of the output


01023 [PDF p.27] prediction of the model estimate.


01024 [PDF p.27] 


01025 [PDF p.27] 1.3.1.4   Model Estimation


01026 [PDF p.27] 


01027 [PDF p.27] The model estimation phase is the consequence of the previous choices of the iden-


01028 [PDF p.27] tification cycle. Commonly the algorithmic solution of the estimation problem, de-


01029 [PDF p.27] fined in terms of the model structure and the identification criterion, is considered


01030 [PDF p.27] here.


01031 [PDF p.27] 


01032 [PDF p.27] 1.3.1.5   Model (In)validation


01033 [PDF p.27] 


01034 [PDF p.27] A crucial question in identification is wether the obtained model is “good enough”


01035 [PDF p.27] for the intended purpose. Prior knowledge and experimental data are both used to


01036 [PDF p.27] confront the estimated model for answering this question. By using experimental


01037 [PDF p.27] data, validation is often accomplished by comparing simulation results of the model


01038 [PDF p.27] estimates to the measurements or by analyzing the model as a predictor of future


01039 [PDF p.27] outputs of the system, based on measured past data.


01040 [PDF p.27]

01042 [PDF p.28] 


01043 [PDF p.28] 1.3.2     General Picture of LPV Identification


01044 [PDF p.28] Next, the LPV identification problem is discussed, defining the notion of LPV sys-


01045 [PDF p.28] tems and formulating the LPV model structures that are currently used in the lit-


01046 [PDF p.28] erature. This sets the stage for the introduction of the state-of-the-art identification


01047 [PDF p.28] approaches.


01048 [PDF p.28] 


01049 [PDF p.28] 1.3.2.1    LPV Systems and the Task of Identification


01050 [PDF p.28] 


01051 [PDF p.28] Based on the original gain-scheduling principle, LPV systems are often viewed as


01052 [PDF p.28] a linear dynamical relation between input signals u and output signals y, where the


01053 [PDF p.28] relation itself is dependent on an external variable, the so-called scheduling signal


01054 [PDF p.28] p. This provides the schematic view presented in Fig. 1.2. The relation can be for-


01055 [PDF p.28] malized as a convolution in terms of u and p, which reads in discrete time (DT) as


01056 [PDF p.28]                                         ∞


01057 [PDF p.28]                                    y = ∑ gi (p)q−i u,                             (1.1)


01058 [PDF p.28]                                        i=0


01059 [PDF p.28] 


01060 [PDF p.28] where q denotes the forward time shift operator, i.e. qi u(k) = u(k + i) and q−i u(k) =


01061 [PDF p.28] u(k − i), u : Z → RnU is the DT input, y : Z → RnY is the DT output, and p : Z → P


01062 [PDF p.28] is the DT scheduling signal of the system with a scheduling space P ⊆ RnP often


01063 [PDF p.28] considered to be compact. The coefficients gi of (1.1) are functions of the scheduling


01064 [PDF p.28] variable and they define the varying linear dynamical relation between u and y. If the


01065 [PDF p.28] functions gi are considered to be dependent only on the instantaneous value of the


01066 [PDF p.28] scheduling signal, i.e. gi : P → RnY ×nU , then their functional dependence is called


01067 [PDF p.28] static. This means that (1.1) has the form


01068 [PDF p.28]

01075 [PDF p.28] 


01076 [PDF p.28] then the functional dependence of gi is called dynamic. An important property of


01077 [PDF p.28] LPV systems is that for a constant scheduling signal, i.e. p(k) = p for all k ∈ Z,


01078 [PDF p.28] (1.1) is equal to a convolution describing an LTI system as each gi (p) is constant.


01079 [PDF p.28] Thus, LPV systems can be seen to be similar to LTI systems, but their signal behav-


01080 [PDF p.28] ior is different due to the variation of the gi parameters. Note that in the literature


01081 [PDF p.28] there are many formal definitions of LPV systems, commonly based on particular


01082 [PDF p.28] model structures with specific parameterizations. The convolution form (1.1) can be


01083 [PDF p.28] seen as their generalization. In identification, we aim to estimate a dynamical model


01084 [PDF p.28] of the system based on measured data, which corresponds to the estimation of the


01085 [PDF p.28] coefficients gi in (1.1). Contrary to the LTI case where gi ∈ R, here gi are func-


01086 [PDF p.28] tions that depend on p, which makes their estimation to be a challenging task. This

01192 [PDF p.31] 1.3.3     LPV-IO Representation Based Methods


01193 [PDF p.31] The existing LPV identification approaches are almost exclusively formulated in


01194 [PDF p.31] discrete-time, they assume static dependence, and they are mainly characterized by


01195 [PDF p.31] the type of the used model structures. As a consequence, the identification methods


01196 [PDF p.31] of the LPV field are typically categorized as either LPV-IO or LPV-SS represen-


01197 [PDF p.31] tations based methods. The resulting categories together with their main proper-


01198 [PDF p.31] ties are investigated in the following sections. First we treat LPV-IO approaches


01199 [PDF p.31] which extend the results of LTI prediction-error identification. A common feature


01200 [PDF p.31] of these methods is that the approaches are derived by focusing on the single-input


01201 [PDF p.31] single-output (SISO) case, i.e. when nY = nU = 1. The following subcategories are


01202 [PDF p.31] distinguished:


01203 [PDF p.31] 


01204 [PDF p.31] 1.3.3.1   Interpolation Approaches


01205 [PDF p.31] 


01206 [PDF p.31] Methods that fall into this category apply the classical gain-scheduling concept:


01207 [PDF p.31] identification of the system for constant scheduling trajectories and interpolation of


01208 [PDF p.31] the resulting, so-called “frozen” models. These methods build on the well-worked


01209 [PDF p.31] out LTI prediction-error framework to achieve high quality estimates of the frozen


01210 [PDF p.31] aspects of the LPV system even in a closed-loop identification setting. Interpolation


01211 [PDF p.31] of the frozen models in an IO from is accomplished in various ways, like on the


01212 [PDF p.31] outputs of the local models [242], or on the inputs [241], or directly on the coeffi-


01213 [PDF p.31] cients [115, 27]. All these interpolation forms result in different global models. A


01214 [PDF p.31] common feature of these approaches is that the interpolation is applied in an ad-


01215 [PDF p.31] hoc manner, most commonly using a polynomial or a spline approach, and that the


01216 [PDF p.31] methods show close relation with the local-linear-modeling framework [121] and


01217 [PDF p.31] with various multiple model approaches as well (see Sec. 1.3.4.3).


01218 [PDF p.31] 


01219 [PDF p.31] 1.3.3.2   Linear Regression Methods


01220 [PDF p.31] 


01221 [PDF p.31] These methods use the LPV-IO model structure resulting from a specific parametriza-


01222 [PDF p.31] tion of the coefficients of (1.4). The corresponding structure is an auto-regressive


01223 [PDF p.31] model with exogenous input (ARX), well known in the LTI identification frame-


01224 [PDF p.31] work. However, in the LPV case, the coefficients are functions of a varying p. Ad-


01225 [PDF p.31]                                                                                nb


01226 [PDF p.31] ditionally, the approaches use a linear parametrization of {ai }ni=1


01227 [PDF p.31]                                                                   a


01228 [PDF p.31]                                                                      and {b j } j=0 with


01229 [PDF p.31] polynomial scheduling dependence. In case of nP = 1, this reads for ai as


01230 [PDF p.31]                                                  n


01231 [PDF p.31]                                  ai (p) = ai0 + ∑ ail pl ,                        (1.9)


01232 [PDF p.31]                                                 l=1


01233 [PDF p.31] 


01234 [PDF p.31] where ail ∈ R. As the resulting model is linear-in-the-parameters, the estimation


01235 [PDF p.31] of {ail } and {b jl } can be obtained by linear regression (see [226, 225, 12, 11]).


01236 [PDF p.31] In analogy, recursive least-squares or instrumental-variable methods can be applied


01237 [PDF p.31] to refine the estimate, building on the concepts of the LTI prediction-error identifi-


01238 [PDF p.31] cation framework (see [57, 13]). In [28] a closed-loop method is proposed for the

01255 [PDF p.32] 1.3.3.3    Set Membership Approaches


01256 [PDF p.32] 


01257 [PDF p.32] Set membership methods have been studied for the identification of LPV-IO models


01258 [PDF p.32] as well. Particular feature of these approaches is that the noise in the measured


01259 [PDF p.32] data is treated as deterministic uncertainty and, instead of a direct estimate of the


01260 [PDF p.32] parameters, a feasible parameter set is calculated. This feasible set represents the


01261 [PDF p.32] set of possible parameter values which satisfy the data equation (1.4) under a prior


01262 [PDF p.32] assumed error bound δe , where e ≤ δe in terms of a given measure  . A direct


01263 [PDF p.32] parameter estimate is often obtained by calculating the mean of the feasible set. In


01264 [PDF p.32] [19], identification of LPV finite impulse response (FIR) models, finite truncation


01265 [PDF p.32] of (1.1), has been studied by this methodology, where the expansion coefficients gi


01266 [PDF p.32] were assumed to be nonlinear functions of a multi-dimensional p. Optimal worst-


01267 [PDF p.32] case experiment design has also been addressed in this context. In [38], this concept


01268 [PDF p.32] has been extended to general LPV-IO models in the form of (1.4). Opposite to [19],


01269 [PDF p.32] the calculation of the feasible parameter set in this case results in a non-convex


01270 [PDF p.32] optimization which is overcome by a polytopic outer approximation.


01271 [PDF p.32]

01276 [PDF p.32] prediction error. The aim is to give better estimates than the linear regression meth-


01277 [PDF p.32] ods. In some approaches this is achieved by using a nonlinear parametrization

01298 [PDF p.33] 1.3.4     LPV-SS Representation Based Methods


01299 [PDF p.33] Other type of approaches use the LPV-SS representation (1.6a–b) or its LFR equiva-


01300 [PDF p.33] lent (1.8) as a model structure by considering specific parametrization of the system


01301 [PDF p.33] matrices. In applications, these approaches are generally more appreciated, as LPV


01302 [PDF p.33] control theory requires a state-space representation and most of the LPV-SS iden-


01303 [PDF p.33] tification methods can also easily handle MIMO plants. The methods of LPV-SS


01304 [PDF p.33] approaches fall into the following sub-categories:


01305 [PDF p.33] 


01306 [PDF p.33] 1.3.4.1   Gradient Methods


01307 [PDF p.33] 


01308 [PDF p.33] These approaches formulate the estimation of the parameter-varying SS matrices


01309 [PDF p.33] as a NL optimization problem solved via gradient-search-based algorithms. Due


01310 [PDF p.33] to the nature of gradient-search optimization, the resulting estimate is often a lo-


01311 [PDF p.33] cally optimal solution of the involved cost function. In [96] and [97], an LFR type


01312 [PDF p.33] of SS model structure is used where the scheduling dependence is extracted as


01313 [PDF p.33] Δ (p) = Diag(I p1 , . . . , I pnP ). The estimation of the linear part is formulated as a NL


01314 [PDF p.33] optimization, which is solved in an iterative scheme based on the gradients of the


01315 [PDF p.33] mean-squared output error. In every step of the estimation, the system matrices can


01316 [PDF p.33] be estimated in a different state basis, i.e. a family of matrix estimates can be given


01317 [PDF p.33] which are all related by state transformations. To eliminate the non-uniqueness of


01318 [PDF p.33] the estimation, in each iteration step, the matrix estimates are restricted to a spe-


01319 [PDF p.33] cific structure. Identifiability issues of such LFR structures are investigated in [98].


01320 [PDF p.33] Other methods have been developed which apply the same methodology, but on


01321 [PDF p.33] the LPV-SS form (1.6a–b) with radial-basis functions based scheduling dependence


01322 [PDF p.33] [215, 214]. In this parametrization, the matrices are formulated as

01335 [PDF p.34] 1.3.4.2   Full-Measurement Approaches

01339 [PDF p.34] Δ (p) = Diag(I p1 , . . . , I pnP ) and D11 = 0, the estimation problem reduces to a linear

01348 [PDF p.34] 1.3.4.3   Multiple-Model Methods


01349 [PDF p.34] 


01350 [PDF p.34] These methods apply the classical gain-scheduling concept of identification simi-


01351 [PDF p.34] lar to the interpolation approaches of the IO case (see Sec. 1.3.3.1). However in


01352 [PDF p.34] this case, interpolation is accomplished via a state-space representation usually in a

01394 [PDF p.35] The family of these methods builds strongly on the concepts of the LTI subspace

01396 [PDF p.35] output-error state-space (MOESP) algorithm (see [221, 220]). During the estima-

01399 [PDF p.35] most methods, E1 and E2 are considered to be constant. The estimation is based

01403 [PDF p.35] LTI case. Other similarities of the LPV subspace approaches are the assumption of


01404 [PDF p.35] affine scheduling dependence (see (1.7)) and the resemblance with bilinear system-


01405 [PDF p.35] identification methods.

01468 [PDF p.36] 1.3.5     Similarity to Other System Classes


01469 [PDF p.36] LPV systems are often considered to be similar in some aspects to other system


01470 [PDF p.36] classes. It has already been mentioned that LPV subspace techniques were inspired


01471 [PDF p.36] by the identification approaches of bilinear systems. These systems can be consid-


01472 [PDF p.36] ered as LPV systems where p is equal to the input of the system and the system


01473 [PDF p.36] dynamics depend linearly on p.

01475 [PDF p.37] 1.4 Challenges and Open Problems                                                  15


01476 [PDF p.37] 


01477 [PDF p.37]    LPV systems can also be seen as the extension of LTV systems. By restricting the


01478 [PDF p.37] coefficients of an LPV system to depend on a fixed linear trajectory of time, instead


01479 [PDF p.37] on a priori unknown trajectory of the scheduling variable, an LTV system results.


01480 [PDF p.37] Due to the structural similarity, many LPV approaches have been inspired by ideas


01481 [PDF p.37] of the LTV framework (IO methods, periodic identification) which do not exploit


01482 [PDF p.37] the priori known linear variation of the time trajectory.


01483 [PDF p.37]    In the fuzzy framework, Takagi-Sugeno (TS) dynamic fuzzy models with linear


01484 [PDF p.37] signal relations are often considered as LPV systems [86]. However, due to the if-


01485 [PDF p.37] then structure of the fuzzy rules, commonly LPV control cannot be applied on such


01486 [PDF p.37] systems and due to other structural differences such an equality of TS and LPV


01487 [PDF p.37] systems is dubious in the general sense. Thus, in the following, TS dynamic fuzzy


01488 [PDF p.37] models are treated as non-LPV systems.

01491 [PDF p.37] 1.4   Challenges and Open Problems


01492 [PDF p.37] 


01493 [PDF p.37] In the previous part we have seen that a wide variety of identification methods is


01494 [PDF p.37] available, approaching the underlying LPV identification problem (see Sect. 1.3.2)


01495 [PDF p.37] from different viewpoints. Many of these approaches are built around an assumed


01496 [PDF p.37] model structure and focusing only on the estimation task, which is just one step


01497 [PDF p.37] of the classical identification cycle. Due to these and many other issues, several


01498 [PDF p.37] challenges and open problems exist, that deserve further investigation. The most


01499 [PDF p.37] crucial questions are collected into the following list:


01500 [PDF p.37] • The current methods use different identification settings, model structures, and


01501 [PDF p.37]   even different views about what an LPV system is. So it is an obvious question


01502 [PDF p.37]   how these concepts and ideas can be brought to a common ground, where they


01503 [PDF p.37]   can be analyzed, compared, and refined.


01504 [PDF p.37] • Often, the validity of the used identification concepts is not investigated. For


01505 [PDF p.37]   example in prediction-error methods, like the least-squares LPV-IO methods,


01506 [PDF p.37]   the formulation of the predictor, or even the description and analysis of the as-


01507 [PDF p.37]   sumed noise structure is often omitted. Except for some recent contributions like


01508 [PDF p.37]   [94, 34, 200], many approaches use linear regression as an optimization tool in-


01509 [PDF p.37]   stead of estimation in a stochastic sense. How to formulate the prediction-error


01510 [PDF p.37]   setting in the LPV case and how to derive well-founded identification approaches


01511 [PDF p.37]   that dwell on the concepts of the classical framework remain questions to be in-


01512 [PDF p.37]   vestigated.


01513 [PDF p.37] • In the SS variants of identification methods, based on the gain-scheduling princi-


01514 [PDF p.37]   ple, state-transformations are applied independently on each LTI-SS model esti-


01515 [PDF p.37]   mate. For example, the frozen models are transformed to a canonical or balanced


01516 [PDF p.37]   form and then they are interpolated. However, such transformed models do not


01517 [PDF p.37]   have a common state, making the results of interpolation unpredictable [189].


01518 [PDF p.37]   Similarly, the problem of local transformations applies when model reduction


01519 [PDF p.37]   is used independently on the frozen models or if the interpolation is based only


01520 [PDF p.37]   on their pole locations. Unexpected problems can also occur in the interpolation


01521 [PDF p.37]   process if the McMillan degree of the local models changes at some interpolation


01522 [PDF p.37] 


01523 [PDF p.38] 16                                                                         1 Introduction


01524 [PDF p.38] 


01525 [PDF p.38]      points. Thus it is also important to investigate how the gain-scheduling principle


01526 [PDF p.38]      can be used in identification such that the interpolation is well structured and


01527 [PDF p.38]      issues of local transformations do not apply.


01528 [PDF p.38] •    Many LPV identification approaches, especially sub-space and gradient-search

01587 [PDF p.39] 1.5     Perspectives of Orthonormal Basis Function Models


01588 [PDF p.39] In view of the previous observations, a central problem of the LPV field is the ab-


01589 [PDF p.39] sence of a model structure which has good representation capabilities with a limited


01590 [PDF p.39] number of parameters, useful for control, and its identification represents a low com-


01591 [PDF p.39] plexity problem. The latter means for example that the model structure is either well


01592 [PDF p.39] applicable in a gain-scheduling type of approach, i.e. it is easily interpolatable with-


01593 [PDF p.39] out the need of local transformations, or its estimation is available through linear


01594 [PDF p.39] regression.

01660 [PDF p.40] 1.5.3    Approximation via OBF Structures


01661 [PDF p.40] In [30] it has been proved that model structures composed from a OBF filter bank


01662 [PDF p.40] followed by a static nonlinearity are general approximators of nonlinear systems


01663 [PDF p.40] with fading memory (NL dynamic systems with convolution representation). This


01664 [PDF p.40] means that a wide class of nonlinear systems can be identified with such OBF model

01669 [PDF p.41] eral approximators, which means that, if the same property can be shown for the


01670 [PDF p.41] LPV case, then these models have a wide representation capability of LPV systems.


01671 [PDF p.41] Based on the general approximator property and the attractive identification proper-


01672 [PDF p.41] ties of OBF models, successful identification approaches based on these structures


01673 [PDF p.41] have been introduced in the NL and the fuzzy field (see [63, 159]). These methods


01674 [PDF p.41] provide low complexity and reliable estimates for the considered classes of systems,


01675 [PDF p.41] giving the hope that similar mechanisms could also be successfully applied in the


01676 [PDF p.41] LPV case.


01677 [PDF p.41]     It is well known in the LTI case that the approximation error, i.e. the resulting


01678 [PDF p.41] bias of the model estimate directly depends on how well the chosen basis functions


01679 [PDF p.41] Φn can represent the dynamics of the system. In terms of gain-scheduling, this refers


01680 [PDF p.41] to the size of the representation error of Φn with respect to each Fp . This refers back


01681 [PDF p.41] to the observation that model structure selection has a prime importance in the LPV


01682 [PDF p.41] case, and as for other type of LPV models, this choice influences the achievable


01683 [PDF p.41] maximal accuracy of the estimates.


01684 [PDF p.41]     In conclusion, the above discussed perspectives yield the observation that iden-


01685 [PDF p.41] tification of LPV systems with OBF models like (1.14) could provide answers to


01686 [PDF p.41] some current challenges of the LPV identification field.

01689 [PDF p.41] 1.6    The Goal of the Book


01690 [PDF p.41] In this chapter it has been shown that there are many open issues and unresolved


01691 [PDF p.41] problems/questions in the area of LPV modeling and identification. Based on this


01692 [PDF p.41] observation, we aim to develop an identification framework in this book where rela-


01693 [PDF p.41] tions of model structures and the concept of estimation can be understood. In fact we


01694 [PDF p.41] intend to extend the prediction-error framework to the LPV case and investigate how


01695 [PDF p.41] we cab benefit from the classical results. Additionally, we also intend to develop an


01696 [PDF p.41] effective LPV identification mechanism, based on the promising properties of OBF


01697 [PDF p.41] expansion models, that overcomes the drawbacks of the existing state-of-the-art so-


01698 [PDF p.41] lutions (see Sect. 1.4).


01699 [PDF p.41]    However, it has been revealed in the previous section that the main obstacle in


01700 [PDF p.41] the formulation of such an identification framework originates from the gaps of LPV


01701 [PDF p.41] system theory. To fill these gaps and give a unified system theoretical framework in


01702 [PDF p.41] the LPV case, which enables the investigation and comparison of model structures


01703 [PDF p.41] and also provides an algebraic tool for manipulations on them, a new system theo-


01704 [PDF p.41] retical framework, which is based on the extension of the LTI behavioral approach


01705 [PDF p.41] [146], is worked out in the first part of the book.


01706 [PDF p.41]    In the sequel we present a theory with new ideas of LPV behaviors, modeling,


01707 [PDF p.41] and identification methods, that have appealing properties and can be applied suc-


01708 [PDF p.41] cessfully to fulfill the aimed objectives. Due to the vast number of problems this


01709 [PDF p.41] book addresses, we also leave many open ends and questions for future research.


01710 [PDF p.41] The exploration of all issues of the LPV identification cycle of general physical sys-


01711 [PDF p.41] tems remains a problem, but the use of orthonormal basis functions, the behavioral

01714 [PDF p.42] 


01715 [PDF p.42] theory, and the proposed prediction-error identification framework open interest-


01716 [PDF p.42] ing and promising perspectives to approach the identification of this system class


01717 [PDF p.42] efficiently.

01720 [PDF p.42] 1.7   Overview of Contents


01721 [PDF p.42] First we start our investigations by introducing in Chap. 2 some basic concepts


01722 [PDF p.42] of system identification with important mathematical and system theoretical tools


01723 [PDF p.42] which are used in the remainder.


01724 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 3 we introduce an LPV behavioral approach that establishes a unified


01725 [PDF p.42] system theoretical framework. In this framework it becomes possible to understand


01726 [PDF p.42] relations of LPV models and the behavioral approach also gives the basic tool to


01727 [PDF p.42] introduce OBFs-based LPV model parameterizations later on.


01728 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 4 we explore LPV-SS canonical forms and equivalence transformations


01729 [PDF p.42] between different representations of LPV systems. The discovered relations provide


01730 [PDF p.42] the tools to analyze and compare LPV model structures.


01731 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 5 the representation of LPV systems by OBF-based series-expansions is


01732 [PDF p.42] investigated. It is shown that finite truncations of these representations can be used


01733 [PDF p.42] as model structures for LPV system identification. Such structures also have wide


01734 [PDF p.42] approximation capabilities.


01735 [PDF p.42]    Discretization of LPV systems is reviewed in Chap. 6. New discretization ap-


01736 [PDF p.42] proaches are introduced together with criteria to choose the discretization step size.


01737 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 7 the modeling of NL systems in a LPV form is investigated and the


01738 [PDF p.42] available solutions for this problem are studied. Using the framework of the LPV


01739 [PDF p.42] behavioral approach, a new mechanism is introduced that solves the LPV model-


01740 [PDF p.42] ing issue of such systems. This approach together with the discretization methods


01741 [PDF p.42] of Chap. 6 are developed with the intention to assist the model-structure selection


01742 [PDF p.42] phase of the identification cycle based on first principle knowledge.


01743 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 8 the basis-selection problem of OBFs-based LPV model structures is


01744 [PDF p.42] considered. The method is based on the clustering of sample poles that result from


01745 [PDF p.42] identification of the system with constant scheduling signals. The effect of noise on


01746 [PDF p.42] identification is also considered and a robust basis-selection procedure is developed


01747 [PDF p.42] based on hyperbolic-geometry results.


01748 [PDF p.42]    In Chap. 9 the extension of the LTI OBFs-based identification approach to the


01749 [PDF p.42] LPV case is developed, relying heavily on the tools derived in the previous chap-


01750 [PDF p.42] ters. The prediction-error framework for the LPV case is established and the model


01751 [PDF p.42] structures of the current approaches are analyzed. Two identification approaches, a


01752 [PDF p.42] global and a local one, are formulated with static dependence of the coefficients.


01753 [PDF p.42] The former approach utilizes the gain-scheduling-based interpolation concept while


01754 [PDF p.42] the latter yields a global estimate based on linear regression. To overcome the


01755 [PDF p.42] limiting assumption of static dependence needed for the parametrization of these


01756 [PDF p.42] approaches, two alternative OBFs-based model structures are worked out. These


01757 [PDF p.42] structures enable the approximation of dynamic dependence of the coefficients


01758 [PDF p.42] through a feedback with only static dependence. An identification approach of such


01759 [PDF p.42] feedback structures is derived through a separable least-squares strategy.

01767 [PDF p.43] Abstract. This chapter is devoted to the introduction of basic concepts that are fun-


01768 [PDF p.43] damental for the theory developed in the subsequent chapters. The notion of or-


01769 [PDF p.43] thonormal basis functions (OBFs) is introduced with a brief overview of the most


01770 [PDF p.43] important relations and properties. Next, the basic concepts and theory of LTI sys-


01771 [PDF p.43] tem identification are reviewed focusing on prediction-error methods. OBFs related


01772 [PDF p.43] parameterizations and the associated identification approaches are also introduced


01773 [PDF p.43] together with the optimality concept of OBF model structures in terms of the Kol-


01774 [PDF p.43] mogorov n-width theory.

02049 [PDF p.48] F(z) are the same (with multiplicity) as the poles of Gb (z), only the terms with i = 0


02050 [PDF p.48] in (2.18) are non-zero. Such a basis is commonly considered to be optimal for F.

02053 [PDF p.48] 2.3.3    Kautz Basis


02054 [PDF p.48] When Gb,i = Gb , ∀i > 0 with ng = 2, the resulting OBFs are called 2-parameter


02055 [PDF p.48] Kautz functions. Such basis sequences can be considered to be adequate for the


02056 [PDF p.48] expansion of systems with dominating second order modes.


02057 [PDF p.48] 


02058 [PDF p.48] 


02059 [PDF p.48] 2.3.4    Laguerre Basis


02060 [PDF p.48] The case when Gb,i = Gb , ∀i > 0 with ng = 1 are called Laguerre functions. As


02061 [PDF p.48] this type of basis sequence in RH2− (E) has only a real pole λ , it can provide an


02062 [PDF p.48] adequate basis for a F ∈ RH2− (E) with a dominating first-order mode.


02063 [PDF p.48] 


02064 [PDF p.48] 


02065 [PDF p.48] 2.3.5    Pulse Basis


02066 [PDF p.48] The case when Gb,i (z) = z−1 , ∀i > 0 are called pulse functions. Based on the expan-


02067 [PDF p.48] sion of the transfer functions of LTI dynamical systems in terms of the pulse basis,


02068 [PDF p.48] the impulse response representation of LTI systems is available.

02138 [PDF p.50] 2.4     Modeling and Identification of LTI Systems


02139 [PDF p.50] When identifying a dynamical system on the basis of experimentally measured data


02140 [PDF p.50] records, the outline of the procedure is summarized in the so-called identification


02141 [PDF p.50] cycle (see Table 1.1). The two most important steps of this cycle are the choices of an


02142 [PDF p.50] appropriate model set and the identification criterion. While the previous describes


02143 [PDF p.50] the set in which the suitable description of the system is sought, the latter defines


02144 [PDF p.50] the aimed performance of the model. The choice of the model set is crucial as it


02145 [PDF p.50] directly influences the maximum achievable accuracy or quality of the identified


02146 [PDF p.50] model in terms of the user-defined criterion. The model set should be as large as


02147 [PDF p.50] possible in order to contain as many candidate models as possible, which reduces


02148 [PDF p.50] the structural or bias error of the optimal model in the set. On the other hand, the


02149 [PDF p.50] number of parameters of the model should be kept as small as possible, because the


02150 [PDF p.50] variability of the identified models increases with increasing number of parameters.


02151 [PDF p.50] The conflict between these issues is the well-known bias/variance trade-off that is


02152 [PDF p.50] present in many estimation problems.


02153 [PDF p.50]    Model structures induced by orthonormal basis functions have attractive proper-


02154 [PDF p.50] ties in terms of the variance/bias trade-off. When appropriately chosen, they require


02155 [PDF p.50] only a limited number of parameters to represent models that can accurately de-


02156 [PDF p.50] scribe the dynamics of the considered system. The choice of basis functions then


02157 [PDF p.50] becomes a principle design issue. In this section, a brief coverage of DT prediction-


02158 [PDF p.50] error system identification is given, based on [105] and [73]. We focus on OBFs


02159 [PDF p.50] based model structures and concepts required for the derivation of the identification


02160 [PDF p.50] approaches of this book.


02161 [PDF p.50] 


02162 [PDF p.50]

02261 [PDF p.52] 2.4.2      Model Structures


02262 [PDF p.52] There are numerous different black-box model structures available for the para-


02263 [PDF p.52] metrization of G(q, θ ) and H(q, θ ). Most of them, collected in Table 2.1, parame-


02264 [PDF p.52] terize the two transfer functions in terms of ratio’s of polynomials RA , . . . , RF ∈ R[ξ ]


02265 [PDF p.52] in the backward time-shift operator q−1 . These structures are known under the


02266 [PDF p.52] acronyms given in the table. The parameter vector θ of these model structures


02267 [PDF p.52] contains the collection of the coefficients of the polynomials. Commonly, the de-


02268 [PDF p.52] nominator polynomials are assumed to be monic to ensure uniqueness of the


02269 [PDF p.52] parametrization. Every model structure or parametrization induces a set of predictor


02270 [PDF p.52] models, commonly called the model set:


02271 [PDF p.52] 


02272 [PDF p.52]                {(G(q, θ ), H(q, θ )) ∈ H2 (E) × H2 (E) | θ ∈ Θ ⊂ Rn } .                                     (2.36)


02273 [PDF p.52] 


02274 [PDF p.52] This concept allows us to distinguish the following situations:


02275 [PDF p.52] • The data generating system (G0 (q), H0 (q)) is in the model set, i.e. an exact rep-


02276 [PDF p.52]   resentation of the data generating system can be found by the applied model


02277 [PDF p.52]   structure.


02278 [PDF p.52] • (G0 (q), H0 (q)) is not in the model set, i.e. no exact representation of the system


02279 [PDF p.52]   exists by the model structure.


02280 [PDF p.52] When the main attention is given to the IO dynamics of the system, i.e. the underly-


02281 [PDF p.52] ing deterministic behavior described by G0 (q), it is attractive to deal with the set of


02282 [PDF p.52] so-called IO models:


02283 [PDF p.52] 


02284 [PDF p.52]                                 {G(q, θ ) ∈ H2 (E) | θ ∈ Θ ⊂ Rn } .                                         (2.37)


02285 [PDF p.52] 


02286 [PDF p.53] 2.4 Modeling and Identification of LTI Systems                                       31


02287 [PDF p.53] 


02288 [PDF p.53] This leads to situations when the IO relation of the plant G0 (q) can be or can not be


02289 [PDF p.53] captured within the chosen model set. Two important properties of the introduced


02290 [PDF p.53] model structures are the following


02291 [PDF p.53] • For some model structures, the expression of the output predictor (2.28) is


02292 [PDF p.53]   linear in the unknown parameters θ , i.e. both the terms (1 − H(q, θ ))−1 and


02293 [PDF p.53]   H(q, θ )−1 G(q, θ ) are polynomials. This property holds for the ARX and FIR


02294 [PDF p.53]   structures and has the major benefit that the LS criterion can be minimized by


02295 [PDF p.53]   solving a set of linear equations.


02296 [PDF p.53] • If G(q, θ ) and H(q, θ ) are independently parameterized, the two transfer func-


02297 [PDF p.53]   tions can be estimated independently. This property holds for the FIR, OE, and


02298 [PDF p.53]   BJ model structures.


02299 [PDF p.53] From these viewpoints it is particulary attractive to consider the FIR model, where


02300 [PDF p.53] both these properties are satisfied.

02303 [PDF p.53] 2.4.3     Properties


02304 [PDF p.53] Next we investigate the statistical properties of the considered model structures in


02305 [PDF p.53] terms of prediction-error identification.


02306 [PDF p.53] 


02307 [PDF p.53] 2.4.3.1   Consistency and Convergence


02308 [PDF p.53] 


02309 [PDF p.53] When applying the quadratic identification criterion (2.30), the asymptotic proper-


02310 [PDF p.53] ties of the resulting parameter estimate can be derived in the situation when Nd → ∞.


02311 [PDF p.53] If the noise in the measured data is normally distributed, the LS estimator is equiv-


02312 [PDF p.53] alent with a maximum likelihood (statistically optimal in an asymptotic sense) es-


02313 [PDF p.53] timator [105]. With other noise distributions, attractive properties also hold (under


02314 [PDF p.53] weak conditions on the noise):


02315 [PDF p.53] • Convergence result: For Nd → ∞, the parameter estimate θ̂Nd converges, i.e.


02316 [PDF p.53]   θ̂Nd → θ ∗ , with probability 1, where θ ∗ = arg minθ ∈Θ Ē{ε 2 (θ )}. This implies


02317 [PDF p.53]   that the asymptotic parameter estimate is independent from the particular noise


02318 [PDF p.53]   realization in the data sequence.


02319 [PDF p.53] • Consistency result: If u is persistently exciting (PE) of a sufficient order, then the


02320 [PDF p.53]   asymptotic parameter estimate θ ∗ has the following properties:


02321 [PDF p.53]    – If the data generating system is in the model set, then G0 (q) = G(q, θ ∗ ) and


02322 [PDF p.53]      H0 (q) = H(q, θ ∗ ).


02323 [PDF p.53]    – If G0 (q) is in the IO model set and additionally G(q, θ ) and H(q, θ ) are inde-


02324 [PDF p.53]      pendently parameterized, then G0 (q) = G(q, θ ∗ ). This means that consistency


02325 [PDF p.53]      of the estimate G(q, θ ) is also obtained if H(q, θ ) is misspecified.


02326 [PDF p.53] Persistency of excitation (PE) for an order n means in this context that the quasi-


02327 [PDF p.53] stationary u, used for excitation during the experiment, satisfy that

02344 [PDF p.54] 2.4.3.2      Asymptotic Bias and Variance


02345 [PDF p.54] 


02346 [PDF p.54] In system identification, one also has to deal with estimation errors. This is due to


02347 [PDF p.54] the fact that information on the system to be estimated is only partially available:


02348 [PDF p.54] finite data records, effect of noise, etc. A well-accepted approach is to decompose


02349 [PDF p.54] the estimation error for G(q, θ̂Nd ) as:


02350 [PDF p.54] 


02351 [PDF p.54]           G0 (q) − G(q, θ̂Nd ) = G0 (q) − G(q, θ ∗) + G(q, θ ∗ ) − G(q, θ̂Nd ).      (2.39)

02353 [PDF p.54]                                           bias                    variance


02354 [PDF p.54] 


02355 [PDF p.54] In this decomposition, the first part is the structural or bias error, usually induced


02356 [PDF p.54] by the fact that the model set is not rich enough to exactly represent the plant. The


02357 [PDF p.54] second part is the noise induced or variance error which is due to noise contribution


02358 [PDF p.54] on the measured data. The bias can be characterized in terms of integral formulas


02359 [PDF p.54] over the frequency domain. Powerful formulas also exist to express variance error if


02360 [PDF p.54] both Nd and the model order tend to infinity [105].


02361 [PDF p.54]    One of the most basic results on variance error is formulated in terms of the


02362 [PDF p.54] variability of asymptotic parameter estimates. In the most general form, the charac-


02363 [PDF p.54] terization follows from the central limit theorem, proving that

02412 [PDF p.55] 2.4.5    Identification with OBFs


02413 [PDF p.55] Considering the classical identification results described in the previous part, it


02414 [PDF p.55] appears that there are two attractive properties of model structures: linear-in-the-


02415 [PDF p.55] parameter property and independent parametrization of the process and noise mod-


02416 [PDF p.55] els. Among the presented classical structures a combination of these two properties


02417 [PDF p.55] can only be found in the FIR structure. However, the main disadvantage of this


02418 [PDF p.55] structure is that it generally requires a large number of parameters to capture the


02419 [PDF p.55] dynamics of the physical system, which implies a relatively large variance of the


02420 [PDF p.55] estimate. Using OBFs instead of the pulse basis like in (2.5) can significantly de-


02421 [PDF p.55] creases the number of required parameters and preserve all the attractive properties.


02422 [PDF p.55] In this section we focus on the model structures:

02425 [PDF p.55]                                        i=0


02426 [PDF p.55] 


02427 [PDF p.55] where {φi }ni=1 with φ0 = 1 are orthonormal basis functions in RH2 (E) with pole lo-


02428 [PDF p.55] cations Λn = [ λ1 . . . λn ]. The unknown series-expansion coefficients of (2.42) are


02429 [PDF p.55] collected into the parameter vector θ = [ w0 . . . wn ] ⊂ Rn+1 . In a general sense,


02430 [PDF p.55] different identification criteria and settings can be applied for OBFs based model


02431 [PDF p.55] structures, like for example frequency domain identification in H2 /H∞ , resulting


02432 [PDF p.55] in attractive alternatives of LTI system identification [73, 50]. In the following we


02433 [PDF p.55] explore the LS prediction-error setting to compare the properties of this model struc-


02434 [PDF p.55] ture to the classical results of other structures. Later, these properties also form the


02435 [PDF p.55] basic motivation why this model structure with the LS prediction-error setting yields


02436 [PDF p.55] an attractive candidate for LPV identification.

02440 [PDF p.56] 2.4.5.1   Least-Squares Identification


02441 [PDF p.56] 


02442 [PDF p.56] Due to the linear-in-the-parameter property of the OBF parametrization, estimation


02443 [PDF p.56] of the parameters in the LS setting similarly follows as in the FIR or ARX cases. The


02444 [PDF p.56] only difference with respect to these model structures is that the regression vector is


02445 [PDF p.56]                           !                                         "


02446 [PDF p.56]                  γ  (k) = u(k) (φ1 (q)u)(k) . . . (φn (q)u)(k) ,


02447 [PDF p.56] 


02448 [PDF p.56] containing filtered versions of the input signal rather than delayed version of u or y.


02449 [PDF p.56] This form of the regressor implies that the LS parameter estimate of (2.42) can be


02450 [PDF p.56] obtained via (2.41). In terms of consistency/bias properties of the estimates all the


02451 [PDF p.56] classical results about FIR structures hold, if u is a white noise signal, i.e. Φu (eiω ) is


02452 [PDF p.56] constant. This means, that if G0 (q) is in the IO model set and the input is white noise,


02453 [PDF p.56] then the model estimate G(q, θ̂Nd ) is unbiased and consistent. This is the case when


02454 [PDF p.56] the true system has a finite series-expansion in terms of the used basis functions.


02455 [PDF p.56] In all other cases, the expansion coefficients of G0 (q) in terms of the finite basis


02456 [PDF p.56] functions are estimated consistently, but a bias results due to the truncated tail of the


02457 [PDF p.56] required infinite expansion. Therefore there is a primal emphasis on the selection of


02458 [PDF p.56] appropriate basis functions, to reduce the bias by ensuring a fast convergence rate


02459 [PDF p.56] of the series-expansion.


02460 [PDF p.56]    A particularly interesting aspect results if the estimation of the parameters is


02461 [PDF p.56] formulated in state-space. As indicated in (2.14a–b), a basis functions based series-


02462 [PDF p.56] expansion model G(q, θ ) can be realized efficiently in two SS forms:

02480 [PDF p.56] initial condition.

02615 [PDF p.58]    As discussed in this section, OBFs-based parametrization can be effectively used


02616 [PDF p.58] for LTI system representation with many fruitful properties, however it is required


02617 [PDF p.58] that the basis function set is “well chosen” with respect to system to be identified. In

02619 [PDF p.58] systems is established, giving the key theorem to solve the basis selection problem


02620 [PDF p.58] of the identification scheme both in the LTI and in the LPV case later on. Before

02623 [PDF p.58] 2.4.5.3   Identification in the MIMO Case


02624 [PDF p.58] 


02625 [PDF p.58] In case of MIMO systems, identification follows similar guidelines as in the SISO


02626 [PDF p.58] case, except that the model structure (2.42) is formulated with MIMO basis func-


02627 [PDF p.58] tions. Due to the FIR structure of OBFs models, the analytic solution of (2.31) is


02628 [PDF p.58] still obtained via a linear regression, however with a more extensive book keeping.


02629 [PDF p.58]     In case the MIMO basis are constructed from scalar basis functions (method 1),


02630 [PDF p.58] all properties in terms of identification trivially extend to MIMO case [128]. How-


02631 [PDF p.58] ever, this model structure has a major disadvantage, namely that specific elements


02632 [PDF p.58] of {Wi } can be insignificantly small for every i > 0, which can result in an over-


02633 [PDF p.58] parametrization, ergo in a significant bias of the estimate. MIMO basis sequences


02634 [PDF p.58] generated by square inner functions via (2.11) (method 2) are not affected by the


02635 [PDF p.58] previous disadvantage, however bias and variance properties of the estimates are


02636 [PDF p.58] not yet clearly understood. See [205] and [72] for more on identification properties


02637 [PDF p.58] of model structures based on this type of MIMO-OBFs.

02640 [PDF p.58] 2.4.6     Pole Uncertainty of Model Estimates


02641 [PDF p.58] In practical situations, identification is unavoidably effected by noise, resulting in


02642 [PDF p.58] uncertainty of the model estimates. The resulting model uncertainties can be char-


02643 [PDF p.58] acterized based on numerous concepts of uncertainty in the parameter or frequency


02644 [PDF p.58] domain. See [67, 105, 127] and [49] for an overview on the available approaches. A


02645 [PDF p.58] well-known fact in the LTI case is that pole locations of a model estimate are gener-


02646 [PDF p.58] ally sensitive to parameter uncertainties, see e.g. [66]. In the following, some basic


02647 [PDF p.58] concepts of pole uncertainty regions are briefly introduced for DT model estimates


02648 [PDF p.58] in the LS setting. The developed concepts are essential for the formulation of the


02649 [PDF p.58] robust basis selection approach in Chap. 8.


02650 [PDF p.58]

02922 [PDF p.63] 2.5    The Kolmogorov n-Width Theory


02923 [PDF p.63] In the identification cycle, one of the key steps is the choice of an adequate model


02924 [PDF p.63] structure, i.e. the model set, which can represent the system to be identified with a


02925 [PDF p.63] relatively small number of statistically meaningful parameters. In the identification


02926 [PDF p.63] approach based on OBF model structures, finding an appropriate model set trans-


02927 [PDF p.63] lates to the search for a set of basis functions Φnnbe , that gives a series-expansion of the


02928 [PDF p.63] system with a fast convergence rate ρ . In LTI system identification, one approach to


02929 [PDF p.63] find appropriate model sets is based on the n-width concept [143], which has been


02930 [PDF p.63] shown to result in appropriate model sets for robust modeling of linear systems


02931 [PDF p.63] [111]. Using this concept, it has been shown in [131] that OBF model structures are


02932 [PDF p.63] optimal in the n-width sense for specific subsets of systems and finding the optimal


02933 [PDF p.63] OBF set for a given system set can be formulated as an optimization problem. In


02934 [PDF p.63] the following, the basic ingredients of this approach for discrete-time, stable, SISO


02935 [PDF p.63] systems are described. Later, this theory is used as the backbone of OBFs selection


02936 [PDF p.63] for the identification of LPV systems.

03066 [PDF p.66] 2.6   Conclusions


03067 [PDF p.66] In this introductory chapter basic definitions and concepts of orthonormal basis


03068 [PDF p.66] functions and the prediction-error identification framework have been introduced


03069 [PDF p.66] with the aim to establish a solid background for our upcoming investigation of mod-


03070 [PDF p.66] eling and identification of LPV systems. Through this chapter we have shown that


03071 [PDF p.66] truncated series-expansion models like OBFs based model structures have attrac-


03072 [PDF p.66] tive properties in LTI system identification. Such model structures not only provide


03073 [PDF p.66] consistent model estimation via simple linear regression (in case of an OE noise


03074 [PDF p.66] model), but need significantly less parameters than FIR models for an adequate ap-


03075 [PDF p.66] proximation of the system and have a direct characterization of the truncation error.


03076 [PDF p.66] We will use these attractive properties to develop a low complexity and efficient


03077 [PDF p.66] identification approach of LPV systems in Chap. 9 using similar truncated series


03078 [PDF p.66] expansion models. Furthermore, we have discussed in Sect. 2.5 that in the context


03079 [PDF p.66] of OBF model structures, the optimal choice of the model set can be characterized


03080 [PDF p.66] by using the Kolmogorov n-width concept. As we will see, this theory will serve as


03081 [PDF p.66] the backbone of the later developed OBF-model-structure-based model set selection


03082 [PDF p.66] approach for LPV systems together with the improved concept of pole uncertainty


03083 [PDF p.66] regions discussed in Sect. 2.4.6. However, before such theories and methods can be


03084 [PDF p.66] introduced first we will study LPV systems and establish the basic system theoreti-


03085 [PDF p.66] cal tools which will enable understanding of model structures and estimation in the


03086 [PDF p.66] LPV context.


03087 [PDF p.66] 


03088 [PDF p.67] Chapter 3


03089 [PDF p.67] LPV Systems and Representations


03090 [PDF p.67] 


03091 [PDF p.67] 


03092 [PDF p.67] 


03093 [PDF p.67] 


03094 [PDF p.67] Abstract. In this chapter, a behavioral framework of LPV systems is introduced


03095 [PDF p.67] as an extension of the LTI behavioral approach. This is done with the intention to


03096 [PDF p.67] give a unified view on LPV system theory, that enables to approach LPV system


03097 [PDF p.67] identification in a well-founded system theoretic sense. First we define LPV dy-


03098 [PDF p.67] namical systems from the behavioral point of view. Then we introduce the algebraic


03099 [PDF p.67] structure in which we formulate kernel, state-space, and input-output representa-


03100 [PDF p.67] tions of LPV systems. We also analyze the properties of LPV systems in terms of


03101 [PDF p.67] state-observability, state-reachability, and dynamic stability.


03102 [PDF p.67] 


03103 [PDF p.67] 


03104 [PDF p.67] 3.1     General Class of LPV Systems


03105 [PDF p.67] In this section, we establish the basics of a behavioral framework for linear parame-


03106 [PDF p.67] ter-varying (LPV) systems where a representation-free definition of such systems


03107 [PDF p.67] can be given and the previously considered concepts of LPV representations and


03108 [PDF p.67] corresponding theories can be re-established. Our main motivation is to set this


03109 [PDF p.67] framework as a tool for the analysis of LPV system identification in a well-founded


03110 [PDF p.67] sense.


03111 [PDF p.67]    One of the key concepts that is required to establish the LPV behavioral frame-


03112 [PDF p.67] work is an algebraic structure with elements describing differential equations, like


03113 [PDF p.67] R[ξ ] (the ring of polynomials with real constant coefficients) used in the LTI case.


03114 [PDF p.67] As we will see, the required structure in the LPV case is based on polynomials


03115 [PDF p.67] with coefficients that are functions of the scheduling variable p and its derivatives


03116 [PDF p.67] (continuous-time) or its time-shifts (discrete-time). The construction of this struc-


03117 [PDF p.67] ture enables us to apply the results of the linear time-varying (LTV) behavioral


03118 [PDF p.67] approach, worked out by [239] and [78]. We use these results to establish three


03119 [PDF p.67] key theorems: the existence of kernel representations, the existence of state-kernel


03120 [PDF p.67] forms, and later in Sect. 3.2 the concept of left/right unimodular transforma-


03121 [PDF p.67] tions. These theorems give the basic building blocks for the derivation of equiva-


03122 [PDF p.67] lence transformations between LPV representations, treated in Chap. 4, which have


03123 [PDF p.67] paramount significance for system identification.

03129 [PDF p.68] 


03130 [PDF p.68]    First, let’s investigate what we call an LPV system from the behavioral point


03131 [PDF p.68] of view and what kind of physical phenomena are represented by this modeling


03132 [PDF p.68] concept.


03133 [PDF p.68] 


03134 [PDF p.68] 


03135 [PDF p.68] 3.1.1       Parameter Varying Dynamical Systems


03136 [PDF p.68] In aerospace engineering, it is well-known that many airplanes, like the F-16 Fight-


03137 [PDF p.68] ing Falcon presented in Fig. 3.1, are nonlinear dynamical systems, but at a constant


03138 [PDF p.68] altitude they can be well approximated as an LTI system [181, 42]. Then, by view-


03139 [PDF p.68] ing the aircraft as a collection of LTI behaviors corresponding to different altitude


03140 [PDF p.68] levels and using the altitude variable as a scheduling between them, we can arrive


03141 [PDF p.68] at an approximation of the global behavior. In this context, the concept of schedul-


03142 [PDF p.68] ing means the selection of the LTI behavior associated with a specific altitude level.


03143 [PDF p.68] This behavior describes the possible continuation of signal trajectories during the


03144 [PDF p.68] time interval in which the aircraft remains at the same altitude. Thus, the result-


03145 [PDF p.68] ing representation of the global behavior involves coefficients that are functions of


03146 [PDF p.68] the scheduling. Such a modeling approach, that was introduced in Chap. 1 as the


03147 [PDF p.68] gain-scheduling principle, defines a parameter-varying (due to scheduling) and lin-


03148 [PDF p.68] ear (in signal relation) system. Such systems are referred as LPV. However, it is


03149 [PDF p.68] important that an LPV system is more than just an array of LTI systems, because


03150 [PDF p.68] the governing scheduling rules or functions also define the dynamical behavior be-


03151 [PDF p.68] tween each scheduling point, i.e. altitude points of this example. The concept of


03152 [PDF p.68] scheduling functions and “frozen” LTI behaviors provides an essential viewpoint on


03153 [PDF p.68] LPV systems which will be frequently used in the development of the identification


03154 [PDF p.68] approaches of Chap. 9.


03155 [PDF p.68]    In the general parameter-varying (PV) framework, the scheduling variable, com-


03156 [PDF p.68] monly denoted by p, is an external1, so-called free signal of the system, that governs


03157 [PDF p.68] the dynamical behavior. From this aspect, the role of p can be understood as an other


03158 [PDF p.68] “time-variable” that determines the change of signal relations. However, the trajec-


03159 [PDF p.68] tory of p is unknown in advance which property distinguishes LPV systems from


03160 [PDF p.68] the LTV system class, where the variations of signal relations is directly associated


03161 [PDF p.68] with time. Based on this, the class of PV systems can be defined as follows:


03162 [PDF p.68] Definition 3.1 (Parameter-varying dynamical system). A parameter-varying dy-


03163 [PDF p.68] namical system S is defined as a quadruple


03164 [PDF p.68] 


03165 [PDF p.68]                                       S = (T, P, W, B),                                 (3.1)


03166 [PDF p.68] 


03167 [PDF p.68] with T the time-axis, P the scheduling space with dimension nP , W the signal space


03168 [PDF p.68] with dimension nW , and B ⊆ (W × P)T the behavior (XT is the standard notation


03169 [PDF p.68] for the collection of all maps from T to X).                                     


03170 [PDF p.68] 1 Note that systems where p is an internal variable (like output, input, or state) are called


03171 [PDF p.68] 


03172 [PDF p.68]      quasi parameter-varying systems. Still, such systems are commonly treated as a PV system


03173 [PDF p.68]      with external scheduling variable, therefore in the upcoming analysis, p is assumed to be


03174 [PDF p.68]      an independent variable. For more on quasi-PV systems, see Chap. 7.
