03246 [PDF p.70] With the previously introduced concepts, we can define LPV systems as follows:


03247 [PDF p.70] Definition 3.3 (LPV system). The parameter-varying system S is called LPV, if the


03248 [PDF p.70] following conditions are satisfied:


03249 [PDF p.70] • W is a vector-space and B p is a linear subspace of WT for all p ∈ BP (linearity).


03250 [PDF p.70] • T is closed under addition.


03251 [PDF p.70] • For any (w, p) ∈ B (a signal trajectory associated with a scheduling trajectory)


03252 [PDF p.70]   and any τ ∈ T, it holds that (w( + τ ), p( + τ )) ∈ B, in other words qτ B = B


03253 [PDF p.70]   (time-invariance).                                                              


03254 [PDF p.70] In terms of Def. 3.3, for a constant scheduling trajectory p(k) ≡ p, time-invariance


03255 [PDF p.70] of S implies time-invariance of Fp . Based on this and the linearity condition of B p ,


03256 [PDF p.70] it holds for an LPV system that for each p ∈ P the associated frozen system Fp is an


03257 [PDF p.70] LTI system, which is in accordance with previous definitions of LPV systems (see


03258 [PDF p.70] [156]). In this way, the projected behaviors of a given LPV system S with respect


03259 [PDF p.70] to constant scheduling trajectories define a set of LTI systems:


03260 [PDF p.70] Definition 3.4 (Frozen system set). Let S = (T, P, W, B) be an LPV system. The

03268 [PDF p.70] This set refers in our example to the LTI behaviors of the aircraft for constant altitude


03269 [PDF p.70] levels. We have already motivated that the LPV system concept is advantageous


03270 [PDF p.70] compared to nonlinear systems, as the relation of the signals is linear. Definition 3.3


03271 [PDF p.70] also reveals the advantage of this system class over LTV systems: the variation of


03272 [PDF p.70] the system dynamics is not associated directly with time, but with the variation of


03273 [PDF p.70] a free signal. Thus, the LPV modeling concept, compared to LTV systems, is more


03274 [PDF p.70] suitable for non-stationary/coordinate dependent physical systems as it describes the


03275 [PDF p.70] underlying phenomena directly (see Example 3.1).

03321 [PDF p.71] In the sequel, we restrict our attention to continuous-time (T = R) and discrete-time


03322 [PDF p.71] (T = Z) systems with finite dimensional and real signal space (W = RnW ) and with


03323 [PDF p.71] finite dimensional, real, and closed scheduling space (P ⊆ RnP ). In fact, we consider


03324 [PDF p.71] LPV systems described by finite order linear differential or difference equations

03326 [PDF p.71] parameter-varying differential/difference systems and denote them with S. A basic


03327 [PDF p.71] property of such systems is that their behaviors B are complete ((w, p) ∈ B ⇔

03332 [PDF p.71] 3.1.2     Representations of Continuous-Time LPV Systems


03333 [PDF p.71] In order to re-establish the concept of LPV representations, we introduce kernel


03334 [PDF p.71] (KR), state-space (SS) and input-output (IO) representations of continuous-time


03335 [PDF p.71] (CT) LPV systems. However, to define these representations, we first have to intro-


03336 [PDF p.71] duce differential equations with varying-coefficients as the representations of LPV

03339 [PDF p.72]

03341 [PDF p.72] ring where equivalence of representations and other system theoretic concepts can


03342 [PDF p.72] be characterized by simple algebraic manipulations.

03707 [PDF p.78] Definition 3.9 (Unimodular polynomial matrix function). Let M ∈ R[ξ ]n×n . Then


03708 [PDF p.78] M is called unimodular, if there exists a M † ∈ R[ξ ]n×n , such that M † (ξ )M(ξ ) = I


03709 [PDF p.78] and M(ξ )M † (ξ ) = I .                                                             


03710 [PDF p.78] Any unimodular matrix operator in R[ξ ]·×· is equivalent to the product of finite


03711 [PDF p.78] many elementary row and column operations [41]:


03712 [PDF p.78] 1. Interchange row (column) i and row (column) j.


03713 [PDF p.78] 2. Multiply on the left (right) a row (column) i by a r ∈ R, r = 0.


03714 [PDF p.78] 3. For i = j, add to row (column) i row (column) j multiplied by ξ n , n ≥ 0.


03715 [PDF p.78] 4. Replace the first element in each of two columns by their highest common left


03716 [PDF p.78]    factor and 0 respectively.

03817 [PDF p.80] 3.1.2.5   Input-Output Representations

03819 [PDF p.80] Another key representation form is the IO representation, which we define from the


03820 [PDF p.80] behavioral point of view in this subsection. Before establishing our definition, we


03821 [PDF p.80] need the concept of IO partition for LPV systems.

03823 [PDF p.80] of dynamical systems into sets of input signals u : R → U and output signals y : R →


03824 [PDF p.80] Y. This is done to distinguish which of them we would like to (or can) actuate as


03825 [PDF p.80] inputs in order to drive the remaining so-called output signals to a desired trajectory


03826 [PDF p.80] of B. The definition of such a IO partition of S, which is commonly non-unique, is

03908 [PDF p.82] 


03909 [PDF p.82] In case of continuous-time LPV systems, the notion of transfer function or frequency


03910 [PDF p.82] response has no meaningful2 interpretation. By using the approximative transfer


03911 [PDF p.82] function calculus of LTV systems [117], some interpretation of these notions can


03912 [PDF p.82] be given for LPV systems. However, these concepts do not satisfy the relations of


03913 [PDF p.82] the LTI case. On the other hand, each element of the frozen system set FS , is an


03914 [PDF p.82] LTI system. Therefore, each Fp ∈ FS has a transfer function Fp (s), a frequency


03915 [PDF p.82] response Fp (iω ), and an impulse response hp (t) with Markov parameters {gi|p }∞ i=0 .


03916 [PDF p.82] The notion of frozen transfer function set or impulse response set can be established


03917 [PDF p.82] for any LPV system. The set of frozen poles or zeros follows similarly.

03919 [PDF p.82] 3.1.2.6      State-Space Representations


03920 [PDF p.82] 


03921 [PDF p.82] Besides partitioning the signals of the system in an IO sense, we often need to


03922 [PDF p.82] introduce additional variables in most modeling exercises to express more conve-


03923 [PDF p.82] niently the relationships of those signals we are particulary interested in. This is


03924 [PDF p.82] motivated by the first principle laws of physics where we can often meet physically


03925 [PDF p.82] non-existing (virtual) variables like the potential field in the well-known Maxwell’s


03926 [PDF p.82] equations. It also can happen that we are just simply not interested in some “inner”


03927 [PDF p.82] variables of the system, like in the voltage drop on a resistor of a space shuttle, if


03928 [PDF p.82] we would like to control its motion around the planet. We call these other, auxiliary


03929 [PDF p.82] variables latent variables. The introduction of latent variables and their associated


03930 [PDF p.82] representations are essential for LPV systems as they give the mathematical concept


03931 [PDF p.82] of signals that corresponds to inner variables or states of the system. In the follow-


03932 [PDF p.82] ing we extend the definition of latent variables and the property of state to the LPV


03933 [PDF p.82] case. Then we introduce the state-kernel form, proving that all latent variable rep-


03934 [PDF p.82] resentations have a first order PV differential equation form. The latter property is


03935 [PDF p.82] used to define SS representations of LPV systems.

03937 [PDF p.82] ifest (non-latent) variables, then as a generalization of (3.24):

04083 [PDF p.85] 3.1.3     Representations of Discrete-Time LPV Systems


04084 [PDF p.85] The concept of discrete-time (DT) parameter-varying dynamical systems is also im-


04085 [PDF p.85] portant for engineering applications. In the following we formulate the behavioral


04086 [PDF p.85] framework for DT-LPV systems. First we investigate the concept of DT parameter-


04087 [PDF p.85] varying systems and then we define their KR, SS and IO representations. To do


04088 [PDF p.85] so, we use the previously developed ring of polynomials R[ξ ] with meromorphic


04089 [PDF p.85] coefficient functions. In the DT case, the time operator q is substituted as the inde-


04090 [PDF p.85] terminate of these polynomials which results in a different non-commutative multi-


04091 [PDF p.85] plication rule in R[ξ ] than in CT case, but the algebraic structure remains the same.


04092 [PDF p.85] This property provides that the previously developed theories extend to the DT case.


04093 [PDF p.85]

04141 [PDF p.86] developed. Similar to the LTI case, the time operator that we use in the discrete-time


04142 [PDF p.86] PV case to define difference equations is the forward-time shift operator q. Such dif-


04143 [PDF p.86] ference equations are used to describe the behavior of DT-LPV systems. However,


04144 [PDF p.86] the operator q has different properties than dtd , used in the CT case. Additionally, q


04145 [PDF p.86] being the time operator also implies that the coefficients in the DT case are depen-


04146 [PDF p.86] dent on p and its time-shifted versions. Due to these differences, in the following we


04147 [PDF p.86] reformulate concepts of coefficient dependence (association of coefficient variables


04148 [PDF p.86] with the scheduling) and commutation rules of multiplication in R[ξ ] in order to


04149 [PDF p.86] define the analog of the concepts of the CT case.


04150 [PDF p.86]    As a first step, we define the variable association of the coefficient functions r ∈ R


04151 [PDF p.86] with elements of p and their forward and backward time-shifts. Similar to the CT


04152 [PDF p.86] case, such a dynamic dependence is needed to establish equivalence transformations


04153 [PDF p.86] (state elimination/construction) between discrete-time SS and IO representations


04154 [PDF p.86] (see Chap. 4 and [189, 202] for the details). Contrary to the CT case, in DT the


04155 [PDF p.86] coefficient functions are required to depend on both forward and backward time-


04156 [PDF p.86] shifts of p. Thus, labeling of the variables must contain positive and negative indexes


04157 [PDF p.86] as well.

04470 [PDF p.91] 3.1.3.4   Input-Output Representations


04471 [PDF p.91] 


04472 [PDF p.91] IO representations are also important for the DT behavioral framework of LPV sys-


04473 [PDF p.91] tems. Beside system theoretical aspects, this type of representations connects the


04474 [PDF p.91] developed behavioral theory to IO models used in the-state-of-the-art of LPV sys-


04475 [PDF p.91] tem identification. In this way, it enables comparison and analysis of IO identifica-


04476 [PDF p.91] tion methods. In the following, we define DT-IO representations from the behavioral


04477 [PDF p.91] point of view, based on the same line of discussion as in the CT case.


04478 [PDF p.91]    For DT-LPV systems, IO partitions are also characterized by Def. 3.11. The


04479 [PDF p.91] existence of IO partition (u, y) implies the existence of matrix polynomials Ry ∈


04480 [PDF p.91] R[ξ ]nY ×nY and Ru ∈ R[ξ ]nY ×nU with Ry full rank, such that (3.53) can be written in


04481 [PDF p.91] a similar form as (3.36). Based on this, it is possible to introduce IO representations


04482 [PDF p.91] of DT-LPV systems as follows:

04623 [PDF p.94] 3.2    Equivalence Classes and Relations


04624 [PDF p.94] In this section, we continue the introduction of the LPV behavioral framework by


04625 [PDF p.94] defining equivalence relations and classes for the introduced representation forms.


04626 [PDF p.94] These are essential aspects of the theory as they characterize which representations


04627 [PDF p.94] describe the same system, providing tools to compare and analyze representation


04628 [PDF p.94] capabilities/validity of LPV models for identification. First we define equality of be-


04629 [PDF p.94] haviors and investigate why this equality needs to be understood in an almost every-


04630 [PDF p.94] where. Then, we define equivalency, equivalence relations and equivalence classes


04631 [PDF p.94] of all representation forms together with the concept of minimality and canonical


04632 [PDF p.94] forms. To do so, we introduce key theorems of left/right side unimodular transfor-


04633 [PDF p.94] mations.


04634 [PDF p.94]    The most important concept to begin with is to define equality with respect to


04635 [PDF p.94] behaviors of PV systems.


04636 [PDF p.94] Definition 3.20 (Equal behaviors of PV systems). Let B1 , B2 ⊆ (W × P)T with


04637 [PDF p.94] W = RnW , P ⊆ RnP , and with T equal to either R or Z. We call B1 and B2 equal, if


04638 [PDF p.94] in case of T = R:


04639 [PDF p.94] 


04640 [PDF p.94]            (w, p) ∈ B1 ∩ C ∞ (R, W × P) ⇔ (w, p) ∈ B2 ∩ C ∞ (R, W × P),


04641 [PDF p.94] 


04642 [PDF p.94] or in the discrete-time case (T = Z):


04643 [PDF p.94] 


04644 [PDF p.94]                              (w, p) ∈ B1 ⇔ (w, p) ∈ B2 .                             


04645 [PDF p.94] Two systems are called equal if they have equal behaviors. However, it is important


04646 [PDF p.94] to remark that Def. 3.20 establishes the concept of equal behaviors in terms of inter-


04647 [PDF p.94] nal, and hence not external equality. This means, that even if two LPV systems have


04648 [PDF p.94] the same behavior in terms of IO signals for a particular IO partition, they are not


04649 [PDF p.94] necessarily equal as their scheduling signals or latent variables can differ. In case of


04650 [PDF p.94] systems with latent variables, equality can be defined in terms of the equality of the


04651 [PDF p.94] manifest behaviors (see Def. 3.29). On the other hand, there also exist systems with


04652 [PDF p.94] equal signal behavior and isomorphic projected scheduling behavior (see Example


04653 [PDF p.94] 3.18). However, due to technical reasons, we do not consider such systems to be


04654 [PDF p.94] equal in the sequel.

05142 [PDF p.102] 3.3     Properties of LPV Systems and Representations


05143 [PDF p.102] In the previous section we have developed the basics of a LPV behavioral frame-


05144 [PDF p.102] work. In order to use this framework as an analysis tool for LPV system identifi-


05145 [PDF p.102] cation, we also need to investigate key properties of systems and representations in


05146 [PDF p.102] terms of dynamic stability and state-observability/reachability. We analyze in this


05147 [PDF p.102] section these concepts using the results of LTV system theory. We also compare


05148 [PDF p.102] the developed results with their counterparts in the existing LPV theory. As the


05149 [PDF p.102] developed behavioral approach addresses a larger set of LPV systems than the state-


05150 [PDF p.102] of-the-art of LPV system theory, the existing LPV concepts follow as special cases


05151 [PDF p.102] of the theory presented in this section.


05152 [PDF p.102] 


05153 [PDF p.102] 3.3.1    State-Observability and Reachability


05154 [PDF p.102] The concepts of state-observability and reachability of LPV-SS system representa-


05155 [PDF p.102] tions are important properties in the LPV case. They are not only key concepts for


05156 [PDF p.102] control and subspace-based identification, but they also provide the formulation of


05157 [PDF p.102] special SS canonical forms. These so-called observability or reachability canoni-


05158 [PDF p.102] cal forms are strongly connected to the observability and reachability matrices of


05159 [PDF p.102] 


05160 [PDF p.103] 3.3 Properties of LPV Systems and Representations                                        81


05161 [PDF p.103] 


05162 [PDF p.103] SS representations and they are required to develop equivalence transformation be-


05163 [PDF p.103] tween different representation domains (see Chap. 4).


05164 [PDF p.103]    In the following discussion, we explore complete state-observability and reacha-


05165 [PDF p.103] bility5 of LPV-SS representations both in CT and DT, based on concepts of the LTV


05166 [PDF p.103] system theory. We show that these properties are equivalent with the existence of in-


05167 [PDF p.103] vertible linear maps for all time instances and scheduling trajectories. Based on this,


05168 [PDF p.103] we define observability and reachability matrices of SS representations. We show


05169 [PDF p.103] that complete state-observability and reachability are very strong properties in the


05170 [PDF p.103] LPV case as only a rather restricted class of representations fulfills them. Moreover,


05171 [PDF p.103] they are not required for minimality nor the generation of observability or reach-


05172 [PDF p.103] ability canonical forms. We show that a weaker property, the so-called structural


05173 [PDF p.103] state-observability/reachability, which defines the state-observability/reachability


05174 [PDF p.103] concept in an almost everywhere sense, is a necessary and sufficient property to


05175 [PDF p.103] generate these canonical forms.


05176 [PDF p.103]    As a first step, we extended the behavioral definitions of complete state-observ-


05177 [PDF p.103] ability and reachability (see [231]) to the LPV case:


05178 [PDF p.103] Definition 3.31 (Complete LPV state-observability). RSS (S) is called completely


05179 [PDF p.103] state-observable, if for all (u, x, y, p), (u, x


05180 [PDF p.103]  , y, p) ∈ BSS it holds that x = x


05181 [PDF p.103]  . 


05182 [PDF p.103] 


05183 [PDF p.103] Definition 3.32 (Complete LPV state-reachability). RSS (S) is called completely


05184 [PDF p.103] state-reachable, if for any given two states x1 , x2 ∈ X and any scheduling signal p ∈


05185 [PDF p.103] BP , there exist an input signal u and an output signal y such that (u, x, y, p) ∈ BSS


05186 [PDF p.103] with x(t1 ) = x1 and x(t2 ) = x2 for some t1 ,t2 ∈ T.                               


05187 [PDF p.103] 


05188 [PDF p.103] The main difference of these definitions with respect to the LTI case follows from


05189 [PDF p.103] the presence of the scheduling signal p that acts as an extra “time-axis” of the sys-


05190 [PDF p.103] tem. By freezing this axis, i.e. using a constant scheduling, these concepts coincide


05191 [PDF p.103] with the original LTI definitions (see [146]). To establish conditions when an LPV-


05192 [PDF p.103] SS representation is completely state-observable or reachable, as a next step, the


05193 [PDF p.103] concept of state-observability and reachability matrices is introduced. Appropriate


05194 [PDF p.103] conditions are derived to formulate when and in which sense the full rank of these


05195 [PDF p.103] matrices implies complete state-observability or reachability. However, the formu-


05196 [PDF p.103] lation of these matrices follows a different track than in the LTI case, due to the


05197 [PDF p.103] non-commutative multiplication on R[ξ ].

05287 [PDF p.105]    Based on the LTI case, one could expect that full rank of OnX , i.e. Rank(OnX ) =


05288 [PDF p.105] nX (full rank in a functional sense), is the necessary and sufficient condition for


05289 [PDF p.105] complete state-observability. However, this not true in the LPV case. It can also


05290 [PDF p.105] be shown that instead of the functional full rank, full rank of OnX for every time


05291 [PDF p.105] instance along every scheduling trajectory, i.e. Rank((OnX  p)(t)) = nX for all t ∈


05292 [PDF p.105] R and p ∈ BP , is a sufficient but not a necessary condition for complete state-


05293 [PDF p.105] observability. To show this and to derive the sufficient and necessary condition for


05294 [PDF p.105] complete state-observability, first introduce a weaker notion of state-observability:


05295 [PDF p.105] 


05296 [PDF p.105] Definition 3.34 (Structural state-observability). RSS (S) with state-dimension nX


05297 [PDF p.105] is called structurally state-observable if its nX -step observability matrix OnX is full


05298 [PDF p.105] (column) rank, i.e. Rank(OnX ) = nX .                                                 


05299 [PDF p.105] 


05300 [PDF p.105] Note that full rank in a functional sense, does not guarantee that OnX is invertible


05301 [PDF p.105] for all t ∈ R and p ∈ BP . Therefore, for specific scheduling trajectories and time


05302 [PDF p.105] instances, reconstructibility of state x by the linear map OnX is not guaranteed. In


05303 [PDF p.105] this way, complete state-observability is not implied. Even if reconstructibility may


05304 [PDF p.105] fail for some scheduling trajectories, for the rest state-observability holds on R. This


05305 [PDF p.105] gives that structural observability can be understood as complete state-observability


05306 [PDF p.105] in an almost everywhere sense. In the following we show that in fact structural state-


05307 [PDF p.105] observability is a necessary condition for complete state-observability.

05727 [PDF p.114] 3.3.1.5   General Properties and Minimality


05728 [PDF p.114] 


05729 [PDF p.114] As a next step we show that structural state-observability/reachability are the nec-


05730 [PDF p.114] essary ingredients to develop observability and reachability canonical forms of SS


05731 [PDF p.114] representations which are similar to their LTI counterparts. Additionally, minimality


05732 [PDF p.114] of LPV-SS representations is implied by structural state-observability instead of the


05733 [PDF p.114] complete concept.


05734 [PDF p.114]    Based on the definition of structural state-observability/reachability, an important


05735 [PDF p.114] corollary is the following:


05736 [PDF p.114] Corollary 3.1. If RSS (S) is structurally state-observable (reachable), i.e.


05737 [PDF p.114] Rank(OnX ) = nX (Rank(RnX ) = nX ), then at least nX number of rows of OnX


05738 [PDF p.114] (columns of RnX ) are linearly independent in the functional sense. This implies that


05739 [PDF p.114] in the SISO case, OnX (RnX ) is invertible.


05740 [PDF p.114] Based on this property, On and Rn can be used to define state-transformations in


05741 [PDF p.114] the behavioral framework and, by using similar argumentation as in the LTI case, to


05742 [PDF p.114] develop canonical forms for LPV-SS representations. Note that, in case of complete


05743 [PDF p.114] state-observability/reachability, On or Rn are invertible for all scheduling trajecto-


05744 [PDF p.114] ries and time instances, which is a much stronger property than the previous one.


05745 [PDF p.114] Thus by requiring this stronger property to generate canonical forms, we would


05746 [PDF p.114] exclude a large set of SS representations that have an equivalent (in the almost ev-


05747 [PDF p.114] erywhere sense) observability/reachability canonical form (see Chap. 4).

05795 [PDF p.115] 3.3.2     Stability of LPV Systems


05796 [PDF p.115] In the literature, there exist various stability concepts of LPV systems, originating


05797 [PDF p.115] either from the concepts of stability along frozen, i.e. constant scheduling trajecto-


05798 [PDF p.115] ries (frozen stability) or stability along arbitrary varying p (global stability). While


05799 [PDF p.115] the first aspect defines stability in the LTI sense of the frozen behaviors, the latter


05800 [PDF p.115] establishes this concept on the full behavior. In many works, LPV stability issues are


05801 [PDF p.115] only discussed for the state-space case with static dependence, involving the notion


05802 [PDF p.115] of state equilibrium points and Lyapunov functions [160, 6], or mixing the concepts


05803 [PDF p.115] of frozen and global stability by considering slow variations of p [164, 176, 155].


05804 [PDF p.115] Here we intend to define stability in the developed behavioral framework, investi-


05805 [PDF p.115] gating dynamic, IO, and Lyapunov stability both in a global and frozen sense. We


05806 [PDF p.115] also show the connection of the derived theory with the existing results of the LPV


05807 [PDF p.115] control synthesis framework.


05808 [PDF p.115] 


05809 [PDF p.115] 3.3.2.1   Global Stability


05810 [PDF p.115] 


05811 [PDF p.115] Global stability is the natural concept of stability for LPV dynamic systems, as it


05812 [PDF p.115] means that small causes produce small effects for any scheduling trajectory. Histor-


05813 [PDF p.115] ically, it originates from LTV system theory [68, 178] and robust control synthesis


05814 [PDF p.115] [240], where the problem of stability over the variations of the system has been first


05815 [PDF p.115] encountered. Let R+   0 denote the set of positive real numbers including 0. Then from


05816 [PDF p.115] the behavioral point of view, this concept extends the notion of dynamic stability for


05817 [PDF p.115] LPV systems as follows:


05818 [PDF p.115] Definition 3.42 (Global dynamic stability). The autonomous LPV dynamical sys-


05819 [PDF p.115] tem S = (T, RnW , P ⊆ RnP , B) is said to be globally dynamically stable, if ((w, p) ∈


05820 [PDF p.115] B) ⇒ (∃ε ∈ R+  0 such that w(t) ≤ ε for all t ≥ 0) (in an arbitrary norm  ). It is


05821 [PDF p.115] 6 Non-reachable systems are very common and they allow a state-minimal representation.


05822 [PDF p.115] 


05823 [PDF p.115]   Consider for instance autonomous systems. Such systems define a unique behavior, but


05824 [PDF p.115]   their state representation is never state-reachable.


05825 [PDF p.115] 


05826 [PDF p.116] 94                                                   3 LPV Systems and Representations


05827 [PDF p.116] 


05828 [PDF p.116] said to be globally unstable, if it is not stable; it is said to be globally dynamically


05829 [PDF p.116] asymptotically stable, if ((w, p) ∈ B) ⇒ (w(t) → 0 as t → ∞).                         


05830 [PDF p.116] The definition strongly builds on the linearity (the only fixed point of the dynamic


05831 [PDF p.116] relation is 0) and time-invariance (stability on t ≥ 0 implies stability on t ≥ t0 for


05832 [PDF p.116] all t0 ∈ R) of the LPV system class. Note that in terms of Def. 3.42 any signal tra-


05833 [PDF p.116] jectory, i.e. signal evolution of the system on the half-line, is bounded no matter the


05834 [PDF p.116] scheduling trajectory it is associated with, and the bound depends on the particular


05835 [PDF p.116] solution w. It is obvious that global stability includes stability with respect to frozen


05836 [PDF p.116] behaviors, as boundedness of w must hold for constant scheduling trajectories as


05837 [PDF p.116] well. This also emphasizes the difference between LPV and LTV systems, as in


05838 [PDF p.116] the latter case stability is defined with respect to only one, linear-trajectory of the


05839 [PDF p.116] scheduling (p(t) = t).


05840 [PDF p.116]     Contrary to the LTI case, conditions of global dynamic stability for LPV-KR


05841 [PDF p.116] representations can not be formulated in terms of eigenvalues or root conditions of


05842 [PDF p.116] polynomials in R[ξ ]. To show this, consider the following argument: In the CT-LTI


05843 [PDF p.116] case, dtd w = rw has solutions on the half-line in the form of w(t) = er w(0), thus


05844 [PDF p.116] the condition r < 0 guarantees boundedness of the solutions. However in the CT-

06042 [PDF p.120] 3.3.2.2    Frozen Stability


06043 [PDF p.120] 


06044 [PDF p.120] Another important aspect of LPV stability is the so-called frozen stability. Stability


06045 [PDF p.120] analysis of the frozen behaviors has been in the focus of LPV control during the


06046 [PDF p.120] gain-scheduling area, before the appearance of global LPV control synthesis tech-


06047 [PDF p.120] niques. At that time, researchers concluded global dynamic stability of the system


06048 [PDF p.120] based on the dynamic stability of the frozen behaviors by assuming appropriately


06049 [PDF p.120] slowly varying scheduling signals [235, 176, 155]. This view has been found mis-


06050 [PDF p.120] leading as the term “appropriate” was not well-defined (see the arguments of [157]


06051 [PDF p.120] and [166]). Today, frozen stability is still important in LPV analysis as it is a neces-


06052 [PDF p.120] sary ingredient for global stability.


06053 [PDF p.120] Definition 3.45 (Frozen stability). Let FS be the frozen system set (see Def. 3.4)


06054 [PDF p.120] of the LPV system S with scheduling space P ⊆ RnP . Then, in the frozen sense, S


06055 [PDF p.120] is


06056 [PDF p.120] • Uniformly asymptotically stable, if for all p ∈ P, Fp ∈ FS is dynamically asymp-


06057 [PDF p.120]   totically stable.


06058 [PDF p.120] • Uniformly stable, if for all p ∈ P, Fp is dynamically stable.


06059 [PDF p.120] • Non-uniformly stable, if it is not uniformly stable but there exists a p ∈ P s.t. Fp


06060 [PDF p.120]   is dynamically stable.


06061 [PDF p.120] • Uniformly unstable, if for all p ∈ P, Fp is dynamically unstable.                  


06062 [PDF p.120] Note that uniform frozen stability of S does not imply global dynamic stability,


06063 [PDF p.120] though the converse is true. In terms of Def. 3.45, the stability of the frozen as-


06064 [PDF p.120] pects of the system is checked separately for each frozen behavior. For example this


06065 [PDF p.120] means the construction of quadratic Lyapunov functions separately for each p ∈ P.


06066 [PDF p.120] If there exists such a common quadratic Lyapunov function which proves stability


06067 [PDF p.120] for all p ∈ P, where P is convex, then in case of linear and static dependence of A, it


06068 [PDF p.120] also implies global dynamic stability in terms of Th. 3.16. This makes an important


06069 [PDF p.120] distinction for systems with dynamic dependence, where the evaluation of A along a


06070 [PDF p.120] constant scheduling trajectory excludes the effect of the dependence on the deriva-


06071 [PDF p.120] tives/time shifts of p. For these systems, a common Lyapunov function of the frozen


06072 [PDF p.120] systems set does not imply global dynamic stability.

06123 [PDF p.122] 3.4    Conclusions


06124 [PDF p.122] In this chapter, we have developed a behavioral framework of LPV systems as an ex-


06125 [PDF p.122] tension of the LTI behavioral approach. The introduced theory has been established


06126 [PDF p.122] to give a unified view on LPV systems and their representations and to enable to ap-


06127 [PDF p.122] proach LPV system identification in a well-founded system theoretic sense. We has


06128 [PDF p.122] shown that the behavioral approach provides a well established view on equivalence


06129 [PDF p.122] relations between LPV representations, gives a clear representation free definition


06130 [PDF p.122] of LPV systems and it is compatible with the existing system theoretical results. It


06131 [PDF p.122] was also shown that the use of dynamic scheduling dependence is necessary in order


06132 [PDF p.122] to establish equivalence relations and also in general to fill the gaps of the existing


06133 [PDF p.122] theory. In the next chapter, we continue by extending the concept of equivalence


06134 [PDF p.122] transformations between different representation domains to the LPV system class.


06135 [PDF p.122] This contribution gives the finishing details of the developed behavioral framework


06136 [PDF p.122] and enables the comparison of different LPV model structures.

06138 [PDF p.123] Chapter 4


06139 [PDF p.123] LPV Equivalence Transformations


06140 [PDF p.123] 


06141 [PDF p.123] 


06142 [PDF p.123] 


06143 [PDF p.123] 


06144 [PDF p.123] Abstract. In this chapter, we continue the discussion of the LPV behavioral frame-


06145 [PDF p.123] work by establishing equivalence transformations between the state-space and the


06146 [PDF p.123] input-output representation domains. These equivalence transformations enable the


06147 [PDF p.123] comparison and analysis of LPV model structures and provide essential tools to


06148 [PDF p.123] formulate the identification approach of this thesis. First we define LPV canonical


06149 [PDF p.123] forms based on the concept of observability and reachability and we give an algo-


06150 [PDF p.123] rithmic scheme to construct them from an existing SS representation of the system.


06151 [PDF p.123] Then, transformations are introduced which provide an equivalent IO representation


06152 [PDF p.123] of a SS representation and vice versa. In both cases, the introduced LPV canonical


06153 [PDF p.123] forms are special cases of the transformation problem, serving as a simple gateway


06154 [PDF p.123] between the representation domains.


06155 [PDF p.123] 


06156 [PDF p.123] 


06157 [PDF p.123] 4.1     State-Space Canonical Forms


06158 [PDF p.123] 


06159 [PDF p.123] Specially structured canonical forms of state-space representations of LPV systems


06160 [PDF p.123] are essential ingredients to accommodate equivalence transformations between the


06161 [PDF p.123] state-space (SS) and the input-output (IO) representation domains. One set of these


06162 [PDF p.123] canonical forms are the so-called observability/reachability canonical forms which


06163 [PDF p.123] are also used in the state-of-the-art of LPV identification and control design.


06164 [PDF p.123]     In this section, LPV canonical forms in continuous-time (CT) and discrete-


06165 [PDF p.123] time (DT) are introduced through a transformation mechanism applied on a given


06166 [PDF p.123] SS representation of the LPV system. Using the concept of structural state-


06167 [PDF p.123] observability/reachability, i.e. the associated observability/reachability matrices,


06168 [PDF p.123] state-transformations are defined, that result in an equivalent SS representation with


06169 [PDF p.123] special structure in the system matrices. It is shown that this special structure implies


06170 [PDF p.123] complete state-observability/reachability of the resulting representation and hence


06171 [PDF p.123] it is called a LPV observability/reachability canonical form. Additionally, the intro-


06172 [PDF p.123] duced canonical forms give a unique representation of their associated equivalence

06182 [PDF p.124]    Besides the derivation of observability/reachability canonical forms, a construc-


06183 [PDF p.124] tion approach for their companion counterparts is introduced. The concept of trans-


06184 [PDF p.124] position of SS representations is also investigated, with the main conclusion that


06185 [PDF p.124] contrary to the LTI case, the transpose of a SS representation in the LPV framework


06186 [PDF p.124] does not have an equal manifest behavior. This means that such a transformation


06187 [PDF p.124] alters the dynamical relation.


06188 [PDF p.124]    It is also investigated how the developed concept of canonical forms relates to


06189 [PDF p.124] applied theories of the current LPV literature. It is shown that the common prac-


06190 [PDF p.124] tice to use LTI theory to compute canonical forms for LPV systems results in SS


06191 [PDF p.124] representations that do not have an equal manifest behavior.

06855 [PDF p.134] show this, consider the following argument:

06924 [PDF p.135] 4.1.5     LTI vs. LPV State Transformation


06925 [PDF p.135] In the previous part, we have seen that through the developed behavioral framework,


06926 [PDF p.135] canonical forms of LPV systems can be similarly formulated as in the LTI case. It


06927 [PDF p.135] has also been emphasized how this framework extends the concepts of LTI system


06928 [PDF p.135] theory to LPV systems by proper handling of the time operators and their effect on


06929 [PDF p.135] scheduling-dependent coefficient functions. Comparing the introduced construction


06930 [PDF p.135] mechanism of LPV canonical forms to the state-of-the-art of the LPV literature,


06931 [PDF p.135] similar mechanisms can be found, which have been developed for CT-SS represen-


06932 [PDF p.135] tations with linear dependence (see [89] as a notable approach). Thus the develop


06933 [PDF p.135] algorithm can be seen as a generalization of these approaches.

07036 [PDF p.137]    In the following we develop these transformations based on the behavioral frame-


07037 [PDF p.137] work. We introduce algorithms to obtain an IO realization of a given LPV-SS rep-


07038 [PDF p.137] resentation and vice-versa, solving the core problem of the existing LPV system


07039 [PDF p.137] theory (see also [202]). We show that the results generalize the theory presented for


07040 [PDF p.137] LTI systems in case the coefficient dependence on the scheduling vector is mero-


07041 [PDF p.137] morphic and dynamic. It is also shown that the canonical forms, developed in the


07042 [PDF p.137] previous part, give special cases of the transformation problem, thus they serve as


07043 [PDF p.137] a simple gateway between the SS and the IO representation domains. Again, it is


07044 [PDF p.137] proved that the common practice of the current LPV literature, namely to apply LTI


07045 [PDF p.137] theory to convert IO models to SS models, provides results which have an unequal


07046 [PDF p.137] manifest behavior.

07141 [PDF p.139] Corollary 4.5. Assume that RSS (S) is minimal, i.e. structurally state-observable.

07209 [PDF p.140] 4.3     From the Input-Output to the State-Space Domain


07210 [PDF p.140] As a next step, the equivalence transformation from the IO to the SS representa-


07211 [PDF p.140] tion domain is considered. To derive such a transformation, a vital ingredient is to


07212 [PDF p.140] construct a state-map for a given IO representation that defines an equivalent SS rep-


07213 [PDF p.140] resentation. This construction can be seen as the counterpart of the previous latent


07214 [PDF p.140] variable elimination. The actual aim is to introduce a latent variable into (4.24) such


07215 [PDF p.140] that it satisfies the state-property, ergo it defines a SS representation of the original


07216 [PDF p.140] system via Th. 3.4.


07217 [PDF p.140]    Generation of a state-map is more involved in the LPV case than for time-


07218 [PDF p.140] invariant systems as the scheduling dependence of the coefficients does not com-


07219 [PDF p.140] mute with time operators as integration, derivation, and time-shift. In order to


07220 [PDF p.140] improve readability of the upcoming rather technical discussion, we first investi-


07221 [PDF p.140] gate the intuitive idea behind the used state-construction mechanism, the so-called


07222 [PDF p.140] cut-and-shift operation. Then this operation is formally defined over the ring R[ξ ]


07223 [PDF p.140] both in CT and in DT. As a next step, state-maps generated by the cut-and-shift pro-


07224 [PDF p.140] cedure are constructed and it is shown that they introduce latent variables satisfying

07501 [PDF p.145] 4.3.5     State-Maps Based on Kernel Representations


07502 [PDF p.145] In the previous part, we have established state-map constructions for kernel rep-

07964 [PDF p.151] In the MIMO case, algorithms (4.54a–b) and (4.66a–b) also provide SS realizations


07965 [PDF p.151] of IO representations, however with different selector matrices (due to the multi-


07966 [PDF p.151] dimension) and with a more complicated path to select independent rows from the


07967 [PDF p.151] shift-map for X. It is only guaranteed that at least na number of rows of the shift-


07968 [PDF p.151] map are independent, thus such a selection is not evident. Similar to the selection


07969 [PDF p.151] schemes generating the SS MIMO canonical representations, only certain selection


07970 [PDF p.151] strategies for X lead to the MIMO observability and reachability canonical forms.


07971 [PDF p.151] Thus minimality of the obtained SS realizations via algorithm (4.54a–b) and (4.66a–


07972 [PDF p.151] b) is not guaranteed in the general sense.


07973 [PDF p.151] 


07974 [PDF p.151] 


07975 [PDF p.151] 4.4     Conclusions


07976 [PDF p.151] In this chapter, we have established equivalence transformations between the state-


07977 [PDF p.151] space and the input-output representation domains. These transformations and the


07978 [PDF p.151] corresponding algorithms have been introduced to enable comparison of LPV model


07979 [PDF p.151] structures and identified models later on and also to provide essential tools to de-


07980 [PDF p.151] velop LPV identification via OBF model structures. Additionally, we have defined


07981 [PDF p.151] observability and reachability canonical SS representations of LPV systems and we


07982 [PDF p.151] have shown that they provide a simple gateway for the conversion between the rep-


07983 [PDF p.151] resentation domains. Furthermore, it has been shown that the transpose of a LPV-SS


07984 [PDF p.151] representation does not have the same manifest behavior, which is a notable differ-


07985 [PDF p.151] ence with respect to the LTI theory. This property also proves that coefficients of


07986 [PDF p.151] canonical forms that structurally seem to be the transpose of each other (like the


07987 [PDF p.151] reachability and observability forms), are not equal. The connection of the intro-


07988 [PDF p.151] duced canonical forms with the applied theories of the current LPV literature has


07989 [PDF p.151] 


07990 [PDF p.152] 130                                              4 LPV Equivalence Transformations


07991 [PDF p.152] 


07992 [PDF p.152] also been investigated. This lead to the conclusion that the common practice to use


07993 [PDF p.152] LTI theory to compute canonical forms or provide a SS realization for LPV systems


07994 [PDF p.152] yields SS representations that do not have an equal manifest behavior. We next ex-


07995 [PDF p.152] plore if a series-expansion representation of LPV systems is available and can be


07996 [PDF p.152] used to establish truncated series-expansion models for the identification of LPV


07997 [PDF p.152] systems just as in the LTI case.

08000 [PDF p.153] LPV Series-Expansion Representations


08001 [PDF p.153]

08004 [PDF p.153] 


08005 [PDF p.153] Abstract. In this chapter, series-expansion representations of LPV systems for a


08006 [PDF p.153] given IO partition are developed using the framework of the behavioral approach.


08007 [PDF p.153] In fact, expansion of DT asymptotically stable LPV systems is considered in terms


08008 [PDF p.153] of OBFs and the connection between this type of expansion and the gain-scheduling


08009 [PDF p.153] principle is explored. It is shown that this series-expansion representation is unique


08010 [PDF p.153] and always exists for the considered system class and in some cases only a finite


08011 [PDF p.153] number of the expansion coefficients are nonzero. This implies that finite truncation


08012 [PDF p.153] of a OBFs-based series-expansion can be used as a model structure for the identifi-


08013 [PDF p.153] cation of asymptotically stable DT-LPV systems similar to the LTI case.


08014 [PDF p.153] 


08015 [PDF p.153] 


08016 [PDF p.153] 5.1     Relevance of Series-Expansion Representations


08017 [PDF p.153] 


08018 [PDF p.153] In the LTI framework, series-expansion representations have proved their usefulness


08019 [PDF p.153] in a number of contexts. They not only characterize a unique representation of the


08020 [PDF p.153] input-output (IO) system dynamics, like impulse-response representations, but they


08021 [PDF p.153] also provide model structures, like orthonormal basis functions (OBFs)-based mod-


08022 [PDF p.153] els, that provide an efficient alternative for LTI system identification. Using such


08023 [PDF p.153] model structures for the identification of LPV systems has a number of attractive


08024 [PDF p.153] proprieties and it would also allow the extension of the OBFs based identification


08025 [PDF p.153] approaches to the LPV case (see the argument of Chap. 1). Based on this, we de-


08026 [PDF p.153] velop in this chapter the concept of series-expansion of LPV systems in terms of


08027 [PDF p.153] OBFs, providing a unique perspective on the representation of the system dynamics


08028 [PDF p.153] with respect to an IO partition. This enables the formulation of the one-step ahead


08029 [PDF p.153] predictor in the LPV prediction-error identification framework and also the intro-


08030 [PDF p.153] duction of model structures as the finite truncation of a OBF series-expansion with


08031 [PDF p.153] respect to a LPV system. These model structures are vital ingredients of the LPV


08032 [PDF p.153] identification approach developed later.


08033 [PDF p.153]    To simplify the discussion and to avoid cases that are complicated but unimpor-


08034 [PDF p.153] tant for the intended identification approach, we restrict the discussion to discrete-


08035 [PDF p.153] time (DT) asymptotically-stable LPV systems.

08042 [PDF p.154] 5.2     Impulse Response Representation of LPV Systems


08043 [PDF p.154] As a first step, we develop the series-expansion representation of DT asymptotically


08044 [PDF p.154] stable LPV systems based on a pulse basis (see Sect. 2.1 for the definition of the


08045 [PDF p.154] pulse basis). LPV systems can not be handled in the frequency domain, thus we


08046 [PDF p.154] develop the concept of series-expansion in terms of the time operator form of the


08047 [PDF p.154] pulse basis. As we will see this results in a convolution based description of the


08048 [PDF p.154] system dynamics. To develop such a description, we first introduce the filter form


08049 [PDF p.154] of an LPV-IO representation. Then we generate the expansion in terms of the pulse


08050 [PDF p.154] basis by recursive substitution of the filter form. We show the uniqueness and the


08051 [PDF p.154] convergence of the resulting expansion coefficients. Additionally we briefly cover


08052 [PDF p.154] how this series-expansion can be generalized to unstable and continuous-time (CT)


08053 [PDF p.154] systems.


08054 [PDF p.154]

08371 [PDF p.160] 5.5     Series Expansions and Gain-Scheduling


08372 [PDF p.160] 


08373 [PDF p.160] There is an interesting relation of the OBF expansion representation and the gain-


08374 [PDF p.160] scheduling principle. This relation helps to understand whether an orthonormal basis


08375 [PDF p.160] is adequate for the series-expansion of the LPV system, i.e. how the rate of conver-


08376 [PDF p.160] gence of the expansion can be characterized. In the following, we explore this re-


08377 [PDF p.160] lation by first showing that for constant scheduling trajectories the OBF expansion


08378 [PDF p.160] representation is equivalent with the series-expansion representations of the frozen


08379 [PDF p.160] system set. As a next step we show, that this equivalence implies that for some LPV


08380 [PDF p.160] systems, KnW optimality of the basis with respect to the frozen system set implies


08381 [PDF p.160] an optimal convergence rate of the series-expansion in the LPV case.

08515 [PDF p.163] 5.6   Conclusions


08516 [PDF p.163] 


08517 [PDF p.163] In this chapter, series-expansion representations of DT asymptotically stable LPV


08518 [PDF p.163] systems for a given IO partition have been developed based on the concepts of


08519 [PDF p.163] the behavioral approach. We investigated expansions in terms of orthonormal basis


08520 [PDF p.163] functions with the intention to use finite truncation of these expansion representa-


08521 [PDF p.163] tions as a model structure for the identification of asymptotically stable DT-LPV


08522 [PDF p.163] systems later on. The developed theory enables the use of the LTI OBF-based iden-


08523 [PDF p.163] tification approach in the LPV case, which is of crucial importance in providing


08524 [PDF p.163] an efficient and theoretically well-founded LPV identification method. The connec-


08525 [PDF p.163] tion between series-expansion representation and the gain-scheduling principle has


08526 [PDF p.163] been explored, showing that the expansion coefficients of the basis sequence char-


08527 [PDF p.163] acterize the scheduling function part of the LPV system, while the basis functions


08528 [PDF p.163] are strongly related to the frozen system set. Based on this connection, it has been


08529 [PDF p.163] proven that KnW optimality of a basis sequence, with respect to the frozen system


08530 [PDF p.163] set of a given LPV system S, implies an optimal convergence rate of the series-


08531 [PDF p.163] expansion in these basis functions in the worst case sense along all possible constant


08532 [PDF p.163] scheduling trajectories. It has been also motivated that for systems with minimal IO


08533 [PDF p.163] representations having static coefficient dependence, optimal convergence rate of


08534 [PDF p.163] the LPV series-expansion with such a basis also holds for every scheduling trajec-


08535 [PDF p.163] tory. As we will see in Chap. 8, these properties have a paramount importance for


08536 [PDF p.163] OBFs-based model structure selection in LPV identification.

08544 [PDF p.164] Abstract. This chapter is devoted to the discretization of LPV systems through the


08545 [PDF p.164] discrete-time projection of their state-space representations. Both exact and approx-


08546 [PDF p.164] imative approaches are developed in a zero-order hold setting. Primary attention is


08547 [PDF p.164] given to the discretization of state-space representations with static coefficient de-


08548 [PDF p.164] pendence. For this case, criteria are derived to assist the choice of the sampling-time


08549 [PDF p.164] in terms of preservation of frozen dynamic stability and acceptable upperbound on


08550 [PDF p.164] the discretization error.


08551 [PDF p.164] 


08552 [PDF p.164] 


08553 [PDF p.164] 6.1     The Importance of Discretization


08554 [PDF p.164] Transformation between LPV systems represented on the continuous-time (CT) and


08555 [PDF p.164] the discrete-time (DT) axis, has primary importance both for system identification


08556 [PDF p.164] and control synthesis:


08557 [PDF p.164]    Implementation of LPV control solutions in physical hardware often meets sig-


08558 [PDF p.164] nificant difficulties, as CT synthesis approaches (see [134, 160]) are preferred over


08559 [PDF p.164] DT solutions (see [6, 133]). The main motivation for this preference is that stabil-


08560 [PDF p.164] ity and performance requirements for LPV systems can be expressed significantly


08561 [PDF p.164] easier in CT, like in a mixed sensitivity setting [240]. As a result, the current design


08562 [PDF p.164] tools focus on continuous-time LPV state-space (SS) controller synthesis, often in


08563 [PDF p.164] an LFR form, requiring efficient discretization of such representations for imple-


08564 [PDF p.164] mentation purposes.


08565 [PDF p.164]    In the LPV modeling framework, first principle LPV models of nonlinear sys-


08566 [PDF p.164] tems are also often derived in a CT form. In LPV system identification, such models


08567 [PDF p.164] serve as a primary source of information to assist adequate model structure selec-


08568 [PDF p.164] tion in terms of order, type of coefficient dependence, etc. However, current LPV


08569 [PDF p.164] identification methods are developed exclusively for DT. This means that DT pro-


08570 [PDF p.164] jection of first principle LPV models is required to assist model structure selection


08571 [PDF p.164] for practical identification.


08572 [PDF p.164]    These issues show how crucial is to well explore and analyze general discretiza-


08573 [PDF p.164] tion of LPV representations. Surprisingly, the existing literature about LPV dis-


08574 [PDF p.164] cretization is very limited. In the early work of [4], three different approaches have

08648 [PDF p.166] 


08649 [PDF p.166] 


08650 [PDF p.166] Sect. 3.1.3, equivalence of CT and DT behaviors under a given sampling-time has


08651 [PDF p.166] been established without any restrictions on the variation of u or p.


08652 [PDF p.166]    On the other hand, the variation of u and p inside a sample interval must be


08653 [PDF p.166] restricted to exactly characterize the effect of these signals on the plant. The reason


08654 [PDF p.166] is similar as in the LTI case. In DT, observations of the CT signals u and p are


08655 [PDF p.166] only available at each sampling-time instant. Thus there is no information about the


08656 [PDF p.166] trajectory of these signals during the sample interval. This means that the output


08657 [PDF p.166] signal can not be uniquely determined, unless the variation of the signals u and p is


08658 [PDF p.166] restricted to a certain class of functions. In the ZOH setting, this function class is


08659 [PDF p.166] chosen to be the piecewise constant (zero-order) class. It is also possible to choose


08660 [PDF p.166] this class wider, including linear, 2nd -order polynomial, etc., functions and in this


08661 [PDF p.166] way to define higher-order hold discretization settings of LPV systems. However, in


08662 [PDF p.166] conclusion it holds true that in any LPV discretization setting, the variation of the


08663 [PDF p.166] scheduling signals must be restricted, otherwise the resulting DT description would


08664 [PDF p.166] not be well-posed.


08665 [PDF p.166]    By applying the ZOH setting for the discretization of a given LPV representa-


08666 [PDF p.166] tion, the piecewise-constant variation of p implies that coefficients with dynamic


08667 [PDF p.166] dependence simplify as the derivatives of p are zero inside the sampling interval.


08668 [PDF p.166] This means, that unless the representation has static dependence, the ZOH setting


08669 [PDF p.166] may result in the loss of certain parts of the original behavior. Based on this, we as-


08670 [PDF p.166] sume that the CT representation to be discretized has static coefficient dependence.


08671 [PDF p.166] Later we explore how this limitation can be overcome, i.e. how the discretization of


08672 [PDF p.166] representations with dynamic dependence can be properly handled.


08673 [PDF p.166]    In conclusion, the introduced discretization setting coincides with the conven-


08674 [PDF p.166] tional setting of the LTI framework. Moreover, the presented setting is also appli-


08675 [PDF p.166] cable to closed-loop controllers in the structure given in Fig. 6.2. This closed-loop


08676 [PDF p.166] setting has also been used in [4]. Note that the assumption that the scheduling vector


08677 [PDF p.166] of the continuous LPV controller is affected by the ZOH setting, i.e. it can only vary


08678 [PDF p.166] in piece-wise manner, also holds in this case.

08819 [PDF p.169] 6.3.2     Approximative State-Space Discretization Methods


08820 [PDF p.169] The complete method is commonly not favored in the LPV literature as it introduces


08821 [PDF p.169] heavy nonlinear dependence on pd , like eTd A(pd ) , which is the main drawback of


08822 [PDF p.169] this approach. Many identification and control synthesis techniques build on the


08823 [PDF p.169] assumption of linear, polynomial or low order rational static dependence on pd ,


08824 [PDF p.169] and hence it is required to develop approximative discretization methods that try to


08825 [PDF p.169] achieve good representation of the original behavior, but with a low complexity of


08826 [PDF p.169] the coefficient dependence. To do that, we systematically extend the approximative


08827 [PDF p.169] discretization methods of the LTI case, by using different approximations of the


08828 [PDF p.169] integral that describes the state-evolution inside the sample-interval.

08958 [PDF p.171] 6.3.2.4     Multi-Step Methods

08965 [PDF p.172] coefficients are assumed to have static dependence. This solution can be numerically


08966 [PDF p.172] approximated via multi-step formulas like the Runge-Kutta, Adams-Moulton, or the


08967 [PDF p.172] Adams-Bashforth type of approaches (see [8]). In commercial engineering software


08968 [PDF p.172] packages, like M ATLAB Simulink, commonly variable step-size implementation of


08969 [PDF p.172] these algorithms assures accurate simulation of continuous-time systems. However


08970 [PDF p.172] in the considered ZOH discretization setting, the step size, i.e. the sampling rate,


08971 [PDF p.172] is fixed and sampled data is only available at past and present sampling instances.


08972 [PDF p.172] This immediately excludes multi-step implicit methods like the Adams-Moulton


08973 [PDF p.172] approaches. Moreover f (x, u, p) can only be evaluated for integer multiples of the


08974 [PDF p.172] sampling-time, as the input only changes at these time instances and the resulting


08975 [PDF p.172] model must be realized as a single rate (not multi-rate) system. Therefore it is com-


08976 [PDF p.172] plicated to apply methods like the Runge-Kutta approach. The family of Adams-


08977 [PDF p.172] Bashforth methods does fulfill these requirements (see [8]). The 3-step version of


08978 [PDF p.172] this type of numerical approach yields the following approximation:

09034 [PDF p.173] 6.4     Discretization Errors and Performance Criteria


09035 [PDF p.173] In the following part, the introduced methods are investigated in terms of the gener-


09036 [PDF p.173] ated discretization error, numerical convergence, and numerical stability. These are


09037 [PDF p.173] used to derive upperbounds on the sampling-time Td , that guarantee a user-defined


09038 [PDF p.173] bounded discretization error and stability preservation with respect to the original


09039 [PDF p.173] CT system. Moreover, the influence of the assumption that no switching effects re-


09040 [PDF p.173] sult from the ZOH actuation is investigated.


09041 [PDF p.173] 


09042 [PDF p.173] 6.4.1    Local Discretization Errors


09043 [PDF p.173] Characterization of the discretization error for each of the introduced approaches is


09044 [PDF p.173] important in order to study how adequate the used approximation is with respect to


09045 [PDF p.173] the original CT behavior. It has been already emphasized that, due to the consid-


09046 [PDF p.173] ered assumptions, the complete method theoretically gives errorless discretization


09047 [PDF p.173] in terms of the ZOH setting. For other approaches we investigate the discretization


09048 [PDF p.173] error in terms of the local unit truncation (LUT) error, which is often applied in


09049 [PDF p.173] numerical analysis (see [8]). This concept describes the error that results in each


09050 [PDF p.173] sampling interval due to discretization.

09260 [PDF p.176] 6.4.2     Global Convergence and Preservation of Stability


09261 [PDF p.176] So far, only the LUT error of the introduced methods has been investigated, giving


09262 [PDF p.176] basic proofs of consistency. As a next step, we investigate global convergence of ap-


09263 [PDF p.176] proximative methods together with their numerical stability (N-stability). The latter


09264 [PDF p.176] concept means that small errors in the initial condition of the discrete-time approxi-


09265 [PDF p.176] mation do not cause the solution to diverge. We show that for the single-step approx-


09266 [PDF p.176] imative discretization methods, N-stability is identical with the preservation of the


09267 [PDF p.176] frozen stability of the original representation. This means that in case of numerical


09268 [PDF p.176] stability, the discretization method does not changes the frozen stability properties


09269 [PDF p.176] of the discretized model, which is a prime requirement of a successful DT approxi-


09270 [PDF p.176] mation of a CT system. To derive adequate criteria for the largest sampling-time for


09271 [PDF p.176] which this property holds (N-stability radius), each method is analyzed and com-


09272 [PDF p.176] putable formulas are derived. Define Z−  0 as the set of all negative integer numbers


09273 [PDF p.176] including 0, and Z+ = Z \ Z−  0 . According to the previously explained line of discus-


09274 [PDF p.176] sion, we introduce the following concepts:

09729 [PDF p.184] In conclusion, for the considered class of LPV representations, the introduced dis-


09730 [PDF p.184] cretization methods of this section give no step-invariant discretization in the ZOH


09731 [PDF p.184] setting (meaning equivalence even in case of switching effects), however they are


09732 [PDF p.184] well applicable methods for practical use. It is important to note that derivation of


09733 [PDF p.184] LPV discretization methods with step-invariant property is also possible, however


09734 [PDF p.184] the resulting discretization approaches are technical and their actual performance


09735 [PDF p.184] gain compared to the previously developed approaches is negligible in practice.

09739 [PDF p.184] Beside stability and discretization error characteristics, there are other properties of

09741 [PDF p.184] resulting DT model. With the previously obtained results, these vital properties are


09742 [PDF p.184] summarized in Table 6.2. From this table it is apparent that the complete method


09743 [PDF p.184] gives errorless conversion at the price of heavy nonlinear dependence of the DT


09744 [PDF p.184] model on pd . As in LPV control synthesis low complexity of the p-dependence is

09999 [PDF p.189] In this chapter, discretization of LPV state-space representations has been investi-

10001 [PDF p.189] trajectories are restricted to be piecewise constant. It has been shown that the ZOH


10002 [PDF p.189] setting provides an adequate discretization concept for SS representations with static


10003 [PDF p.189] dependence. Extending the approaches of the LTI discretization theory, both exact


10004 [PDF p.189] and approximative methods have been developed in the ZOH setting for the dis-


10005 [PDF p.189] cretization of LPV-SS representations. These approaches have been developed to


10006 [PDF p.189] provide tools that assist DT model structure selection based on first-principle CT


10007 [PDF p.189] models. Using the results of the numerical analysis field, the introduced methods


10008 [PDF p.189] have been investigated in terms of numerical consistency, convergence, and stabil-


10009 [PDF p.189] ity. Criteria have been developed for the choice of sampling-time that guarantees

10025 [PDF p.191] Abstract. With the motivation to provide tools for model-structure selection in LPV


10026 [PDF p.191] identification, in this section modeling of physical systems described by nonlinear


10027 [PDF p.191] differential equations is studied in the LPV framework. It is investigated how such


10028 [PDF p.191] a nonlinear system can be realized or approximated by a LPV system, giving mod-


10029 [PDF p.191] els of the original behavior in terms of LPV representations. First an overview is


10030 [PDF p.191] presented of the available LPV modeling methods. Then, an algorithmic approach


10031 [PDF p.191] is introduced that ensures errorless conversion of nonlinear differential equations


10032 [PDF p.191] into LPV kernel representations. The approach explores adequate choices of the


10033 [PDF p.191] scheduling variable. Based on equivalent sate-space, input-output or orthonormal


10034 [PDF p.191] basis functions based representation of the resulting kernel form, an adequate choice


10035 [PDF p.191] of a model structure can be obtained for the LPV identification of the physical


10036 [PDF p.191] system.


10037 [PDF p.191] 


10038 [PDF p.191] 


10039 [PDF p.191] 7.1     Towards Model Structure Selection


10040 [PDF p.191] 


10041 [PDF p.191] A crucial ingredient of any system identification procedure is the choice of model


10042 [PDF p.191] structure, that describes the model set in which the optimal candidate is to be found.


10043 [PDF p.191] If this structure is well-founded with respect to the system to be identified, then all


10044 [PDF p.191] other ingredients, like experiment design, criterion selection, estimation, etc. can


10045 [PDF p.191] contribute successfully to the validity of the end result. Commonly, a poor choice of


10046 [PDF p.191] the model set directly results in a poor estimate of the system.


10047 [PDF p.191]     LPV models have considerably more freedom in parametrization than the class of


10048 [PDF p.191] LTI models. This is due to the presence of functional and often dynamic dependence


10049 [PDF p.191] of the model parameters on the scheduling. Thus LPV model-structure selection is


10050 [PDF p.191] even a more sensitive question than in the LTI case. Furthermore, due to the lack


10051 [PDF p.191] of a general LPV validation theory, mis-modeled dynamics only show up in the


10052 [PDF p.191] performance loss of the designed controllers.


10053 [PDF p.191]     In LPV identification, initiatives has only recently appeared to assist model-


10054 [PDF p.191] structure selection based on measured data [75, 200]. Commonly, the sole source


10055 [PDF p.191] of information available for this decision is in the form of first principle laws or

10062 [PDF p.192] expert’s knowledge. Such knowledge is mostly presented in terms of nonlinear dif-


10063 [PDF p.192] ferential equations, which must be transformed to or approximated by an LPV rep-


10064 [PDF p.192] resentation to facilitate model structure selection in this setting. In this chapter, the


10065 [PDF p.192] concept of LPV modeling of nonlinear dynamical systems is investigated. The in-


10066 [PDF p.192] tention is to give a practical way of using first principle laws and knowledge in the


10067 [PDF p.192] decision process of LPV model structures, appropriate for the identification of the


10068 [PDF p.192] underlying system. Such a process is inevitable for successful identification in the


10069 [PDF p.192] general LPV framework, as it interprets key information about the order and type of


10070 [PDF p.192] functional dynamical dependencies on the scheduling signal and even about which


10071 [PDF p.192] signal(s) can be used for scheduling purposes.

10074 [PDF p.192] 7.2    General Questions of LPV Modeling


10075 [PDF p.192] Before the first papers on LPV identification methods appeared, modeling of phys-


10076 [PDF p.192] ical systems in a LPV form was dominated by the gain-scheduling principle (see


10077 [PDF p.192] Chap. 1). Motivated by the early approaches of LPV control, the available nonlin-


10078 [PDF p.192] ear (NL) description of the system was linearized in several operating/equilibrium


10079 [PDF p.192] points resulting in a collection of local LTI descriptions of the plant. These “local ”


10080 [PDF p.192] descriptions were interpolated to obtain a global approximation of the physical sys-


10081 [PDF p.192] tem on the entire operation regime. However, unknown coefficients/relations of the


10082 [PDF p.192] NL model still had to be estimated beforehand. This concept has resulted in many


10083 [PDF p.192] linearization-based LPV modeling approaches trying to approximate the NL system


10084 [PDF p.192] in a LPV state-space (SS) form.


10085 [PDF p.192]     For direct approximation of the NL system with an LPV model, LPV identifica-


10086 [PDF p.192] tion methods has appeared soon (see Chap. 1). However, these approaches only aim


10087 [PDF p.192] at the identification of an underlying “true LPV system” with completely known


10088 [PDF p.192] structural information. It has been seemingly forgotten that the true aim has always


10089 [PDF p.192] been the approximation of the NL physical system. Additionally, many of these ap-


10090 [PDF p.192] proaches has followed the gain-scheduling principle by identifying local LTI models


10091 [PDF p.192] and interpolating them.


10092 [PDF p.192]     Due to higher performance demands and the still existing gap between LPV iden-


10093 [PDF p.192] tification methods and practical applications, a new generation of LPV modeling


10094 [PDF p.192] approaches have appeared, formulating LPV modeling from a different perspective


10095 [PDF p.192] than gain-scheduling. These approaches aim at the transformation of the original NL


10096 [PDF p.192] representation into a particular LPV form by using substitution or other mathemat-


10097 [PDF p.192] ical manipulations. However, the resulting methods are only able to handle certain


10098 [PDF p.192] sub-classes of NL systems. So the natural question, what kind of systems can the


10099 [PDF p.192] LPV framework describe accurately, has remained unanswered.


10100 [PDF p.192]     Till today, both the control and identification literature on LPV systems typically


10101 [PDF p.192] takes the existence of the plant in a LPV form as a starting point. It is commonly


10102 [PDF p.192] not pointed out how the underlying nonlinear system is transformed to this LPV


10103 [PDF p.192] form. On the other hand, the available LPV modeling approaches are focusing only


10104 [PDF p.192] on particular subclasses of LPV representations. The question whether a significant


10105 [PDF p.192] loss of generality is introduced by the used assumptions usually remains uninvesti-


10106 [PDF p.192] gated. This shows that LPV modeling of NL systems deserves much more attention


10107 [PDF p.192] 


10108 [PDF p.193] 7.3 Modeling of Nonlinear Systems in the LPV Framework                                173


10109 [PDF p.193] 


10110 [PDF p.193] and research in order to understand what can be represented by LPV systems and


10111 [PDF p.193] how the best description for a given NL system can be found in the LPV system


10112 [PDF p.193] class. This is why we give in this section an overview on the available approaches,


10113 [PDF p.193] comparing and evaluating their modeling concepts.


10114 [PDF p.193]    To set the stage for the upcoming discussion we state the following questions that


10115 [PDF p.193] are intrinsical for the analysis or development of an LPV description with respect to


10116 [PDF p.193] a physical system:


10117 [PDF p.193] • The scheduling variable, that governs the dynamics of LPV models, has a crucial


10118 [PDF p.193]   role in the validity or in the approximation quality of the LPV description. Thus,


10119 [PDF p.193]   in the process of formulating an LPV model, one of the most important ques-


10120 [PDF p.193]   tions is which variables of the original system can be selected as the scheduling


10121 [PDF p.193]   variable in order to obtain an equivalent LPV description.


10122 [PDF p.193] • Another question is whether LPV modeling needs to be formulated in terms of


10123 [PDF p.193]   systems or in terms of particular representations. The latter concept is commonly


10124 [PDF p.193]   used to consider LPV modeling as an approximation of a given state-space equa-


10125 [PDF p.193]   tion, which is a subjective description of the NL system. On the other hand, the


10126 [PDF p.193]   former concept focuses on the approximation/description of the original behav-


10127 [PDF p.193]   ior. Thus formulating modeling on the level of systems provides more freedom


10128 [PDF p.193]   and focuses on the “natural aim” of a modeling problem.


10129 [PDF p.193]    These general considerations are the guidelines by which we explore in the fol-


10130 [PDF p.193] lowing how a a reliable model-transformation approach can be formulated to sup-


10131 [PDF p.193] port both identification and control design in the LPV framework.


10132 [PDF p.193] 


10133 [PDF p.193] 


10134 [PDF p.193] 7.3     Modeling of Nonlinear Systems in the LPV Framework


10135 [PDF p.193] In the following, an overview is presented about the state-of-the-art methods of ap-


10136 [PDF p.193] proximation/equivalent realization of NL systems by an LPV form. Our intention is


10137 [PDF p.193] to give a general picture about the difficulties and the available solutions of this task.


10138 [PDF p.193] To do so, first we define the class of NL systems we consider. These nonlinear sys-


10139 [PDF p.193] tems characterize the first-principle laws of the behavior that we want to capture in


10140 [PDF p.193] the LPV framework. Then we define a particular class of LPV systems, the so-called


10141 [PDF p.193] quasi-LPV systems, that commonly result in the presented modeling approaches. As


10142 [PDF p.193] a next step, we give a SS representation of the introduced NL systems. This repre-


10143 [PDF p.193] sentation is often the starting point of the existing LPV modeling methods. We also


10144 [PDF p.193] motivate that using such a representation as a starting point implies the assumption


10145 [PDF p.193] of prior chosen state variables and IO partition, which might restrict the generality


10146 [PDF p.193] of the resulting LPV description. After this, we systematically present the available


10147 [PDF p.193] approaches, sorted into categories.


10148 [PDF p.193] 


10149 [PDF p.193]

10152 [PDF p.193] restrict our attention in the sequel to this domain. We consider real, finite dimen-


10153 [PDF p.193] sional, continuous-time NL systems in the following form:

10185 [PDF p.194]    In the LPV framework, models commonly originate from nonlinear dynamic sys-


10186 [PDF p.194] tem representations via the gain-scheduling approach. However, linearization of GNL


10187 [PDF p.194] at different operating points in W and then interpolating the resulting LTI models


10188 [PDF p.194] by an operating point dependent function implies that the scheduling signal p of the


10189 [PDF p.194] obtained LPV description is dependent on w. In this way, the fundamental assump-


10190 [PDF p.194] tion of the LPV framework, namely the property of freedom for p does not hold in


10191 [PDF p.194] this case. Therefore, these descriptions are often referred to as quasi-LPV systems


10192 [PDF p.194] (see [102]). In the developed LPV framework, we define these systems as follows:


10193 [PDF p.194] Definition 7.2 (Quasi-LPV system). A PV dynamical system S = (T, P, W, B)


10194 [PDF p.194] with signals w and scheduling variable p is called quasi-LPV, if it satisfies Def-


10195 [PDF p.194] inition 3.3 without p being a free variable, i.e. B p is not a linear subspace


10196 [PDF p.194] of WT .                                                                         


10197 [PDF p.194] Note that if some components of p are free signals, then the system is still consid-


10198 [PDF p.194] ered to be quasi-LPV. During the dawn of the gain-scheduling era, LPV systems


10199 [PDF p.194] have been defined with the concept of exogenous/external and thus free scheduling


10200 [PDF p.194] signal (see [165]), opening the possibility of the later development of popular and


10201 [PDF p.194] theoretically well-founded optimal control solutions for such systems. However in


10202 [PDF p.194] the practical application, this assumption has been commonly neglected, treating


10203 [PDF p.194] LPV models with non-free scheduling signal as if their scheduling signal would be


10204 [PDF p.194] a free variable of the system [17]. Even if such an assumption introduces conser-


10205 [PDF p.194] vatism into the model, and thus the control design applied to it, this masking of


10206 [PDF p.194] the dynamical relation made reliable control of many heavily nonlinear processes

10246 [PDF p.195] The family of these methods applies linearization theory on a given SS representa-


10247 [PDF p.195] tion (7.2a–b) of the NL system to obtain local LTI models in a state-space form and

10251 [PDF p.195] Su ∈ Rn2 ×nU (see Sect. 4.3.5), which select these components, then we can write that


10252 [PDF p.195] p = Col(Sx x, Su u) with nP = n1 + n2. The following subcategories of these methods


10253 [PDF p.195] are distinguished:
