10308 [PDF p.197]     Additionally, it is an important observation that the PV differential equation


10309 [PDF p.197] (7.6a–b) is not an LPV-SS representation as it contains the remainder terms γx


10310 [PDF p.197] and γu . These remainder terms can not be eliminated in general due to their time


10311 [PDF p.197] dependent nature. In many cases, the remainder terms are either considered as an


10312 [PDF p.197] additional input/disturbance in (7.6a–b) or eliminated locally from (7.5a–b) by sub-


10313 [PDF p.197] tracting them from the signal variables (u, y, x), then the locally altered LTI models


10314 [PDF p.197] are interpolated to obtain a global model. While the previous approach leads to a


10315 [PDF p.197] conservative model, the latter method results in an alteration of the state-space as,


10316 [PDF p.197] due to the local transformations, the local states do not have the same meaning any


10317 [PDF p.197] more. This may lead to a complete misfit of the approximation. An exceptional case


10318 [PDF p.197] is when n = 1, so the system is linearized in only one point. In such case no interpo-


10319 [PDF p.197] lation is needed, i.e. g1 = 1. Then by redefining the state as x̆ = x − x1 , the input as


10320 [PDF p.197] ŭ = u − u1, and the output as y̆ = y − g(p1) an LTI-SS approximation of GNL results


10321 [PDF p.197] via (7.6a–b). Proper elimination of the remainder terms is only available in this case.


10322 [PDF p.197]     In the general sense, linearization in the equilibrium points is a serious restriction


10323 [PDF p.197] that may lead to poor transient performance and inability to preserve stability char-


10324 [PDF p.197] acteristics of (7.2a–b). Therefore, an adequate approximation capability requires


10325 [PDF p.197] the assumption of slowly varying scheduling. However, such an assumption is often


10326 [PDF p.197] unrealistic as x and u are not slowly varying signals. To improve the approxima-


10327 [PDF p.197] tion capabilities of this approach many alternative linearization methods have been


10328 [PDF p.197] considered like higher order series-expansion based linearization [14] or the refor-


10329 [PDF p.197] mulation of the mean value theorem [31].


10330 [PDF p.197]     Furthermore, interpolation has its own pitfalls as well. If the local LTI models


10331 [PDF p.197] resulting from the linearization are transformed to a canonical form to accomplish


10332 [PDF p.197] interpolation, then the effect of local transformations can completely alter the be-


10333 [PDF p.197] havior (see [130] for an example). In this way, the resulting LPV representation


10334 [PDF p.197] may not be able to reproduce the dynamical aspects of the original NL form (see


10335 [PDF p.197] Example 7.1 and [189]). Similar errors result if the interpolation is applied through


10336 [PDF p.197] the transfer functions of the local LTI models to get a mixed scheduling and fre-


10337 [PDF p.197] quency dependent description and then applying LTI realization theory to obtain the


10338 [PDF p.197] LPV form (see [125] for an example). In [142], the interpolation problem of the


10339 [PDF p.197] local models is formulated in an optimization sense to reduce the complexity of the


10340 [PDF p.197] resulting dependence of the SS matrices on p. As the procedure avoids any local


10341 [PDF p.197] manipulations of the SS matrices, it provides a reliable way for efficient generation


10342 [PDF p.197] of (7.6a–b).

10383 [PDF p.198] 7.3.2.2   Multiple Linearizations around a Single Equilibrium Point


10384 [PDF p.198] 


10385 [PDF p.198] This approach originates from the Fuzzy control framework, where it is used to


10386 [PDF p.198] obtain linear Takagi-Sugeno (TS) dynamic fuzzy models, which under certain re-


10387 [PDF p.198] strictions can be viewed as quasi-LPV systems [86]. The basic idea is to linearize


10388 [PDF p.198] the NL-SS representation at multiple points of X × U around a single equilibrium


10389 [PDF p.198] point. Then the resulting local models are interpolated in a similar fashion as in the


10390 [PDF p.198] previous part. The method leads to a LPV model that performs well during tran-


10391 [PDF p.198] sient operation, because the framework allows some of the local LTI models to be


10392 [PDF p.198] associated with transient operating regimes. If the system stays close to the used


10393 [PDF p.198] equilibrium point, no restrictions concerning slowly varying trajectories is needed.


10394 [PDF p.198] However, a principal disadvantage is that this approach is not suited for NL models


10395 [PDF p.198] with multiple equilibria.

10398 [PDF p.198] 7.3.2.3   Linearization along a Nominal Trajectory


10399 [PDF p.198] 


10400 [PDF p.198] This approach was introduced in the early 1990s when LPV controllers were typi-


10401 [PDF p.198] cal scheduled in a open-loop sense based on a chosen reference trajectory (intended


10402 [PDF p.198] operation trajectory of the plant) or fixed auxiliary input variables (typical operation


10403 [PDF p.198] trajectories). These user-defined signals were used to describe a nominal trajectory


10404 [PDF p.198] of system operation. Linearizing the NL model along this nominal signal trajec-


10405 [PDF p.198] tory gives an LPV model (see [164, 102] for examples of this approach). It is an


10406 [PDF p.198] advantage of this approach that the resulting LPV description can cover transient


10407 [PDF p.198] operation of the plant along the used nominal trajectory, however such a description


10408 [PDF p.198]

10411 [PDF p.199] also suffers from the drawback that the performance may be poor when the system is


10412 [PDF p.199] operating far away from it. As the time-variation of the system is considered along a


10413 [PDF p.199] pre-chosen trajectory of p, the resulting models resemble a LTV system rather than


10414 [PDF p.199] a LPV system.

10418 [PDF p.199] Linearization of the NL system at points in the state space that may not be equilibria


10419 [PDF p.199] has been considered in numerous approaches (see [76, 102, 121, 122]) The benefit


10420 [PDF p.199] of this concept is that the transient (off-equilibrium) dynamics of the LPV approx-


10421 [PDF p.199] imation may be significantly improved. The LPV model is obtained by selecting a


10422 [PDF p.199] set of linearization points pi = Col(xi , ui ) with (xi , ui ) ∈ X × U, i ∈ IN1 and using


10423 [PDF p.199] Jacobian linearization of the nonlinear functions f and g around these points in the


10424 [PDF p.199] sense of (7.5a–b). The only difference is that in (7.5a) an extra term f (pi ) appears if


10425 [PDF p.199] pi is not an equilibrium point. Then the local models are interpolated as described by


10426 [PDF p.199] (7.6a–b) and the remainder terms are considered as disturbances, extra input chan-


10427 [PDF p.199] nels or they are locally eliminated to form a global LPV model. This approach has


10428 [PDF p.199] the same features as the equilibrium-points-based linearization with all the pitfalls


10429 [PDF p.199] of interpolation and local state transformations. An additional problem rises how-


10430 [PDF p.199] ever from the selection of linearization points {pi }ni=1 . Equidistant selection on the


10431 [PDF p.199] space X × U may seem tempting, but it might happen that due to the dynamical


10432 [PDF p.199] changes of GNL , a non-equidistant selection with dense samples in specific regions


10433 [PDF p.199] of X × U can lead to far better approximations (see [123] for details).

10651 [PDF p.203] Automated model transformation is based on the exploration of all possible ways


10652 [PDF p.203] of reformulating the NL system as a quasi-LPV model with the smallest possible


10653 [PDF p.203] conservatism. Such a technique can also be seen as a substitution method. Recently


10654 [PDF p.203] the approach, introduced in [90], has appeared in this context, formulating the con-


10655 [PDF p.203] version concept in terms of an algorithm.


10656 [PDF p.203]    The proposed procedure starts with the description (7.2a) and by relying on sym-


10657 [PDF p.203] bolic manipulations it assumes the separation of f to irreducible additive terms, i.e.


10658 [PDF p.203] the ith row of f is decomposed as:

10668 [PDF p.203] state as a coefficient αi jk (x, u) = fi j (x, u)/xk in the ith row and kth column of A. As in

10680 [PDF p.204]    By using all assignment possibilities, a set of LPV-SS representations is gener-


10681 [PDF p.204] ated, each corresponding to (7.2a). These representations are tested for complexity


10682 [PDF p.204] and the most adequate LPV description is selected by the user. The exact way of


10683 [PDF p.204] this test and the selection of the most suitable assignment is not formulated in the


10684 [PDF p.204] approach. Thus, these tests remain to the intuition of the user. The same procedure


10685 [PDF p.204] can be executed for the output equation (7.2b) as well. The whole approach depends


10686 [PDF p.204] on how well the simplification of the nonlinear terms can be achieved. As simpli-


10687 [PDF p.204] fication of symbolic terms is not unique in general, the complexity of the resulting


10688 [PDF p.204] model can vary with different symbolic solvers (see [71] for an overview of the re-


10689 [PDF p.204] quired symbolic manipulation techniques). A more serious problem, which has been


10690 [PDF p.204] already mentioned in the linearization part, arises when non-factorizable terms are


10691 [PDF p.204] divided by signal components. Such operations can result in the alteration of the


10692 [PDF p.204] behavior around the origin. It can also happen that no element of u can be lifted out


10693 [PDF p.204] from any summands and thus the generation procedure results in an autonomous


10694 [PDF p.204] quasi-LPV description.


10695 [PDF p.204]    Another technique that falls into this category develops an automated transfor-


10696 [PDF p.204] mation of a nonlinear model to an linear fractional representation (LFR) by using


10697 [PDF p.204] symbolic manipulation techniques (see [71, 211]). A disadvantage of this method,


10698 [PDF p.204] implemented in the LFR toolbox of M ATLAB, is that it assumes the nonlinear model


10699 [PDF p.204] to be in the form (7.11a–b) with also a set of algebraic constraints. In this way it


10700 [PDF p.204] avoids the crucial part of the modeling, namely the generation of the quasi-LPV


10701 [PDF p.204] form (7.11a–b). This technique shows resemblance with other multiple modeling


10702 [PDF p.204] methods and implements a particular way of model reduction with respect to LFRs.


10703 [PDF p.204]    Using the tools offered by the LFR toolbox, the previous approach has been re-


10704 [PDF p.204] cently improved in [46] and [37] by establishing a transformation method between


10705 [PDF p.204] quasi-LPV forms and nonlinear models formulated in the M ODELICA environment


10706 [PDF p.204] as first order differential algebraic equations (DAEs) with uncertain parameters. The


10707 [PDF p.204] transformation is based on triangulization of the DAEs and solving them recursively


10708 [PDF p.204] to obtain a set of system equations. Then uncertain parameters and remaining non-


10709 [PDF p.204] linear terms are extracted to the Δ block to form the scheduling dependency of the


10710 [PDF p.204] resulting description. The latter implies that the original latent variables of the DAEs


10711 [PDF p.204] are forced to be the state variables of the resulting LFR and that there is no control


10712 [PDF p.204] over what is chosen to be the scheduling variable. Despite these problems and some


10713 [PDF p.204] restrictions in the allowed nonlinear relationships between the signals themselves


10714 [PDF p.204] and the uncertain parameters, this approach offers an attractive way of automated


10715 [PDF p.204] model conversion.

10718 [PDF p.205] 


10719 [PDF p.205] 7.3.6    Summary of Existing Techniques


10720 [PDF p.205] In conclusion, the existing techniques for transformation of NL systems to a quasi-


10721 [PDF p.205] LPV form are either based on linearization-based approximation or substitution


10722 [PDF p.205] techniques. Linearization techniques are commonly easily applicable for this pur-


10723 [PDF p.205] pose, but they suffer from serious disadvantages in terms of non-eliminatable affine


10724 [PDF p.205] reminder terms, pitfalls of interpolation, selection of adequate linearization points,


10725 [PDF p.205] and the loss of general representation of the nonlinear dynamics. On the other hand,


10726 [PDF p.205] substitution techniques are based on mathematical manipulations that are only appli-


10727 [PDF p.205] cable for some class of NL systems. Commonly they preserve the original dynamic


10728 [PDF p.205] behavior, however for the general class of NL systems they may result in loss of


10729 [PDF p.205] validity or even stability (e.g. division by signal elements).


10730 [PDF p.205]    A common feature of all approaches is that they use a SS representation of the


10731 [PDF p.205] system as a starting point, thus they try to achieve good approximation with respect


10732 [PDF p.205] to a prior chosen state variable. As a consequence the scheduling variable of the


10733 [PDF p.205] resulting LPV description is composed from the priori chosen state and input vari-


10734 [PDF p.205] ables. This restriction can severely reduce the search-space where an adequate LPV


10735 [PDF p.205] representation of the original NL behavior can be found as rewriting (7.2a–b) to


10736 [PDF p.205] another state-basis may result in a simplified/better transformation to a LPV form.


10737 [PDF p.205]    All of the approaches do not pay attention how the scheduling variable is chosen


10738 [PDF p.205] and what kind of effects a particular choice of p has on the obtained LPV behavior.


10739 [PDF p.205] Seemingly it does not matter that components of x which are inner variables or


10740 [PDF p.205] components of u which are free variables are used for p.


10741 [PDF p.205]    As a general conclusion, existing transformation possibilities to a LPV form are


10742 [PDF p.205] conservative, non-unique, and the validity of the resulting model is based on the skill


10743 [PDF p.205] of the user. On the other hand, to support LPV identification and control of physical


10744 [PDF p.205] systems, the LPV modeling phase must be accomplished carefully, exploring the


10745 [PDF p.205] best possibility of transformation of the first principle laws into an LPV form, with-


10746 [PDF p.205] out ad hoc selection of state signals and scheduling variables. Based on this conclu-


10747 [PDF p.205] sion, in the next section the possibilities to accomplish this task are investigated and


10748 [PDF p.205] a model transformation procedure is proposed, that can tackle this problem using


10749 [PDF p.205] the powerful theoretical framework of the developed LPV behavioral approach.

10751 [PDF p.205] 


10752 [PDF p.205] 7.4     Translation of First Principle Models to LPV Systems


10753 [PDF p.205] 


10754 [PDF p.205] As a next step, a transformation method is investigated that converts first principle


10755 [PDF p.205] laws represented by (7.1) into a LPV kernel (KR) representation. The procedure


10756 [PDF p.205] gives the freedom to consider all possibilities of transformation, not restricted by


10757 [PDF p.205] preselected state or IO partition or particular formulation of the nonlinear dynam-


10758 [PDF p.205] ical relationship like a SS representation. In fact, the method explores all possible


10759 [PDF p.205] transformations that are applicable for general NL dynamical systems, to convert the


10760 [PDF p.205] specific NL behavior into an LPV behavior. Then the obtained LPV-KR representa-


10761 [PDF p.205] tions are categorized by complexity and transformed to an LPV-SS or IO realization


10762 [PDF p.205] based on the equivalence transformation theory of Chap. 3. To assist LPV model


10763 [PDF p.205] 


10764 [PDF p.206] 186                                                  7 LPV Modeling of Physical Systems


10765 [PDF p.206] 


10766 [PDF p.206] structure selection, the discretization theory developed in Chap. 6 is applied to ob-


10767 [PDF p.206] tain DT descriptions of the original behavior.


10768 [PDF p.206]    The developed transformation mechanism is based on similar concepts like the


10769 [PDF p.206] approach of [90], however the proposed method is constructed in a more structured


10770 [PDF p.206] way, where the validity of the transformation is guaranteed in the applied formulas.


10771 [PDF p.206] In the following, a brief outline of the procedure is presented to give insight into


10772 [PDF p.206] the theoretical concept instead of technicalities. First we define the exact problem


10773 [PDF p.206] setting we consider.

10839 [PDF p.207] 7.4.2     The Transformation Algorithm


10840 [PDF p.207] In the following, an algorithm is applied on the simplified differential equation to


10841 [PDF p.207] explore all possibilities of its transformation to an LPV form and in this way to


10842 [PDF p.207] solve Problem 7.1. We follow a similar strategy as the algorithm of [90] but in


10843 [PDF p.207] a different setting. First we separate the rows of f in (7.1) into summands. Then


10844 [PDF p.207] we factorize the nominator of these summands in a specific way to lift out signal


10845 [PDF p.207] variables in a product form. Next we collect all factorization possibilities and their


10846 [PDF p.207] associated coefficients in terms of factors into a decision tree. By selecting a route


10847 [PDF p.207] in the resulting tree we assign elements of w to signals or scheduling variables and


10848 [PDF p.207] use their associated coefficients to form a LPV-KR representation. In the process


10849 [PDF p.207] we assume that all summands are factorizable. This assumption is relaxed later. The


10850 [PDF p.207] proposed algorithm reads as follows:

10965 [PDF p.209]           nals give the simplest models of the NL system. From these candidates,


10966 [PDF p.209]           representations with free scheduling signals have priority. Further distinc-


10967 [PDF p.209]           tion can be the maximal order of derivatives of the leafs. Based on these,


10968 [PDF p.209]           the resulting valid representations can be ordered in terms of complexity,


10969 [PDF p.209]           to assist selection by the user.

10973 [PDF p.209] GNL , the PV behavior can be considered to be equal with the original NL behavior

10975 [PDF p.209] complexity ordering derived in Step 6. In this way, a solution for our transformation


10976 [PDF p.209] problem, i.e. for Problem 7.1 is obtained. Next, the behavioral approach is applied


10977 [PDF p.209] on the chosen representation to obtain a full row rank KR representation together


10978 [PDF p.209] with an SS or IO realization of the resulting LPV system. With the introduced dis-


10979 [PDF p.209] cretization theory, this methodology serves as a model selection tool for DT-LPV


10980 [PDF p.209] identification routines.

11087 [PDF p.211] 7.4.3    Handling Non-Factorizable Terms


11088 [PDF p.211] Now we investigate the case, when not all summand terms { fi j } are factorizable. In


11089 [PDF p.211] that case, there is little chance for the elimination of these terms and to enable the

11229 [PDF p.214] 7.4.4    Properties of the Transformation Procedure


11230 [PDF p.214] It can be concluded that the proposed method can transform a wide class of NL


11231 [PDF p.214] systems satisfying Definition 7.1. An advantage of the method is that it provides


11232 [PDF p.214] a systematic way of conversion, examining all possibilities of an equivalent LPV


11233 [PDF p.214] realization. By checking validity of the derived LPV representation with respect to


11234 [PDF p.214] the behavior of the original NL system, it provides a successful tool to solve Prob-


11235 [PDF p.214] lem 7.1. Additionally, the algorithm gives a structured selection of the scheduling


11236 [PDF p.214] variable p highlighting when not only a quasi-LPV but a true LPV formulation is


11237 [PDF p.214] possible.


11238 [PDF p.214]    However, the approach has disadvantages as well. One of them is the heavy de-


11239 [PDF p.214] pendence on symbolic recognition of summands and possible ways of factorization.


11240 [PDF p.214] Thus the performance of the algorithm is clearly limited by the available symbolic


11241 [PDF p.214] computational tools. Another disadvantage is that investigating all possible LPV-KR


11242 [PDF p.214] representations that can be obtained from the generated decision tree can be quite


11243 [PDF p.214] demanding in case of large signal dimensions or a complicated f . Moreover, in case


11244 [PDF p.214] of large scale systems, computing and comparing the possible IO partitions of the


11245 [PDF p.214] resulting LPV descriptions is hopeless.


11246 [PDF p.214]    It may also happen for some cases that no valid transformation of the NL dy-


11247 [PDF p.214] namic system is available via the proposed algorithm. Commonly, there is little


11248 [PDF p.214] chance of any ad-hoc transformation to succeed if the proposed method does not


11249 [PDF p.214] work as the original system description is minimal and all possibilities are inves-


11250 [PDF p.214] tigated. That means that some sort of approximation technique must be applied in


11251 [PDF p.214] advance. In principle, it must be accepted that not every NL system can be appropri-


11252 [PDF p.214] ately transformed to an LPV form, which is especially true for systems not satisfying


11253 [PDF p.214] Definition 7.1. Examples for such dynamical relations are systems with delays, hys-


11254 [PDF p.214] teresis, or non-functional signal relations like if-then rules. In such cases, the LPV


11255 [PDF p.214] framework may be inappropriate for dealing with the system dynamics without con-


11256 [PDF p.214] siderable approximation.


11257 [PDF p.214]    Comparing the proposed approach of model transformation to the available ap-


11258 [PDF p.214] proaches presented in Sect. 7.3, it can be concluded that this method gives adequate


11259 [PDF p.214] transformation for a much wider class of NL systems. The selection of the schedul-


11260 [PDF p.214] ing variable follows a more structured procedure, without the ad hoc selection of


11261 [PDF p.214] input, output, or latent variables. This gives the flexibility to find the most efficient


11262 [PDF p.214] form of transformation. In case of non-factorizable terms, approximation is inher-


11263 [PDF p.214] ently involved in the transformation, similar to the methods of Sect. 7.3, which result


11264 [PDF p.214] in an approximation of the original behavior up to a specific precision.


11265 [PDF p.214] 


11266 [PDF p.215] 7.5 Conclusions                                                                     195


11267 [PDF p.215] 


11268 [PDF p.215] 7.5    Conclusions


11269 [PDF p.215] In this chapter, modeling of physical systems described by nonlinear differential


11270 [PDF p.215] equations has been studied in the LPV framework. Our motivation has been to derive


11271 [PDF p.215] tools that can assist model structure selection in LPV identification.


11272 [PDF p.215]    First we investigated the general questions of LPV modeling and the available


11273 [PDF p.215] approaches. One of the major conclusions has been that instead of the transforma-


11274 [PDF p.215] tion of a given mathematical description of the NL system to a LPV description,


11275 [PDF p.215] the modeling problem needs to be approached from the perspective of a search for


11276 [PDF p.215] a LPV system with equal behavior. This also implies that there is a prime emphasis


11277 [PDF p.215] on the selection of the scheduling vector, i.e. which variables of the original sys-


11278 [PDF p.215] tem are used as scheduling variables in order to find an equivalent LPV description.


11279 [PDF p.215] The latter gives that the common starting point of the available approaches: the use


11280 [PDF p.215] of a priori chosen state-space representation of the NL system, has the danger that


11281 [PDF p.215] the prespecified state variable can seriously lower the realization possibilities in the


11282 [PDF p.215] LPV system class. Furthermore, it has been shown that for linearization based meth-


11283 [PDF p.215] ods any local transformation of the obtained linearized models can seriously alter


11284 [PDF p.215] the result of their interpolation, i.e. the behavior of the obtained LPV description


11285 [PDF p.215] may not even resemble the original NL system.


11286 [PDF p.215]    By showing the open problems of LPV modeling, in Sect. 7.4 a transformation


11287 [PDF p.215] algorithm has been proposed that aims at the exploration of all possible LPV systems


11288 [PDF p.215] that are equivalent with respect to a given dynamical NL system and selecting that


11289 [PDF p.215] specific description which preserves the original behavior the best. The approach


11290 [PDF p.215] is formulated in terms of conversion of a NL differential equation to a PV form,


11291 [PDF p.215] avoiding the problems related to other conversion tools. The developed technique


11292 [PDF p.215] provides a useful tool to assist the identification methods of the LPV field with


11293 [PDF p.215] structural information about the plant and ease the choice of parametrization of the


11294 [PDF p.215] coefficient dependencies.

11297 [PDF p.216] Optimal Selection of OBFs

11302 [PDF p.216] Abstract. In this chapter, selection of the optimal basis, i.e. the basis with the fastest


11303 [PDF p.216] convergence rate, for the series-expansion of LPV systems is investigated. In fact,


11304 [PDF p.216] we consider the situation when information about the system is only available in


11305 [PDF p.216] terms of measured data records of the frozen signal behavior. Solution of this prob-


11306 [PDF p.216] lem is crucial to provide a model structure selection tool for LPV identification


11307 [PDF p.216] based on truncated series-expansion models. In case of an optimal basis, a fast con-


11308 [PDF p.216] vergence rate of the expansion representation implies that only the estimation of a


11309 [PDF p.216] few expansion coefficients is necessary for a good approximation of the system. By


11310 [PDF p.216] using the concept of Kolmogorov n-width optimality of the basis with respect to the


11311 [PDF p.216] frozen behaviors, we derive a practically applicable algorithm, that provides opti-


11312 [PDF p.216] mal basis selection based on fuzzy clustering of estimated “frozen” poles. The pole


11313 [PDF p.216] estimates are the results of LTI identification of the system with constant scheduling


11314 [PDF p.216] trajectories. To consider the effect of noise on the estimation of the frozen poles, a


11315 [PDF p.216] robust version of the algorithm is also developed using the strong relation between


11316 [PDF p.216] the Kolmogorov n-width theory and hyperbolic geometry.


11317 [PDF p.216] 


11318 [PDF p.216] 


11319 [PDF p.216] 8.1     Perspectives of OBFs Selection


11320 [PDF p.216] The concept of modeling discrete-time asymptotically stable LPV systems with or-


11321 [PDF p.216] thonormal basis functions (OBFs) based truncated series expansions has been in-


11322 [PDF p.216] troduced in Chap. 5 to develop an effective model structure for LPV identification.


11323 [PDF p.216] However, practical application of this concept requires the selection of basis func-


11324 [PDF p.216] tions that guarantees a fast convergence rate of the LPV expansion representation


11325 [PDF p.216] of a system. The reason is that using a truncated expansion with a fast convergence


11326 [PDF p.216] rate, i.e. only a finite number of OBFs from the basis sequence, a model results that


11327 [PDF p.216] approximates the system well with only a few expansion coefficients.


11328 [PDF p.216]    In Sect. 5.5, it has been motivated that to achieve a fast convergence rate of the


11329 [PDF p.216] LPV expansion representation, a necessary condition is to use a basis which has fast


11330 [PDF p.216] convergence rate with respect to FS , the set of transfer functions of the frozen system


11331 [PDF p.216] set for the considered input-output (IO) partition. In order to characterize optimal-


11332 [PDF p.216] ity of the convergence rate with respect to a given transfer function set, like FS , we

11338 [PDF p.217] 


11339 [PDF p.217] have introduced the worst-case concept of the Kolmogorov n-width (KnW) theory in


11340 [PDF p.217] Sect. 2.5. However, to use this concept to choose an n-width optimal basis, it is re-


11341 [PDF p.217] quired to know the pole locations of FS , i.e. the region ΩP , which contains the points


11342 [PDF p.217] where not all transfer functions in FS are analytic. If reliable first-principle knowl-


11343 [PDF p.217] edge is available to calculate ΩP , then by solving the min-max problem of (2.62),


11344 [PDF p.217] optimal basis selection in the KnW sense can be achieved for the system. However,


11345 [PDF p.217] in an identification scenario, such knowledge might not be available. Therefore, if


11346 [PDF p.217] no reliable first-principle information is available about ΩP , selection of the basis


11347 [PDF p.217] has to be based on measured data records of the system. In this chapter, we consider


11348 [PDF p.217] the situation when data records of some frozen behaviors of the LPV system are


11349 [PDF p.217] available. Estimating LTI models based on these data records, result in pole samples


11350 [PDF p.217] of ΩP . Based on these sample poles, we aim at the derivation of a basis selection


11351 [PDF p.217] mechanism, that is capable to accomplish the following objectives:


11352 [PDF p.217] • Reconstruction of ΩP based on the sample pole locations.


11353 [PDF p.217] • Determination of the set of KnW optimal OBFs with respect to ΩP .


11354 [PDF p.217] The method we propose to solve these objectives simultaneously is based on the


11355 [PDF p.217] fusion of the KnW theory and the fuzzy c-means (FcM) clustering approach (see


11356 [PDF p.217] [22, 79]). These theories are applied together to derive KnW optimal basis functions


11357 [PDF p.217] by the clustering of the sample pole locations. The resulting mechanism guarantees


11358 [PDF p.217] optimality in the KnW sense for the obtained basis functions with poles at the cluster


11359 [PDF p.217] centers in case the fuzzyness parameter approaches infinity. In this way it provides


11360 [PDF p.217] a trade-off between the optimality of the chosen basis and the complexity of the


11361 [PDF p.217] optimization.

11364 [PDF p.217] 8.2    Kolmogorov n-Width Optimality in the Frozen Sense


11365 [PDF p.217] As a first step, we investigate the KnW optimality concept of orthonormal basis


11366 [PDF p.217] functions with respect to a LPV system in a frozen sense. To do so we revisit the


11367 [PDF p.217] KnW theory presented in Sect. 2.5 and we highlight properties that are important


11368 [PDF p.217] for the discussion of the basis selection mechanism. As the presented KnW theory


11369 [PDF p.217] is formulated in the SISO case, we restrict the discussion to SISO asymptotically


11370 [PDF p.217] stable LPV systems in the following. The basis selection problem for MIMO LPV


11371 [PDF p.217] systems is postponed till Chap. 9.

11373 [PDF p.217] set FS for a given IO partition of the LPV system S. In Sect. 2.5 it has been al-

11375 [PDF p.217] function Gb ∈ H2− (E), such that the Hambo basis sequence Φn∞g generated by Gb

11377 [PDF p.217] transfer function set. This optimality means that among all Hambo bases, the linear


11378 [PDF p.217] combination of the set of ng (ne + 1) functions Φnnge has the smallest worst-case rep-


11379 [PDF p.217] resentation error (in the H2 norm). In this sense, optimality means also the fastest

11381 [PDF p.217] basis sequence Φn∞g . In other words, a KnW optimal basis for FS provides series-

11523 [PDF p.220] 8.3     The Fuzzy-Kolmogorov c-Max Clustering Approach


11524 [PDF p.220] In the following we introduce a particular data clustering algorithm, proposed in


11525 [PDF p.220] [196], which is the extension of the fuzzy c-means (FcM) clustering approach used


11526 [PDF p.220] in a wide collection of applications like pattern recognition, data analysis, image


11527 [PDF p.220] processing and fuzzy modeling (see [22, 79]). As we will show, the proposed ap-


11528 [PDF p.220] proach is able to effectively handle the reconstruction problem of ΩP jointly with


11529 [PDF p.220] the solution of (8.4). First, in section 8.3.1, we formulate the exact problem setting


11530 [PDF p.220] for the clustering approach to interpret our basis selection goal. Then we charac-


11531 [PDF p.220] terize the optimal solution of the clustering problem and introduce the extension of


11532 [PDF p.220] the FcM algorithm. As a next step, in Sect. 8.3.2, we show how the derived optimal


11533 [PDF p.220] solution provides an answer for the original basis selection problem of Sect. 8.2.


11534 [PDF p.220] Numerical properties of the derived algorithm are investigated together with practi-


11535 [PDF p.220] cal aspects, like the use of adaptive cluster merging (ACM) in this setting. At last,


11536 [PDF p.220] a simulation example is presented to show the effectiveness of the introduced basis


11537 [PDF p.220] selection mechanism.


11538 [PDF p.220]

11540 [PDF p.220] 8.3.1    The Pole Clustering Algorithm


11541 [PDF p.220] Objective-function-based fuzzy clustering algorithms, such as FcM, partitions the


11542 [PDF p.220] data into overlapping groups, so-called clusters, where each data element is asso-


11543 [PDF p.220] ciated with a set of membership levels with respect to these clusters. These levels


11544 [PDF p.220] indicate the strength of the association between that data element and a particular


11545 [PDF p.220] cluster. In this way, fuzzy clustering is a process of assigning these membership lev-


11546 [PDF p.220] els such that the resulting clusters describe the underlying structure within the data


11547 [PDF p.220] [79]. This enables the determination of the region ΩP on the basis of the observed


11548 [PDF p.220] poles by exploring the underlying data coherency.


11549 [PDF p.220]    Let nc > 1 be the number of clusters (pole regions) to be used to reconstruct ΩP .


11550 [PDF p.220] Note that due to the uniform frozen asymptotic stability of FS , it is guaranteed that


11551 [PDF p.220] ΩP ⊆ D, i.e. all sample poles zk are in the unit disc D. Thus, let D be the clustering


11552 [PDF p.220] space and let Z = {zk }Nk=1


11553 [PDF p.220]                           z


11554 [PDF p.220]                              ⊂ D, be the set of observed poles for clustering. In fuzzy


11555 [PDF p.220] clustering, a cluster is defined by two ingredients: a center (or prototype) υi ∈ D,


11556 [PDF p.220] i ∈ In1c and a membership function μi : D → [0, 1]. While the former defines the


11557 [PDF p.220] central point, the latter describes the “degree of membership” to the cluster for all


11558 [PDF p.220] z ∈ D. Note that the shapes of fuzzy clusters are not described by hard borders but


11559 [PDF p.220] by the commonly bell-like shape of the membership functions on D. Introduce also

11806 [PDF p.224] (see (8.1)) is with respect to Z. In practice, uniformly random choices for V0 are


11807 [PDF p.224] suggested. Initial partitions based on the distribution of Z can also be used (V0 cho-


11808 [PDF p.224] sen as random elements of Z, V0 is given as the points of a circle around the mean


11809 [PDF p.224] of Z, etc.) however they limit the possibilities to explore all local minima, while


11810 [PDF p.224] random initialization based on a uniform distribution gives equal probability.


11811 [PDF p.224]    In the rare case of singularity of the resulting partition (some dik = 0), Th. 8.2


11812 [PDF p.224] does not hold. Such a phenomenon can only happen in extreme situations when for


11813 [PDF p.224] example nc ≈ Nz . In that case, an optimal partition can contain some clusters whose


11814 [PDF p.224] cluster center is equal to sample pole locations. Singularity of the partition can also


11815 [PDF p.224] result if the samples of ΩP do not describe any data coherency, suggesting that ΩP

11825 [PDF p.225] is not a region but a finite set of isolated points. In such cases, the best solution in


11826 [PDF p.225] the KnW sense is to assign a dedicated OBF with respect to some sampled poles.


11827 [PDF p.225] However, when ΩP is a region, this solution should be avoided, as the reconstruction


11828 [PDF p.225] of ΩP based on the pole samples is required before choosing the basis functions.


11829 [PDF p.225] Thus, to assist the validity of the reconstruction, nc must be chosen a priori such


11830 [PDF p.225] that it correctly describes the separated pole regions of ΩP . This can be achieved


11831 [PDF p.225] by visual inspection of the sampled poles, by trial-and-error or by using automated


11832 [PDF p.225] selection (see Sect. 8.3.2.4).

11834 [PDF p.225] 8.3.2.2   Optimization and Numerical Conditioning


11835 [PDF p.225] 


11836 [PDF p.225] While Step 3 in Algorithm 8.1, i.e. the membership update, can be analytically


11837 [PDF p.225] computed through (8.11a), Step 4, i.e. the cluster center update, requires the so-


11838 [PDF p.225] lution of (8.11b). The optimization defined by (8.11b) is a minimization problem


11839 [PDF p.225] with quadratic constraints (QC)s, where γ is the optimization variable and ν is the


11840 [PDF p.225] decision variable. Based on [162], it is possible to derive sum-of-squares (SoS) re-


11841 [PDF p.225] laxations of such constraints, through which (8.10) is turned into a linear matrix in-


11842 [PDF p.225] equality (LMI). The resulting convex minimization of γ , based on these constrains,


11843 [PDF p.225] is a linear semi definite programming (LSDP) problem that can be efficiently solved


11844 [PDF p.225] by a variety of (interior-point-based) solvers like SeDuMi [183] or CSDP etc. Al-


11845 [PDF p.225] ternatively, bisection-based recursive search (see [8]) can also be used to obtain the


11846 [PDF p.225] minimization of {γi } with respect to (8.10). In each step of this bisection-based


11847 [PDF p.225] minimization, every QCs with a fixed τ is rewritten as a LMI constraint. Checking


11848 [PDF p.225] feasibility of the constraints indicates how to proceed with the minimization of γi


11849 [PDF p.225] (see [193] for the details).


11850 [PDF p.225]     For high values of m, the QCs (8.10) become numerically ill-conditioned, which

11859 [PDF p.225] 8.3.2.3   Termination Criterion


11860 [PDF p.225] 


11861 [PDF p.225] In Algorithm 8.1, the cost function Jm “flattens” when m increases. This yields that


11862 [PDF p.225] for high values of m, Jm is almost constant for all points of UnNcz × Dnc except in the


11863 [PDF p.225] close neighborhood of its local minima where its value decreases quickly. To avoid


11864 [PDF p.225] unnecessary termination of the algorithm on the flat surface of the cost function, the


11865 [PDF p.225] relative evolution of Jm , in each iteration step l, has to be checked in a windowed


11866 [PDF p.225] sense:

11868 [PDF p.225]                    1−                                          < εt                (8.14)

11874 [PDF p.226] termination constant. If in step l (8.14) is satisfied, then the relative evolution of Jm


11875 [PDF p.226] has been small in the considered window, so the optimization is terminated. Expe-


11876 [PDF p.226] rience has shown, that for m ∈ [5, 10], the threshold εt = 0.99 with n = 3 usually


11877 [PDF p.226] works well.

11879 [PDF p.226] 8.3.2.4   Cluster Merging


11880 [PDF p.226] 


11881 [PDF p.226] The determination of the number of “natural” pole groups in Z, i.e. the best suitable


11882 [PDF p.226] nc for clustering, is important for the successful application of the FKcM method.


11883 [PDF p.226] Similarity-based adaptive cluster merging (ACM) can be effectively used for this


11884 [PDF p.226] purpose [196]. The basic idea of ACM is the following: a measure of similarity is


11885 [PDF p.226] introduced with respect to cluster pairs. Then, in each iteration step of Algorithm


11886 [PDF p.226] 8.1, a cluster pair is merged when its similarity between iterations changes negli-


11887 [PDF p.226] gibly (characterized with a threshold εs ∈ [0, 1]) and if also this pair is the most


11888 [PDF p.226] similar of all cluster pairs. However, merging is only applied if the similarity mea-


11889 [PDF p.226] sure exceeds a certain threshold value, εa ∈ [0, 1]. In FcM clustering, commonly the


11890 [PDF p.226] so-called inclusion similarity measure is applied (see [83]) and εa is taken as an


11891 [PDF p.226] adaptive threshold εa = (nc − 1)−1 , where εa is the value of the threshold and


11892 [PDF p.226]                        (l)     (l)                 (l)


11893 [PDF p.226]   (l)


11894 [PDF p.226] nc the remaining number of clusters in iteration l. In [83] this adaptive threshold


11895 [PDF p.226]                                                                                      (0)


11896 [PDF p.226] has been observed empirically to work well if the initial number of clusters nc


11897 [PDF p.226]             (0)


11898 [PDF p.226] satisfies: nc < 12 Nz .


11899 [PDF p.226]     In [196] it has been shown that starting from a large nc , the use of the ACM strat-


11900 [PDF p.226] egy in the FKcM algorithm gives the possibility to “adequately”choose the number


11901 [PDF p.226] of clusters to describe the region ΩP , associated with the samples Z. In the consid-


11902 [PDF p.226] ered problem setting, adequateness means that for the reconstructed region Ωε , in


11903 [PDF p.226] which width sense we search for KnW optimal OBFs, where the basis functions are


11904 [PDF p.226] associated with the cluster centers. If the available information, the sampling of ΩP ,


11905 [PDF p.226] is dense, then in the optimal solution of Problem 8.1: Ωε ≈ ΩP . This implies that


11906 [PDF p.226] the ACM provides an effective choice of the width, i.e. the value of n in which the


11907 [PDF p.226] KnW basis is searched for ΩP with the proposed algorithm. However in terms of


11908 [PDF p.226] Proposition 2.1, the setting of Problem (8.1) implies that repetitive basis poles can


11909 [PDF p.226] also be part of the optimal solution. With ACM, these solutions are not accessible as


11910 [PDF p.226] repetitive poles result in perfectly similar clusters which are immediately joined. As


11911 [PDF p.226] a result, the ACM only yields convergence to partitions with distinct cluster centers.


11912 [PDF p.226] This means that the choice of the adequate width in the KnW sense is restricted such


11913 [PDF p.226] that the optimal basis poles for the adequate width must be distinct.

12076 [PDF p.229] • The values of Nav , which are based on the results of 10 runs starting from random

12259 [PDF p.233] 8.4     Robust Extension of the FKcM Approach


12260 [PDF p.233] During the development of the FKcM approach, we have assumed that some sam-


12261 [PDF p.233] ples of ΩP are given. These samples have been used as a data set, i.e. a source


12262 [PDF p.233] of information on which the developed basis selection tool is based on. We have


12263 [PDF p.233] motivated that such samples are available in practice either based on first principle


12264 [PDF p.233] information or as the poles of model estimates of the frozen system set FS . These


12265 [PDF p.233] model estimates are considered to be the result of LTI identification of the LPV sys-


12266 [PDF p.233] tem with constant scheduling signals. However, system identification is in practice


12267 [PDF p.233] always affected by noise, thus the pole locations of the estimated models are the re-


12268 [PDF p.233] alizations of an underlying probability function of the frozen poles. This means that


12269 [PDF p.233] selecting basis functions, based on estimated poles, carries the risk that the result of


12270 [PDF p.233] the basis selection by the FKcM method is significantly effected by the noise. In this


12271 [PDF p.233] section, we aim to provide a robust solution of the previously considered basis se-


12272 [PDF p.233] lection problem by reformulating the developed FKcM approach, such that it takes


12273 [PDF p.233] into account the uncertainty of the pole estimates.


12274 [PDF p.233] 


12275 [PDF p.233] 


12276 [PDF p.233] 8.4.1    Questions of Robustness


12277 [PDF p.233] In prediction-error identification, each estimated pole can be associated with an un-


12278 [PDF p.233] certainty region in the complex plain for a certain level of confidence. In the classical


12279 [PDF p.233] literature, ellipsoidal regions are quantified that are the results of the linearization


12280 [PDF p.233] of the map from parameters θ to pole locations {λ }. In Sect. 2.4.6, an alternative


12281 [PDF p.233] approach of [223] has been introduced that characterizes pole uncertainty regions


12282 [PDF p.233] of the model estimates without linearization. The approach leads to a (possibly dis-


12283 [PDF p.233] connected) uncertainty region P(Qθ , α ) ⊂ C for which it holds that


12284 [PDF p.233] 


12285 [PDF p.233]                     λ̂1 , . . . , λ̂n ∈ P(Qθ , α ),   with probability ≥ α            (8.18)


12286 [PDF p.233] 


12287 [PDF p.233] where {λ̂1 , . . . , λ̂n } are the poles of the model estimate. Note that this uncertainty


12288 [PDF p.233] concept is still necessarily conservative as it disregards covariance of the pole es-


12289 [PDF p.233] timates. However, later it will be shown that the locations of the possible pole es-


12290 [PDF p.233] timates, i.e. possible poles of a transfer function set, are formulated in the same


12291 [PDF p.233] worst-case sense as the KnW theory. Based on this, it is clear that by using the un-


12292 [PDF p.233] certainty regions provided by this approach as data objects in both the reconstruction


12293 [PDF p.233] problem of ΩP and the KnW optimization problem, the basis selection task can be


12294 [PDF p.233] solved in a robust sense.


12295 [PDF p.233]    In the original problem of FKcM clustering, the samples of ΩP form a finite


12296 [PDF p.233] set of points Z in D. Because of the fact that Z is finite, both the reconstruction


12297 [PDF p.233] problem and the minimization of (8.4) can be analytically computed and solved via


12298 [PDF p.233] the proposed algorithm. However, if Z is not a finite set but a collection of complex


12299 [PDF p.233] regions, i.e. uncertainty sets, it is not trivial how to calculate ρ in (8.4) with respect


12300 [PDF p.233] to these regions or how to obtain the worst-case KM distance used in the FKcM


12301 [PDF p.233] algorithm as the dissimilarity measure dik . Subsequently the problem rises how to


12302 [PDF p.233] solve the selection problem of the OBFs poles by using the FKcM mechanism.


12303 [PDF p.233] 


12304 [PDF p.234] 8.4 Robust Extension of the FKcM Approach                                          215


12305 [PDF p.234] 


12306 [PDF p.234]    To provide answers for these questions, in Sect. 8.4.2 we first show that by using


12307 [PDF p.234] results of hyperbolic geometry, (8.3) and its 1-width version, the so-called Kol-


12308 [PDF p.234] mogorov measure, can be analytically computed if the regions in Z are hyperbolic


12309 [PDF p.234] circles or hyperbolic segments. However, shapes of uncertainty regions can vary ar-


12310 [PDF p.234] bitrary, thus to use the developed hyperbolic results, the regions must be covered by


12311 [PDF p.234] a collection of hyperbolic circles or hyperbolic segments. In Sect. 8.4.2 a practically


12312 [PDF p.234] applicable multistep procedure is developed that covers complex regions with the


12313 [PDF p.234] union of hyperbolic circles. In this way the KnW optimization problem (8.4) and


12314 [PDF p.234] also the reconstruction problem of ΩP by the clustering of pole uncertainty regions


12315 [PDF p.234] can be solved along a similar line of reasoning as in Sect. 8.3. This robust extension


12316 [PDF p.234] of the FKcM clustering is developed in Sect. 8.4.4 and its properties are investigated


12317 [PDF p.234] again in terms of optimality of the solution, numerical convergence, etc. It is shown


12318 [PDF p.234] that the resulting algorithm provides the selection of asymptotically optimal OBFs


12319 [PDF p.234] in the KnW sense for the local behaviors of S even in case of significant measure-


12320 [PDF p.234] ment noise. This property is also illustrated through an example.

12323 [PDF p.234] 8.4.2    Basic Concepts of Hyperbolic Geometry


12324 [PDF p.234] In order to develop the required geometrical tools, the basic aspects of the 2-


12325 [PDF p.234] dimensional Poincaré disc model of hyperbolic geometry are introduced in the se-


12326 [PDF p.234] quel. It is also shown how hyperbolic geometry can be used to generalize the results


12327 [PDF p.234] of the KnW theory.


12328 [PDF p.234]    The 2-dimensional Poincaré model provides a conformal disc model, where


12329 [PDF p.234] points of the geometry are in a complex disc. The lines are segments of circles


12330 [PDF p.234] that lie inside the disc, where the circles themselves are orthogonal to the boundary


12331 [PDF p.234] of the disc, or the segments are part of a diameter of the disc (see Fig. 8.6). Be-


12332 [PDF p.234] fore defining these objects, it is motivated why this geometric model has important


12333 [PDF p.234] relations to the KnW theory.


12334 [PDF p.234]    We have already discussed that the Kolmogorov measure (see Definition 8.1) is


12335 [PDF p.234] equal to the cost function of the 1-width Kolmogorov problem (ng = 1) (see (8.3)).


12336 [PDF p.234] Based on this property, the KM had an important role as a dissimilarity measure in


12337 [PDF p.234] the FKcM algorithm to formulate KnW optimality of the obtained solution in an


12338 [PDF p.234] asymptotic sense. Additionally, this observation has an important consequence for


12339 [PDF p.234] geometrical objects in D which are convex in terms of the KM. Namely, that in the


12340 [PDF p.234] ng = 1 case, the solution of (8.4) with respect to regions equivalent with these ob-


12341 [PDF p.234] jects can be found through LMI’s based optimization. We will see that this property


12342 [PDF p.234] provides an efficient way to solve the heavy nonlinear optimization problem that


12343 [PDF p.234] (8.4) represents and is also the key ingredient to handle the robust basis selection


12344 [PDF p.234] problem. In the following, we first introduce some simple convex objects in the KM


12345 [PDF p.234] sense and additional geometrical tools that are required in the second part to develop


12346 [PDF p.234] three key results for the above mentioned property.

12348 [PDF p.234] hyperbolic lines which are introduced through the concept of i-lines (see Fig. 8.6.a)


12349 [PDF p.234] and their orthogonality in C:

12560 [PDF p.239] 8.4.3     Pole Uncertainty Regions as Hyperbolic Objects


12561 [PDF p.239] In the robust basis selection problem the results of hyperbolic geometry will be ap-


12562 [PDF p.239] plied on pole uncertainty regions. However, the pole uncertainty regions of Sect.


12563 [PDF p.239] 2.4.6 do not necessary coincide with hyperbolic objects. Thus, it is required to ap-


12564 [PDF p.239] proximate these regions by a coverage of hyperbolic objects in order to apply the


12565 [PDF p.239] developed results. In the following, a simple pragmatic procedure for this approxi-


12566 [PDF p.239] mation is briefly explained.


12567 [PDF p.239]      In principle it is true that, if an identified transfer function G(q, θ̂Nd ) has a real


12568 [PDF p.239] valued pole, then the pole-uncertainty region P(Qθ , α ) of G(q, θ̂Nd ) (for a given con-


12569 [PDF p.239] fidence level α ) contains segments of the real axis. Therefore, these segment parts


12570 [PDF p.239] of P(Qθ , α ) can be associated with h-segments without the need of any approxi-


12571 [PDF p.239] mation. In case G(q, θ̂Nd ) has a complex pole pair, then P(Qθ , α ) contains complex


12572 [PDF p.239] regions which come in complex conjugate pairs. Depending on the uncertainty of


12573 [PDF p.239] the model estimate, these complex regions can merge into one another, and can also


12574 [PDF p.239] encircle parts of D which seemingly do not contain any of the estimated or original


12575 [PDF p.239] pole locations (see Sect. 2.4.6). Thus complex pole uncertainty regions can occur in


12576 [PDF p.239] complicated shapes. However, with a simple methodology, quite effective coverage


12577 [PDF p.239] of such shapes can be achieved by h-discs.


12578 [PDF p.239]      Let Ω be a separate, complex region in P(Qθ , α ). Due to the method of [198], the


12579 [PDF p.239] separated regions are distinguished during the calculation of P(Qθ , α ). Assume that


12580 [PDF p.239] an equidistant gridding of D is given with step size τ ∈ R+ and the set of grid points


12581 [PDF p.239] is denoted by Q. Let Q+ = Ω ∩ Q be the grid points in Ω and let Q− = Q \ Q+ .


12582 [PDF p.239] Next, define D0 as a collection of√equidistant Euclidian discs with centers at each


12583 [PDF p.239] points of Q+ and with radii r = 22 τ . In this way, a coverage of Ω is obtained by


12584 [PDF p.239] an unnecessary large number of Euclidian discs determining uniquely their h-disc


12585 [PDF p.239] counterparts. This is used as the initialization of the iterative optimization procedure


12586 [PDF p.239] of Algorithm 8.2 to find an efficient disc-coverage based on a fixed number of n discs


12587 [PDF p.239] with unequal radii.

12589 [PDF p.239] furthest from the points of Q− and its radii can be increased by 22 τ , without


12590 [PDF p.239] causing the discs to contain any point of Q− . In case of a tie, an arbitrary disc is

12824 [PDF p.243] 8.4.5     Properties of the Robust FKcM


12825 [PDF p.243] As a next step we investigate the properties of the robust extension of the FKcM


12826 [PDF p.243] algorithm. It is shown that KnW optimality of the resulting cluster centers (if the


12827 [PDF p.243] solution is the global minima of (8.28)) holds again in an asymptotic sense (m → ∞).


12828 [PDF p.243] Practical implementation of the algorithm is also discussed together with how the


12829 [PDF p.243] conservatism of the used pole uncertainty concept influences the procedure.

12905 [PDF p.244] In order to derive an algorithmic solution of Problem 8.2 in terms of Th. 8.8, it is


12906 [PDF p.244] important to define the regions Zk as inequality constrains. Such form would enable


12907 [PDF p.244] to use (8.29) as a quadratic constraint and apply the same LMIs based optimization


12908 [PDF p.244] as in the FKcM case. Using the hyperbolic geometry, each uncertainty region can


12909 [PDF p.244] be represented in the following way:


12910 [PDF p.244] • If Zk is an h-segment then for z ∈ Zk it holds that

12919 [PDF p.244] 


12920 [PDF p.244] As the resulting descriptions define an inequality (see 8.34) or a set of quadratic con-


12921 [PDF p.244] straints (see 8.35) thus (8.30b) is equivalent with a minimization problem with QCs


12922 [PDF p.244] where γ is the optimization variable and ν is the decision variable. As the structure


12923 [PDF p.244] of these constraints is similar as in the non-robust case, it is possible to derive SoS


12924 [PDF p.244] relaxations through which (8.29) and (8.34) turn into LMIs. The resulting LSDP can


12925 [PDF p.244] be efficiently solved by LMI solvers. Alternatively, bisection-based recursive search


12926 [PDF p.244] can be used to obtain the minimization of γi in (8.30b). Also numerical conditioning


12927 [PDF p.244] of Ul can relax the computational need of the LMI’s based optimization and the ter-


12928 [PDF p.244] mination criterion of the overall algorithm can be established similar to the original


12929 [PDF p.244] FKcM method. For details on these items see Sect. 8.3.2. Similarity-based ACM


12930 [PDF p.244] (see Sect. 8.3.2.4) can also be used for the determination of the number of “natural”


12931 [PDF p.244] groups in Z, i.e. the best suitable nc for clustering, which is also important for the


12932 [PDF p.244] successful application of the robust FKcM method.

12934 [PDF p.244] 8.4.5.3   Conservatism of the Pole Uncertainty Concept


12935 [PDF p.244] 


12936 [PDF p.244] The approach of calculating pole uncertainty regions, presented in Sect. 2.4.6,


12937 [PDF p.244] projects ellipsoidal uncertainty regions of parameter estimates to regions in the com-


12938 [PDF p.244] plex plane. It has been already explained in Sect. 2.4.6 that these regions represent


12939 [PDF p.244] the set of possible pole locations of the model with respect to the parameter uncer-


12940 [PDF p.244] tainties with the given confidence level. However, the covariance of the poles, i.e.


12941 [PDF p.244] which poles occur together in the model estimate with the given confidence level,


12942 [PDF p.244] is disregarded in this representation. Thus, the projection is inherently conservative


12943 [PDF p.244] as for a pole uncertainty region P of a 5th order LTI model it is not guaranteed that


12944 [PDF p.244] for any 5 arbitrary chosen points {λ1 , . . . , λ5 } in P there exists a parameter vec-


12945 [PDF p.244] tor θ in the ellipsoidal parameter uncertainty region such that the model associated


12946 [PDF p.244] with θ has poles {λ1 , . . . , λ5 }. In other words, neglecting the covariance between


12947 [PDF p.244] the pole estimates introduces conservatism. However, it is true that for any point


12948 [PDF p.244] in P it is guaranteed that there exist 4 other points in P, such that these 5 points


12949 [PDF p.244] 


12950 [PDF p.245] 226                                                          8 Optimal Selection of OBFs


12951 [PDF p.245] 


12952 [PDF p.245] correspond to the pole locations of a model whose parameters are in the ellipsoidal


12953 [PDF p.245] parameter uncertainty region. This means that the pole uncertainty regions obtained


12954 [PDF p.245] by this method contain all possible, including the worst-case pole locations that


12955 [PDF p.245] can occur due to the uncertainty of the obtained model. However, such worst-case


12956 [PDF p.245] conservatism completely matches the worst-case concept of the KnW theory (see


12957 [PDF p.245] Sect. 2.5). Thus the conservatism of the projection does not affect the basis selec-


12958 [PDF p.245] tion mechanism. This is an important observation which underlines the validity of


12959 [PDF p.245] the presented approach.

12962 [PDF p.245] 8.4.6     Simulation Example


12963 [PDF p.245] In the following an example is given to visualize the applicability of the robust basis


12964 [PDF p.245] selection mechanism and to enable comparison with the original FKcM method.


12965 [PDF p.245] In this example it is shown that disregarding pole uncertainties during the basis


12966 [PDF p.245] selection process can result in a lower worst-case convergence rate of the obtained


12967 [PDF p.245] basis functions.


12968 [PDF p.245] 


12969 [PDF p.245] 8.4.6.1   Data Generation


12970 [PDF p.245] 


12971 [PDF p.245] Consider again the asymptotically stable SISO LPV system S given by the LPV-IO


12972 [PDF p.245] representation (8.17). By using constant scheduling signals with values {0.6; 0.6 +


12973 [PDF p.245] τ ; . . . ; 0.8}, where τ = 0.04, 6 local LTI-IO representations of S are obtained,


12974 [PDF p.245] whose pole locations are samples of ΩP (see Fig. 8.2a). We use fewer constant


12975 [PDF p.245] scheduling points in this case than before, to make the results and the figures more


12976 [PDF p.245] transparent. The LTI models, associated with constant scheduling signals, in this


12977 [PDF p.245] example are estimated. The identification of each frozen model has been based on


12978 [PDF p.245] a OE parametrization and 250 samples long measured IO signals of the system.


12979 [PDF p.245] The measurements contained additive white output noise ε with normal distribution


12980 [PDF p.245] N (0, 0.1) and a white input signal u with uniform distribution U(−1, 1). Using the


12981 [PDF p.245] pole uncertainty concept of Sect. 2.4.6, the pole uncertainty regions {Pi }6i=1 of the


12982 [PDF p.245] estimated models have been calculated with confidence level α = 99%. The result-


12983 [PDF p.245] ing uncertainty regions consist of Nz = 6 · 5 complex regions {Ωk }Nk=1      z


12984 [PDF p.245]                                                                                 which are


12985 [PDF p.245] presented in Figures 8.9a–b. In Fig. 8.9a, the estimated frozen poles are denoted by


12986 [PDF p.245] ◦ with a color indicating the constant scheduling trajectory they are associated with


12987 [PDF p.245] (deep red p1 = 0.6 ↔ yellow p6 = 0.8). The perimeter lines of the pole uncertainty


12988 [PDF p.245] regions are given in Fig. 8.9b with a color indicating which poles they are associated


12989 [PDF p.245] with. Based on these figures, the resulting uncertainty regions are relatively large,


12990 [PDF p.245] prognosticating that using only the estimated poles by the non-robust algorithm can


12991 [PDF p.245] result in a serious performance degradation of the obtained solution. In order to de-


12992 [PDF p.245] rive an OBF set for S based on the robust FKcM mechanism, a hyperbolic coverage


12993 [PDF p.245] {Zk }Nk=1   z

13300 [PDF p.250] 8.5    Conclusions


13301 [PDF p.250] In this chapter, optimal basis selection for series expansion of LPV systems has been


13302 [PDF p.250] investigated in the case when only measured data records of the frozen signal behav-


13303 [PDF p.250] ior are available. The solution of this problem is crucial to provide a practical model


13304 [PDF p.250] structure selection tool for LPV identification based on truncated series-expansion


13305 [PDF p.250] models. In case of an optimal basis, a fast convergence rate of the expansion rep-


13306 [PDF p.250] resentation implies that only the estimation of a few coefficients is necessary for a


13307 [PDF p.250] good approximation of the system.


13308 [PDF p.250]    A crucial conclusion that we could draw is that a practically applicable and ef-


13309 [PDF p.250] fective basis selection can be formulated based on estimated pole locations of the


13310 [PDF p.250] system with respect to constant scheduling trajectories. By reconstruction of the


13311 [PDF p.250] pole manifest set of the system based on these sample pole locations and finding


13312 [PDF p.250] the KnW optimal basis with respect to the reconstructed regions adequate selection


13313 [PDF p.250] of the basis follows. We could see that both of these tasks can be efficiently solved


13314 [PDF p.250] in one step by using a modified fuzzy clustering approach. This approach is also


13315 [PDF p.250] applicable in situations where the measurement noise has a significant effect on the


13316 [PDF p.250] sample pole estimates, as by the use of hyperbolic geometry the basis selection al-


13317 [PDF p.250] gorithm can be robustified with respect to pole uncertainty regions. In conclusion


13318 [PDF p.250] the algorithms, developed in this chapter, provide effective tools for model structure


13319 [PDF p.250] selection in terms of LPV truncated series-expansion models. In the next chapter


13320 [PDF p.250] we will see how all tools developed so far, enable the identification of LPV systems


13321 [PDF p.250] through a simple and effective approach.


13322 [PDF p.250] 


13323 [PDF p.251] Chapter 9


13324 [PDF p.251] LPV Identification via OBFs


13325 [PDF p.251] 


13326 [PDF p.251] 


13327 [PDF p.251] 


13328 [PDF p.251] 


13329 [PDF p.251] Abstract. All the theory that has been introduced so far has served the sole purpose


13330 [PDF p.251] of providing tools to formulate identification of general LPV systems in a well-


13331 [PDF p.251] established manner. Building on the developed tools, a widely applicable identifi-


13332 [PDF p.251] cation approach is proposed in this chapter by using model structures that originate


13333 [PDF p.251] from truncated OBF expansion representations of LPV systems. First, under the


13334 [PDF p.251] assumption of static dependence of the expansion coefficients, two identification


13335 [PDF p.251] methods, a local and global one, are developed for the introduced model structures.


13336 [PDF p.251] While the local approach uses the gain-scheduling principle: identification with con-


13337 [PDF p.251] stant scheduling signals and interpolation of the resulting LTI models, the global


13338 [PDF p.251] approach provides a direct LPV model estimate via linear regression based on data


13339 [PDF p.251] records with varying scheduling trajectories. The approaches are analyzed in terms


13340 [PDF p.251] of variance, bias, consistency, and applicability together with the validation of the


13341 [PDF p.251] model estimates. Finally, to enable the estimation of modes with dynamic coeffi-


13342 [PDF p.251] cient dependencies, a modified feedback-based OBF model structure is proposed


13343 [PDF p.251] and estimation in this framework is formulated through a separable least-squares


13344 [PDF p.251] strategy.


13345 [PDF p.251] 


13346 [PDF p.251] 


13347 [PDF p.251] 9.1     Aim and Motivation of an Alternative Approach


13348 [PDF p.251] In the previous chapters we have built up an extensive LPV system theoretical


13349 [PDF p.251] framework to provide understanding of model structures and to develop tools for


13350 [PDF p.251] their analysis. Based on this framework it has been shown that a series-expansion


13351 [PDF p.251] representation of discrete-time asymptotically stable LPV systems is available in


13352 [PDF p.251] terms of orthonormal basis functions (OBFs). Based on the motivation given in


13353 [PDF p.251] Chap. 1, we aim to use finite truncations of such representations as models for the


13354 [PDF p.251] identification of LPV systems in the classical least-squared (LS) setting. We will


13355 [PDF p.251] show that these structures:


13356 [PDF p.251] • provide an easily scalable trade-off between model complexity and accuracy of


13357 [PDF p.251]   the estimate,


13358 [PDF p.251] • simplify identification and control design,


13359 [PDF p.251]

13364 [PDF p.252] 


13365 [PDF p.252] • do not suffer from locally changing system order,


13366 [PDF p.252] • they extend the results of LTI system identification.


13367 [PDF p.252] We also formulate the prediction-error setting for LPV identification, in order to


13368 [PDF p.252] analyze the stochastical properties of estimation in these model structures and to


13369 [PDF p.252] be able to investigate possible noise model concepts. This provides the final tool in


13370 [PDF p.252] order to compare identification algorithms of the LPV field.


13371 [PDF p.252]    The aim of this chapter is to give a set of identification approaches that are capa-


13372 [PDF p.252] ble to deliver theoretically well-founded model estimates in the LPV framework, ac-


13373 [PDF p.252] complishing our primary objective. Here we do not pursue the proper exploration of


13374 [PDF p.252] the other two steps of the identification cycle: experiment design and model valida-


13375 [PDF p.252] tion, though some basic results about these issues are briefly covered in the analysis


13376 [PDF p.252] of the identification approaches. The proper treatment of these steps is reserved for


13377 [PDF p.252] further studies. Our intention is to open a new and sound alternative for the existing


13378 [PDF p.252] identification literature and to stimulate the development of a future generation of


13379 [PDF p.252] LPV identification approaches.

13381 [PDF p.252] 


13382 [PDF p.252] 9.2     OBFs Based LPV Model Structures


13383 [PDF p.252] LPV model structures based on truncated OBF expansion representations are intro-


13384 [PDF p.252] duced in this section. The structures are defined by using the concepts of the classi-


13385 [PDF p.252] cal prediction-error setting. Thus first, characterization of this setting is developed


13386 [PDF p.252] in the LPV case. Due to the absence of a transfer function type of description of


13387 [PDF p.252] LPV systems, the process and noise models are formulated based on their impulse-


13388 [PDF p.252] response representation. This gives the possibility to develop one-step-ahead predic-


13389 [PDF p.252] tors in this framework. As a next step, the proposed model structures, as truncated


13390 [PDF p.252] OBF expansion representations are formulated with an output-error (OE) type of


13391 [PDF p.252] noise models. Based on the fact that the coefficients can appear on the left or on


13392 [PDF p.252] the right-side of the basis functions in the expansion, different model structures can


13393 [PDF p.252] be introduced. Finally, important properties of the proposed model structures are


13394 [PDF p.252] investigated and compared to other model structures of the LPV identification field.


13395 [PDF p.252]

13397 [PDF p.252] 9.2.1    The LPV Prediction-Error Framework


13398 [PDF p.252] As a starting point, we assume that a non-autonomous, SISO, asymptotically stable


13399 [PDF p.252] LPV system S = (Z, P, W, B) is given in discrete-time (DT) with scheduling signal


13400 [PDF p.252] p. We aim at the identification of this system based on a predefined input-output (IO)


13401 [PDF p.252] partition (u, y). We suppose that S is equivalent with the deterministic part of the


13402 [PDF p.252] data generating physical system (i.e. the deterministic part of the physical system


13403 [PDF p.252] corresponds to an LPV system with the considered scheduling signal). Based on


13404 [PDF p.252] first principles information, it is possible in practice to select scheduling variables


13405 [PDF p.252] for a plant that yield an LPV equivalent (see the procedure developed in Sect. 7.4).

13710 [PDF p.258] 9.2.3     Properties of Wiener and Hammerstein OBF Models


13711 [PDF p.258] As a next step, important properties of the introduced models are investigated from


13712 [PDF p.258] the viewpoint of system identification. First we prove that the W-LPV OBF and H-


13713 [PDF p.258] LPV OBF models are general approximators of LPV systems, so by these models,


13714 [PDF p.258] LPV systems can be approximated with arbitrary precision. Then we explore how a


13715 [PDF p.258] locally changing McMillan degree of the system, which is a crucial problem in the


13716 [PDF p.258] interpolation-based identification methods, affects these model structures. Next we


13717 [PDF p.258] show why these model structures are beneficial in the prediction-error setting and


13718 [PDF p.258] 


13719 [PDF p.259] 9.2 OBFs Based LPV Model Structures                                                   241


13720 [PDF p.259] 


13721 [PDF p.259] how estimates in these structural forms can be used for control design, i.e. that these


13722 [PDF p.259] models are compatible with the existing LPV control theory.


13723 [PDF p.259] 


13724 [PDF p.259] 9.2.3.1   General Approximation Property


13725 [PDF p.259] 


13726 [PDF p.259] It has been show in Chap. 5 that an asymptotically stable discrete-time LPV systems


13727 [PDF p.259] has a series-expansion representation in terms of an arbitrary basis for RH2− (E).


13728 [PDF p.259] For such an approximation-free representation, infinitely many basis functions, Φn∞g ,


13729 [PDF p.259] are required in the general case. This implies that using a finite number of basis


13730 [PDF p.259] functions, Φnnge , restricts the class of realizable LPV systems. Thus, it is important to


13731 [PDF p.259] investigate the approximation capabilities of these models.


13732 [PDF p.259]     In the work of [30], it has been proved for nonlinear Wiener models that, if the


13733 [PDF p.259] LTI part is an OBF filter bank, then such models are general approximators of non-


13734 [PDF p.259] linear systems with fading memory (NL dynamic systems with convolution rep-


13735 [PDF p.259] resentation). This means that, if the number of the OBFs in the filter bank tends


13736 [PDF p.259] to infinity, then the best achievable approximation error of the output trajectories


13737 [PDF p.259] converges to zero in an arbitrary norm, under the condition that the correct static


13738 [PDF p.259] nonlinearity is used in the weighting block.


13739 [PDF p.259]     Now consider the LPV case. In Chap. 5 it has been shown that the series-


13740 [PDF p.259] expansion of asymptotically stable LPV systems in terms of an orthonormal ba-


13741 [PDF p.259] sis Φn∞g is convergent. It has also been highlighted, that such series expansions in


13742 [PDF p.259] general only exist, if the expansion coefficients have dynamic dependence. Further-


13743 [PDF p.259] more, it has been shown that the expansion coefficients yield a sequence, which


13744 [PDF p.259] converges to zero for each scheduling trajectory. For a given basis sequence Φn∞g ,


13745 [PDF p.259] the worst-case approximation error of a truncated expansion representation is

13768 [PDF p.259] Property 9.1 (General LPV approximation) W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models are


13769 [PDF p.259] general approximators of LPV systems.


13770 [PDF p.259] This result means that, by extending the basis function set of these models, ap-


13771 [PDF p.259] proximation of general LPV systems can be achieved with arbitrary precision. An


13772 [PDF p.259] additional property is that, in practice, careful selection of the basis functions can


13773 [PDF p.259] ensure almost error free representation of the frozen transfer function set FS of S


13774 [PDF p.259] with a limited number of OBFs (see Chap. 8). Such a basis function set has fast con-

13779 [PDF p.260] the general approximator property, the proposed model structures offer an efficient


13780 [PDF p.260] approximation structure for identification.


13781 [PDF p.260]    There is also an important difference with respect to the previously mentioned


13782 [PDF p.260] nonlinear counterpart of this result. In the nonlinear case, a necessary condition of


13783 [PDF p.260] the general approximator property is that the static nonlinearity must contain all


13784 [PDF p.260] possible combinations of the products of the output signals y̆i j of the filter bank.


13785 [PDF p.260] Due to the linear signal relation of the LPV setting, this condition is not required for


13786 [PDF p.260] Property 9.1, i.e. the linear combination of y̆i j with meromorphic PV coefficients is


13787 [PDF p.260] sufficient.


13788 [PDF p.260] 


13789 [PDF p.260] 9.2.3.2   McMillan Degree Property


13790 [PDF p.260] 


13791 [PDF p.260] An additional property of the introduced model structures is that they are well struc-


13792 [PDF p.260] tured against changes of the McMillan degree in the frozen system set FS of S.


13793 [PDF p.260] It is generally true that, if for a constant scheduling signal p(t) = p the associated


13794 [PDF p.260] Fp ∈ FS has a lower McMillan degree than the rest of the systems in FS , then


13795 [PDF p.260] this does not imply that any of the coefficient functions {wi j } of the OBF series-


13796 [PDF p.260] expansion is zero for p. This shows that these model parameterizations are not af-


13797 [PDF p.260] fected by problems that are common for LPV-SS or IO representations based model


13798 [PDF p.260] structures (see Chap. 1).


13799 [PDF p.260] 


13800 [PDF p.260] 9.2.3.3   Linear in the Coefficients Property


13801 [PDF p.260] 


13802 [PDF p.260] The third, but equally important property of W-LPV OBF and H-LPV OBF models


13803 [PDF p.260] is that they are linear in the coefficients θ , i.e. both in predictor equations (9.22) and


13804 [PDF p.260] (9.25) the coefficients {wi j } appear linearly. This means that for a LS identification


13805 [PDF p.260] criterion and with a linear parametrization of {wi j }, the estimation problem of these


13806 [PDF p.260] coefficient functions has an analytic solution.


13807 [PDF p.260] 


13808 [PDF p.260] 9.2.3.4   Models for Control


13809 [PDF p.260] 


13810 [PDF p.260] The proposed models are also efficiently applicable for LPV control design.


13811 [PDF p.260] Through (9.23a–b) and (9.26a–b), a SS realization of the estimated models is avail-


13812 [PDF p.260] able. Such SS forms have a trivial LFR realization if the coefficients {wi j } have


13813 [PDF p.260] polynomial or rational dependence on p. Therefore the existing LPV control ap-


13814 [PDF p.260] proaches, which are exclusively formulated for SS representations, can be directly


13815 [PDF p.260] applied. Due to the fact, that both in (9.23a) and (9.26a) the matrix A is constant,


13816 [PDF p.260] optimal control design greatly simplifies with respect to these model estimates. The


13817 [PDF p.260] reason is that global dynamic stability of models with constant A can be always


13818 [PDF p.260] expressed by a Lyapunov equation with non-parameter dependent, i.e. constant P


13819 [PDF p.260] (see Sect. (3.3.2)). The only disadvantage is that many control approaches assumes


13820 [PDF p.260] static dependence of the matrices. This implies, that dependence of {wi j } must be


13821 [PDF p.260] restricted to static dependence, i.e. wi j ∈ R|nP , to provide models to which these


13822 [PDF p.260] control solutions can be applied. However, for the general approximator property,


13823 [PDF p.260] 


13824 [PDF p.261] 9.2 OBFs Based LPV Model Structures                                                             243


13825 [PDF p.261] 


13826 [PDF p.261] dynamic dependence of the coefficients is required, which means that the restric-


13827 [PDF p.261] tion to static dependence reduces the representation capabilities of the models. This


13828 [PDF p.261] issue is explored further in Sect. 9.3 and 9.4.
