13937 [PDF p.263] 


13938 [PDF p.263] 9.2.4.3   Similarity to the Nonlinear Wiener and Hammerstein Models


13939 [PDF p.263] 


13940 [PDF p.263] By comparing NW and NH models to the introduced structures, the structural simi-


13941 [PDF p.263] larity is immediate. However, there are some fundamental differences:


13942 [PDF p.263] • In the NW and NH case, a static nonlinearity is assumed on the output/input of


13943 [PDF p.263]   the LTI part. In the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF case, the “nonlinearity” is entering


13944 [PDF p.263]   through a dynamic dependence on p, which can be composed of external (strict


13945 [PDF p.263]   LPV systems) and internal (quasi-LPV systems) variables alike. Assuming that p


13946 [PDF p.263]   is equal to u or y, NW and NH models can be viewed as special cases of W-LPV


13947 [PDF p.263]   and H-LPV OBF models under minor restrictions on the static nonlinearities (see


13948 [PDF p.263]   Sect. 7.4.3).


13949 [PDF p.263] • The LTI parts of W-LPV and H-LPV OBF are respectively single-input multiple-


13950 [PDF p.263]   output (SIMO) and multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems as opposed to


13951 [PDF p.263]   the SISO LTI part of NW and NH models1 .


13952 [PDF p.263] 


13953 [PDF p.263] 


13954 [PDF p.263] 9.2.5     Identification of W-LPV and H-LPV OBF Models


13955 [PDF p.263] In the following, a general outline of LPV identification based on W-LPV and H-


13956 [PDF p.263] LPV OBF models is presented. The major steps of the identification cycle: model


13957 [PDF p.263] structure selection, identification criterion selection, and estimation are considered.


13958 [PDF p.263] Our aim is to set the stage for the upcoming discussion of LPV-OBF identification


13959 [PDF p.263] approaches, which are based on particular choices with respect to these steps.


13960 [PDF p.263] 


13961 [PDF p.263] 9.2.5.1   OBF Selection


13962 [PDF p.263] 


13963 [PDF p.263] In the case of W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models, there is a primal emphasis on the


13964 [PDF p.263] model structure selection step of the identification cycle. This is due to the fact that


13965 [PDF p.263] selection of the finite OBF set, that defines the structure, effects the approximation


13966 [PDF p.263] capabilities in terms of the convergence rate of the series-expansion with respect to


13967 [PDF p.263] 1 Originally both Wiener and Hammerstein proposed their models with SIMO and MISO


13968 [PDF p.263] 


13969 [PDF p.263]   LTI parts, but because of the complexity of the problem, the LTI part has been simplified


13970 [PDF p.263]   to be SISO [25, 105].

13975 [PDF p.264] gence rate, negligible approximation error, i.e. bias can be achieved. Beside selec-


13976 [PDF p.264] tion of an adequate basis it is also important to decide how many of the functions in


13977 [PDF p.264] the chosen basis function sequence are considered in the model, i.e. in which degree


13978 [PDF p.264] the expansion is truncated. This decision directly effects the efficiency of the model


13979 [PDF p.264] structure in terms of the number of coefficients to be estimated.

13981 [PDF p.264] cussed in Chap. 7, where an algorithm has been proposed to assist basis selection

13983 [PDF p.264] locations of the system can be characterized, and based on this pole set, the optimal

14096 [PDF p.266] 9.3      Identification with Static Dependence


14097 [PDF p.266] In the previous part, we have developed truncated OBF expansion models, as the


14098 [PDF p.266] basic ingredients of a well-posed LPV identification approach. As a next step, we


14099 [PDF p.266] show how these model structures can be efficiently identified in the prediction-error


14100 [PDF p.266] setting, such that the obtained models are directly applicable for control design.


14101 [PDF p.266] First we clarify the exact identification setting (parametrization, identification cri-


14102 [PDF p.266] terion, etc.) in which we aim to derive the model estimates. Then we develop our


14103 [PDF p.266] approaches using either the gain-scheduling identification strategy (local approach)


14104 [PDF p.266] or a linear regression based strategy with varying scheduling trajectory (global


14105 [PDF p.266] approach). We only treat the SISO case. The MIMO extension of the developed


14106 [PDF p.266] approaches is covered later. The methods are analyzed in terms of variance, bias,


14107 [PDF p.266] consistency and validation of the model estimates is also investigated. Finally, a


14108 [PDF p.266] simulation example is studied to visualize the performance of the approaches.


14109 [PDF p.266] 


14110 [PDF p.266] 


14111 [PDF p.266] 9.3.1      The Identification Setting


14112 [PDF p.266] In the previous parts, we have seen that a common feature of all LPV model struc-


14113 [PDF p.266] tures, either based on SS, IO, or series-expansion representations, is that to represent


14114 [PDF p.266] general LPV systems they need dynamic dependence in the parametrization of their


14115 [PDF p.266] coefficients. However, LPV control design approaches often assume only static de-


14116 [PDF p.266] pendence of the model estimate. On the other hand, it is hard to handle the extra


14117 [PDF p.266] degree of freedom that dynamic dependence constitutes in an estimation problem.


14118 [PDF p.266]

14433 [PDF p.272] 9.3.5     Properties


14434 [PDF p.272] In this part the properties of the introduced identification approaches are investi-


14435 [PDF p.272] gated. First we analyze the restriction of the used linear parametrization with static


14436 [PDF p.272] dependence in the identification of general LPV systems and we characterize that


14437 [PDF p.272] subclass of LPV systems where no bias results. Next we motivate when the use of


14438 [PDF p.272] a global approach or a local approach is more fruitful in practice. Then we show


14439 [PDF p.272] convergence and consistency of the parameter estimates. By using similarity of the


14440 [PDF p.272] identification methods with respect to LTI prediction-error identification, we charac-


14441 [PDF p.272] terize basic results about variance and bias of the estimates. Finally, (in)validation


14442 [PDF p.272] issues are discussed in the introduced framework together with the estimation of


14443 [PDF p.272] initial conditions.


14444 [PDF p.272] 


14445 [PDF p.272] 9.3.5.1   Representation Capabilities via Static Dependence


14446 [PDF p.272] 


14447 [PDF p.272] It is important to investigate the effects of the linear parametrization with static


14448 [PDF p.272] dependence on the representation capabilities of the models. From the SS repre-


14449 [PDF p.272] sentation form of the models (see (9.23a–b) and (9.26a–b)) it is obvious that the


14450 [PDF p.272] assumption of static dependence restricts the class of representable LPV systems


14451 [PDF p.272] to systems which have a SS representation with static p-dependence only in the C


14452 [PDF p.272] (see (9.23a)–b) or in the B (see (9.26a)–b) system matrices. This means that sys-


14453 [PDF p.272] tems that have no representation that satisfies these conditions are not in the model


14454 [PDF p.272] class. Hence, due to parametrization, a modeling error inevitably occurs during the


14455 [PDF p.272] identification process in these cases. Additionally, the linear parametrization of the


14456 [PDF p.272] expansion coefficients (see (9.38a–b)) implies that systems that are identifiable in


14457 [PDF p.272] the considered way are further restricted to have a SS representation where only the


14458 [PDF p.272] C (or B) matrix depends on p and the functional dependence is the linear combina-


14459 [PDF p.272] tion of the used functions ψi j . This underlines that selection of these functions based


14460 [PDF p.272] on prior information is an important part of the model structure selection process.


14461 [PDF p.272]     A second consequence of the parametrization (9.38a–b) rises with respect to the


14462 [PDF p.272] general approximator property of the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models. We have


14463 [PDF p.272] seen in the general case that increasing ne lowers the achievable approximation er-


14464 [PDF p.272] ror with these models. However, in case of static dependence, increasing ne enlarges


14465 [PDF p.272] Span{Φnnge } which means that the worst-case representation error in the KnW sense


14466 [PDF p.272] is lowered with respect to the frozen system set of the data generating system. How-


14467 [PDF p.272] ever, an increase in ne may not lower the representation error of the LPV system


14468 [PDF p.272] in a global sense as the modeling error can be significantly dominated by the miss-


14469 [PDF p.272] ing non-static p-dependence of the expansion coefficients. This results in the loss


14470 [PDF p.272] of the general approximator property, meaning that the approximation capability of


14471 [PDF p.272] the model is restricted by the absence of dynamic coefficient dependence. Thus in-


14472 [PDF p.272] creasing ne in the hope of better accuracy can easily result in over-parametrization


14473 [PDF p.272] in this case.


14474 [PDF p.272]     We will see that despite the theoretically presented restrictions of the applied


14475 [PDF p.272] parametrization, commonly in a practical situation, adequate approximation of the


14476 [PDF p.272] data generating system can be achieved by the resulting model estimates. It is an


14477 [PDF p.272]

14479 [PDF p.273] 


14480 [PDF p.273] important remark that the global method is also applicable in the situations where


14481 [PDF p.273] the coefficients of the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF model structures are not assumed


14482 [PDF p.273] to be static. As the estimation algorithm is independent from the choice of the ψi j

14489 [PDF p.273] 9.3.5.2   Informativity of Data Sets and Persistency of Excitation


14490 [PDF p.273] 


14491 [PDF p.273] In order to estimate an adequate model in a given model set, most prediction-error


14492 [PDF p.273] algorithms require persistency of excitation in terms of DNd collected from the sys-


14493 [PDF p.273] tem. This condition is required to guarantee consistency and convergence of the


14494 [PDF p.273] estimates (see Sect. 2.4.3). In order to analyze the estimation in the defined LPV-


14495 [PDF p.273] OBFs model structures, a characterization of the data sets satisfying this condition


14496 [PDF p.273] is required.


14497 [PDF p.273]     In the LTI case persistency of excitation is associated with the notion of an infor-


14498 [PDF p.273]                                            Nd −1


14499 [PDF p.273] mative data set. Let DNd = {y(k), u(k)}k=0       be a data set of quasi-stationary u and y


14500 [PDF p.273] collected from the data generating system, and let WNd (θ , DNd ) be an identification


14501 [PDF p.273] criterion. DNd is called informative with respect to a parametric model set with pa-


14502 [PDF p.273] rameters θ and a given WNd if any two models in the model set can be distinguished


14503 [PDF p.273] under WNd (θ , DNd ) [56]. Basically this means that if the model set is globally iden-


14504 [PDF p.273] tifiable (no two different parameters θ1 and θ2 give rise to the same predictor) and


14505 [PDF p.273] the data set DNd is informative, then WNd (θ , DNd ) has a global optimum in the


14506 [PDF p.273] statistical sense. The latter is the essential requirement for consistency of any min-


14507 [PDF p.273] imization method. The notion of persistency of excitation of order n relates in the


14508 [PDF p.273] LTI case to an informative DNd with respect to a model structure with n parameters.


14509 [PDF p.273] The latter is equivalent to the possibility of statistically uniquely estimating a nth


14510 [PDF p.273] order FIR filter based on DNd .


14511 [PDF p.273]     In the LPV case there are numerous differences. First of all, the requirements for


14512 [PDF p.273]                                                                                  nψ


14513 [PDF p.273] identifiability imply that the linear combinations of the used functions {ψl }l=0    in the


14514 [PDF p.273] coefficient parametrization provide inequivalent dynamical behaviors of the model


14515 [PDF p.273] structure for each θ . Moreover, the notion of an informative data set in the LPV case


14516 [PDF p.273] is not equivalent to the condition of persistency of excitation with a given order.


14517 [PDF p.273] First of all, the model parameters θ are related to signals ψl (p)φi j (q)u and not only


14518 [PDF p.273]                                                                    nψ


14519 [PDF p.273] the time-shifted versions of u and y, thus the functions {ψl }l=0     and the scheduling


14520 [PDF p.273] trajectory p together also influence the estimation of θ . Moreover, the estimation of


14521 [PDF p.273] the parameters of a LPV-FIR filter, irrelevant to the coefficient parametrization, is


14522 [PDF p.273] not equivalent with the estimation of LPV-ARX models or LPV-OBF models due


14523 [PDF p.273] to the non-commutativity of multiplication by q. This means that the terminology


14524 [PDF p.273] of persistency of excitation with order n is ill-defined in the LPV case. Instead, the


14525 [PDF p.273] informativity of the data sets with respect to the assumed coefficient parametrization


14526 [PDF p.273] and model order must be satisfied in order to ensure consistency and convergence


14527 [PDF p.273] 


14528 [PDF p.274] 256                                                       9 LPV Identification via OBFs


14529 [PDF p.274] 


14530 [PDF p.274] of the estimation. However, conditions for data sets to be informative have not been


14531 [PDF p.274] investigated directly in the LPV literature.


14532 [PDF p.274]    For the case of LPV-ARX models with polynomial dependence of the coefficients


14533 [PDF p.274] on the parameters, conditions for persistency of excitation have been studied in [57]


14534 [PDF p.274] and [225], unknowingly also addressing the question of informativity of the data


14535 [PDF p.274] set. In these works it is assumed that a LPV system is a family of LTI systems, each


14536 [PDF p.274] associated with a point in P. If the dependence on p is polynomial of order nψ , then


14537 [PDF p.274] the LPV system identification can be realized by identifying at least nψ LTI models


14538 [PDF p.274] operating at distinct values of P, and using these to determine the coefficients of the


14539 [PDF p.274] polynomial dependence based on the interpolation principle. This means that a data


14540 [PDF p.274] set DNd is informative if


14541 [PDF p.274] • p visits at least nψ different points p1 , . . . , pnψ ∈ P.


14542 [PDF p.274] • Each sequence of u associated with a pl must be persistently exciting with respect


14543 [PDF p.274]   to the LTI model corresponding to pl .


14544 [PDF p.274] • The number of revisits of each pl must be large enough to approximate the er-


14545 [PDF p.274]   godicity condition in a given neighborhood around the considered points of P.


14546 [PDF p.274] These conditions are rather conservative from a number of viewpoints. A LPV sys-


14547 [PDF p.274] tem can be considered as a set of LTI systems associated with points of P, but these


14548 [PDF p.274] systems share a common memory so they can describe the continuation of the signal


14549 [PDF p.274] trajectories when p changes. This means that in terms of the above given conditions


14550 [PDF p.274] the variation of p must be infinitely slow in order to consider these systems to be


14551 [PDF p.274] independent LTI systems. However, ergodicity requires basically that the number of


14552 [PDF p.274] revisits of the chosen points must be infinite in the general case, which means that


14553 [PDF p.274] the p should vary as fast as possible to revisit these points more often. This shows


14554 [PDF p.274] that the above given conditions are too conservative for practical use. In [225], an


14555 [PDF p.274] improved version of this approach has been developed which tries to overcome the


14556 [PDF p.274] problem of conservativeness, but since it is based on the same principle of indepen-


14557 [PDF p.274] dent LTI system estimation, the question whether a data set is informative in the


14558 [PDF p.274] LPV case remains open. However, in practice, the absence of a solid criterion re-


14559 [PDF p.274] stricts the user to the paradigm to excite the system as much as possible in order to


14560 [PDF p.274] guarantee consistency and convergence of the estimation.

14732 [PDF p.278] 9.3.5.7   (In)validation


14733 [PDF p.278] 


14734 [PDF p.278] In general, reliable (in)validation of LPV model estimates is a theoretically hard


14735 [PDF p.278] task. One problem is that uncertainty of the model estimates has not been investi-


14736 [PDF p.278] gated in the LPV framework and, on the other hand, it is difficult to judge how the


14737 [PDF p.278] estimated model relates or fits to the available first principle knowledge.


14738 [PDF p.278]     In general, only (in)validation through model simulation is available, comparing


14739 [PDF p.278] the model output with respect to measured data records which are assumed to be


14740 [PDF p.278] informative. Here the richness of p in terms of excitation has a prime importance,


14741 [PDF p.278] as with slowly varying scheduling trajectories, model estimates with significantly


14742 [PDF p.278] different transient behavior can seem to be both valid models of the plant. Error


14743 [PDF p.278] measures like MSE, BFR and VAF, introduced in Sect. 2.4.7, can be successfully


14744 [PDF p.278] used to accommodate comparison of the simulated and measured signals and to


14745 [PDF p.278] decide on the validity of the model estimates. However, in case of an invalidated


14746 [PDF p.278] model estimate, it is hard to give any indication how to identify the system with a


14747 [PDF p.278] better end result (reconfiguration of the model structure, more exciting (u, p), other


14748 [PDF p.278] type of identification method, etc.).


14749 [PDF p.278]     Additionally, for the introduced models, (in)validation can also be accomplished


14750 [PDF p.278] based on the residual signal ε in the one-step-ahead prediction error (9.15). The


14751 [PDF p.278] residual can be easily computed for the proposed models as the inverse of the noise


14752 [PDF p.278] model is 1. Applying residual analysis, similar to the LTI case, the hypothesis that


14753 [PDF p.278] ε is white noise or ε is uncorrelated with the past inputs can be tested. If these


14754 [PDF p.278] hypothesis tests result in rejection, then the deficiency of the applied model structure


14755 [PDF p.278] is implied. The only problem is that due to the approximative nature of the applied


14756 [PDF p.278] model structure (both in terms of the finite series expansion and in terms of the


14757 [PDF p.278] assumption of static dependence), some unmodeled dynamics of the system always


14758 [PDF p.278] contribute to the residual term. This implies that, based on residual analysis, the


14759 [PDF p.278] models are most likely to be rejected. Thus, in the following, we only consider


14760 [PDF p.278] (in)validation in terms of simulations and error measures.


14761 [PDF p.278] 


14762 [PDF p.278] 9.3.5.8   Initial Conditions


14763 [PDF p.278] 


14764 [PDF p.278] In practice, slow dynamics of the system, safety considerations, or high costs of long


14765 [PDF p.278] measurements often result in data records which are collected with non-zero initial


14766 [PDF p.278] conditions of the plant. For these data sets, the initial conditions need to be estimated


14767 [PDF p.278] during the identification process. In the LTI case the identification framework of


14768 [PDF p.278] OBFs supports estimation of initial conditions (see [73]), which can be efficiently


14769 [PDF p.278] applied in the local algorithm to estimate initial conditions of the frozen systems of


14770 [PDF p.278] S. Therefore, further investigation of initial condition estimation is only interesting


14771 [PDF p.278] for the global identification approach.

14802 [PDF p.279] 9.3.5.9    (Quasi) LPV System Identification


14803 [PDF p.279] 


14804 [PDF p.279] There is an important aspect of the proposed identification methods if the data gen-


14805 [PDF p.279] erating system is a quasi LPV system. For quasi LPV systems, generally, p cannot


14806 [PDF p.279] be held constant, as the scheduling is an internal signal of the system like elements


14807 [PDF p.279] of the state or output variables. Thus, for this case, only the global method is applica-


14808 [PDF p.279] ble, as the local approach needs identification of the system with respect to constant


14809 [PDF p.279] scheduling trajectories. Violation of the freedom of p, how this affects the previous


14810 [PDF p.279] results and what happens in case p is influenced by noise are not well understood


14811 [PDF p.279] phenomena and these questions are in the focus of current research.


14812 [PDF p.279] 


14813 [PDF p.279] 9.3.5.10    Global versus Local Approach


14814 [PDF p.279] 


14815 [PDF p.279] As demonstrated both the global and the local approaches provide attractive ways of


14816 [PDF p.279] identifying an LPV system an obvious question is when to use which approach. In


14817 [PDF p.279] most situations the global approach is considered to be a more attractive candidate


14818 [PDF p.279] as it provides estimation of the system with a varying trajectory of p, giving a better


14819 [PDF p.279] possibility to approximate the global dynamic behavior of the system instead of just


14820 [PDF p.279] the frozen aspects. As shown, estimation in the global case can be formulated in a


14821 [PDF p.279] simple least-squares setting and cumbersome problems of interpolation are avoided


14822 [PDF p.279] due to the fixed functional dependencies of the parametrization. The theoretically


14823 [PDF p.279] 


14824 [PDF p.280] 262                                                       9 LPV Identification via OBFs


14825 [PDF p.280] 


14826 [PDF p.280] better understood behavior of the stochastic nature of estimation in the global setting


14827 [PDF p.280] also suggests that it is a theoretically more sound approach than the local method if


14828 [PDF p.280] informativity of the measured data set can be guaranteed in the application.


14829 [PDF p.280]    However, practical use of LPV identification on industrial problems often turns


14830 [PDF p.280] out to favor different properties. In most practical applications, identification is must


14831 [PDF p.280] be accomplished in a closed-loop setting due to instability of the plant or because


14832 [PDF p.280] the current production can not be disturbed in the favor of identification. In terms


14833 [PDF p.280] of the local approach, the well worked out methods of the LTI framework can be


14834 [PDF p.280] fully used to solve the identification problem in a divide-and-conquer manner. This


14835 [PDF p.280] implies that closed-loop identification is practically feasible via this approach. For


14836 [PDF p.280] the global case, closed-loop identification in the general sense is not well worked


14837 [PDF p.280] out even though some recent research directions are promising [210, 94, 28].


14838 [PDF p.280]    The use of frequency-based identification is also supported in the local setting.


14839 [PDF p.280] The latter is important in mechatronic applications where the often tight model-


14840 [PDF p.280] ing specifications with respect to the frozen behaviors are only available in the fre-


14841 [PDF p.280] quency domain. Such specifications can often not be addressed in the global setting.


14842 [PDF p.280] On the other hand interpolation can result in unexpected global behavior as the lo-


14843 [PDF p.280] cal identification approach only focuses on the frozen behaviors. However, such a


14844 [PDF p.280] drawback can be avoided by using data with varying p to assist the interpolation.


14845 [PDF p.280]    As a general receipt the use of the global approach is advised whenever there is


14846 [PDF p.280] enough possibility to perturb the system for an informative data record and if the


14847 [PDF p.280] model specifications are not given in the frequency domain. In other situations the


14848 [PDF p.280] use of a local approach is advised due to its higher capability to meet the target


14849 [PDF p.280] performance under the given information content of available data sets.

14852 [PDF p.280] 


14853 [PDF p.280] In Chap. 1 it has been discussed that the attractive properties of truncated OBF


14854 [PDF p.280] expansion representations inspired some identification approaches in the NL and


14855 [PDF p.280] the fuzzy field. In order to position the developed approaches with respect to those


14856 [PDF p.280] methods, i.e. to clarify the connection or dissimilarities, the following properties are


14857 [PDF p.280] important:


14858 [PDF p.280] • In the nonlinear case, the method of [63] uses Wiener and Hammerstein type of


14859 [PDF p.280]   models where the LTI part is the linear combination of a filter bank of OBFs.


14860 [PDF p.280]   We have already shown that these models result as “special cases”of W-LPV and


14861 [PDF p.280]   H-LPV OBF models in the quasi-LPV case. In [159], the used model structure


14862 [PDF p.280]   contains fuzzy membership functions associated with a (Laguerre) basis function


14863 [PDF p.280]   in the filter bank.


14864 [PDF p.280] • In our approach, the OBFs, the backbone of the model structures, are optimized


14865 [PDF p.280]   for S, while in the methods of [159] and [63] they are assumed to be chosen by


14866 [PDF p.280]   the user.


14867 [PDF p.280] • In [63], the LTI part is parameterized and estimated as a linear combination of


14868 [PDF p.280]   the chosen basis functions simultaneously with the estimation of the static non-


14869 [PDF p.280]   linearity. Similarly in [159], both the LTI part and the fuzzy part are identified

14872 [PDF p.281] 


14873 [PDF p.281]   together. In our approach, the parametrization is focused on the expansion coef-

14876 [PDF p.281] • Both the proposed and the NL/fuzzy approaches use the least-squares criterion

15117 [PDF p.285] 9.4    Approximation of Dynamic Dependence


15118 [PDF p.285] In the previous part, OBFs-based model structures have been introduced for the


15119 [PDF p.285] identification of LPV systems, with the main intention to give flexible models that


15120 [PDF p.285] are able to describe general LPV systems, simplify identification, are useful for con-


15121 [PDF p.285] trol, and are unaffected by the difficulties present in the identification of LPV-SS or


15122 [PDF p.285] IO models. It has been shown that to describe any LPV system, the coefficients


15123 [PDF p.285] of the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models, similar to the coefficients of other LPV


15124 [PDF p.285] models, need to have dynamic dependence on p. We have motivated that dynamic


15125 [PDF p.285] dependence presents an extra freedom of the parametrization and is not supported


15126 [PDF p.285] by the existing control approaches. To overcome this problem, in Sect. 9.3 the coef-


15127 [PDF p.285] ficients have been restricted to static dependence. This assumption led to a novel and


15128 [PDF p.285] efficient identification approach of W-LPV and H-LPV OBF model structures based


15129 [PDF p.285] on the LS criterion. However, the drawback of the assumption has also been pointed


15130 [PDF p.285] out: it limits the class of representable LPV systems. In this section an alternative


15131 [PDF p.285] of LPV truncated OBF expansion models and its identification approach is intro-


15132 [PDF p.285] duced with the intention to improve the representation capabilities of the previously


15133 [PDF p.285] considered model structures and parametrization, but without the use of dynamic


15134 [PDF p.285] dependence. In fact the idea that we will apply is the introduction of an additional


15135 [PDF p.285] feedback-loop around each basis component of the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF model


15136 [PDF p.285] structures with a gain incorporating also static dependence (see Figures 9.8 and 9.9).


15137 [PDF p.285] In this way, the filter bank of OBFs as a dynamical LTI system is “reused”to provide


15138 [PDF p.285] dynamic expansion coefficients. This implies that these modified structures can ap-


15139 [PDF p.285] proximate a much wider class of LPV systems than W-LPV and H-LPV OBF mod-


15140 [PDF p.285] els with static dependence. The introduction of feedback-based weighting leads to

15292 [PDF p.288] 9.4.2     Properties of Wiener and Hammerstein Feedback Models


15293 [PDF p.288] In order to show the importance of the introduced feedback based model structures,


15294 [PDF p.288] their key properties are investigated in this section.


15295 [PDF p.288] 


15296 [PDF p.288] 9.4.2.1   Representation of Dynamic Dependence


15297 [PDF p.288] 


15298 [PDF p.288] First, the representation capabilities of the feedback based model structures are dis-


15299 [PDF p.288] cussed:


15300 [PDF p.288] Property 9.1 (Representation of dynamic dependence). Let S be an asymptotically


15301 [PDF p.288] stable LPV system and Φn∞g ⊂ RH2− (E) be a Hambo basis. Consider a Wiener-


15302 [PDF p.288] feedback model MWF (Φnnge , θ , BP ) of S with coefficients wi j and vi j having static


15303 [PDF p.288] dependence. If MWF (Φnnge , θ , BP ) is asymptotically stable, then its deterministic


15304 [PDF p.288] part has a convergent series-expansion in terms of Φn∞g . If there is a feedback co-


15305 [PDF p.288] efficient vi j of MWF (Φnnge , θ , BP ) which is dependent on p, i.e. not constant, then


15306 [PDF p.288] 


15307 [PDF p.289] 9.4 Approximation of Dynamic Dependence                                            271


15308 [PDF p.289] 


15309 [PDF p.289] the coefficients of the series-expansion have dynamic dependence, otherwise all ex-


15310 [PDF p.289] pansion coefficients have static dependence.


15311 [PDF p.289] Obviously the same property holds for the Hammerstein case. For a proof see Ap-


15312 [PDF p.289] pendix A.4. Note that in terms of Property 9.1, a WF-LPV or a HF-LPV OBF model


15313 [PDF p.289] can be considered to be equivalent with a W-LPV or a H-LPV OBF model with


15314 [PDF p.289] dynamic coefficient dependence. However, the converse does not hold in general.


15315 [PDF p.289] Thus, through static weighting functions wi j , vi j ∈ R|nP the feedback based OBF


15316 [PDF p.289] models can approximate general LPV systems. It is trivial that such an approxi-


15317 [PDF p.289] mation is more adequate than using W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models with static


15318 [PDF p.289] coefficient dependence. In fact, those models are special cases of the WF-LPV OBF


15319 [PDF p.289] and HF-LPV OBF structures. Equations (9.62a–b) and (9.65a–b) imply that the WF-


15320 [PDF p.289] LPV and HF-LPV OBF structures can approximate static scheduling dependence in


15321 [PDF p.289] the A matrix as well as static scheduling dependence in the autoregressive part, see


15322 [PDF p.289] (9.60a–b) and (9.63a–b). However, this improved representation capability comes


15323 [PDF p.289] at a price, namely that due to the feedback, stability of the model is not internally


15324 [PDF p.289] guaranteed like in the W-LPV or the H-LPV OBF case.


15325 [PDF p.289] 


15326 [PDF p.289] 9.4.2.2   General Approximation Property


15327 [PDF p.289] 


15328 [PDF p.289] Based on the previous part, a WF-LPV or a HF-LPV OBF model can only approx-


15329 [PDF p.289] imate and not represent an arbitrary LPV system S. So the general approximator


15330 [PDF p.289] property does not hold in this case as it would require dynamic dependence of W


15331 [PDF p.289] and V . However, these models have a series-expansion representation with coeffi-


15332 [PDF p.289] cients incorporating dynamic dependence, thus they give better approximations of


15333 [PDF p.289] general LPV systems than W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models restricted to have static


15334 [PDF p.289] dependence.


15335 [PDF p.289] 


15336 [PDF p.289] 9.4.2.3   Loss of Linearity in the Coefficients


15337 [PDF p.289] 


15338 [PDF p.289] The second price to be paid is that, by the introduction of the feedback loop, the


15339 [PDF p.289] linear-in-the-coefficients property of the original series-expansion structure is lost.


15340 [PDF p.289] The resulting predictors (9.61a–b) and (9.64a–b) are bilinear in the coefficients.


15341 [PDF p.289] 


15342 [PDF p.289] 9.4.2.4   McMillan Degree Property


15343 [PDF p.289] 


15344 [PDF p.289] Due to the fact that the introduced feedback based structures are still based on trun-


15345 [PDF p.289] cated series expansions, just like the W-LPV and H-LPV OBF models, they are well


15346 [PDF p.289] structured against changes of the McMillan degree in the frozen system set FS .


15347 [PDF p.289] 


15348 [PDF p.289] 9.4.2.5   Models for Control


15349 [PDF p.289] 


15350 [PDF p.289] The existing approaches of LPV control theory are also directly applicable for es-


15351 [PDF p.289] timates with the introduced model structures. Through (9.62a–b) and (9.65a–b),

15547 [PDF p.293] 9.4.4     Properties


15548 [PDF p.293] In the following important properties of the introduced identification approach of


15549 [PDF p.293] WF-LPV and HF-LPV OBF models are investigated. It is motivated that the sep-


15550 [PDF p.293] arable least-squares estimation scheme is convergent and the obtained parameter


15551 [PDF p.293] estimates are local minima or saddle points of the LS criterion.


15552 [PDF p.293] 


15553 [PDF p.293] 9.4.4.1   Convergence of the Iterative Estimation Scheme


15554 [PDF p.293] 


15555 [PDF p.293] In the proposed identification scheme, the coefficients wi j and vi j are parameterized


15556 [PDF p.293] linearly via (9.66), resulting in a set of unknown parameters {θiwjl } and {θivjl }. Due


15557 [PDF p.293] to the bilinear relationship in which these parameters appear in the one-step-ahead


15558 [PDF p.293] predictors (9.61a) and (9.64a), a separable least-squares algorithm is applied to


15559 [PDF p.293] tackle the minimization of the LS criterion. It is a cardinal question if this iterative


15560 [PDF p.293] scheme is convergent, i.e. is it guaranteed that the value of the LS criterion decreases


15561 [PDF p.293] in each consecutive iteration step. In each iteration cycle of this scheme, one set of


15562 [PDF p.293] the parameters is fixed, {θiwjl } or {θivjl }, in order to form a linear regression based


15563 [PDF p.293] estimation of the other set by minimizing the mean squared error of the residual.


15564 [PDF p.293] This results in a steepest descend type of iterative optimization in the search for the


15565 [PDF p.293] optimal LS prediction error. For such a separable least squares strategy, it is well


15566 [PDF p.293] known that it is convergent and the convergence point is a saddle point or a local


15567 [PDF p.293] minimum of the cost function [62]. The exact convergence point is characterized


15568 [PDF p.293] by the initial choice of {θivjl } in Step 3c. The estimates converge to that point of the


15569 [PDF p.293] 


15570 [PDF p.294] 276                                                       9 LPV Identification via OBFs


15571 [PDF p.294] 


15572 [PDF p.294] parameter space Θ whose associated region of attraction, based on the given data set,


15573 [PDF p.294] contains the initial choice of {θivjl }. Similar to the numerical optimization schemes


15574 [PDF p.294] of LTI OE or Box-Jenkins models, the global optimum of (9.37) can only be ob-


15575 [PDF p.294] tained by starting the iterative search from different initial values and comparing the


15576 [PDF p.294] results [105].


15577 [PDF p.294] 


15578 [PDF p.294] 9.4.4.2   Unstable Model Estimates


15579 [PDF p.294] 


15580 [PDF p.294] A further problem may arise in cases where the resulting model estimate is unstable,


15581 [PDF p.294] even if S is asymptotically stable. This phenomenon is due to the fact that the feed-


15582 [PDF p.294] back weighting is tuned on a particular, finite scheduling trajectory. As this feedback


15583 [PDF p.294] tuning can be thought of as the reoptimization of the basis with respect to DNd , the


15584 [PDF p.294] finite data length and the excitation capabilities of the input and scheduling signals


15585 [PDF p.294] directly effect the estimation. Thus, even if the resulting model is stable with respect


15586 [PDF p.294] to the scheduling trajectory in DNd it is not guaranteed that it is stable for any other


15587 [PDF p.294] p ∈ BP .


15588 [PDF p.294] 


15589 [PDF p.294] 9.4.4.3   Practical Use and (In)validation


15590 [PDF p.294] 


15591 [PDF p.294] Local minima and the possibility of unstable model estimates do not necessarily cre-


15592 [PDF p.294] ate problems in practice. If the resulting model passes the validation test it should


15593 [PDF p.294] be an acceptable model [105]. The problem is that the only theoretically sound


15594 [PDF p.294] (in)validation approach of the model estimates is based on simulation. By comput-


15595 [PDF p.294] ing error measures of the difference of simulated and measured outputs, the qualities


15596 [PDF p.294] of the model estimates can be compared. As is shown in the example of Sect. 9.4.5,


15597 [PDF p.294] the proposed method quickly converges in practice and provides a reliable estimate


15598 [PDF p.294] of LPV systems.


15599 [PDF p.294] 


15600 [PDF p.294] 


15601 [PDF p.294] 9.4.4.4   Consistency, Variance, and Bias of the Estimates


15602 [PDF p.294] 


15603 [PDF p.294] In the previous section, the linear-in-the-parameter property of the used model struc-


15604 [PDF p.294] tures in the one-step-ahead predictor enabled results on the consistency, variance,


15605 [PDF p.294] and bias of the resulting model estimates. In the feedback case, the linear-in-the-


15606 [PDF p.294] parameter property is lost, due to the bilinear relationship of the coefficients. Thus


15607 [PDF p.294] the previously developed results do not hold in this case. In nonlinear system iden-


15608 [PDF p.294] tification, there are many results on the consistency, variance, and bias of model


15609 [PDF p.294] estimates obtained via different types of separable least-squares strategies. How-


15610 [PDF p.294] ever, none of these results seem to apply to the considered model structures and


15611 [PDF p.294] estimation strategies used here. Investigation of consistency, variance, and bias of


15612 [PDF p.294] the estimation mechanism remains the subject of future research for the feedback


15613 [PDF p.294] based model structures.

15641 [PDF p.295] 9.4.5      Example


15642 [PDF p.295] In this section applicability of the WF-LPV OBF model structure and its identifi-


15643 [PDF p.295] cation approach for the approximation of general LPV systems is shown through


15644 [PDF p.295] an example. Comparison is made with the static-coefficient-function based Wiener


15645 [PDF p.295] OBF model structure to show that by using the proposed feedback structure, better


15646 [PDF p.295] performance of the model estimates can be achieved.


15647 [PDF p.295]    As in the previous case, the asymptotically stable LPV system S3 is considered


15648 [PDF p.295] which has been studied in Sect. 8.3.3. The IO representation of S3 , RIO (S3 ) is de-


15649 [PDF p.295] fined by (8.17). This system has also been identified in Sect. 9.3.6 by using the


15650 [PDF p.295] basis functions set Φ80 obtained via the FKcM algorithm with fuzzyness m = 25 and


15651 [PDF p.295] nc = 8.


15652 [PDF p.295]    Here we aim at the identification of S3 with the WF-LPV and W-LPV OBF model


15653 [PDF p.295] structures. To ensure fair comparison of the results, both model structures are used


15654 [PDF p.295] with basis functions Φ80 and the coefficients in W are parameterized as 2nd -order


15655 [PDF p.295] polynomials in p. In the feedback case, the coefficients in V are parameterized as


15656 [PDF p.295] 3rd -order polynomials. These orders have been found optimal after several trial and


15657 [PDF p.295] error experiments. Identification of S3 with the global approach has been accom-


15658 [PDF p.295] plished 100 times in 4 different noise settings with both the Wiener and the Wiener-


15659 [PDF p.295] feedback model structures. The data records for each identification have been


15660 [PDF p.295] generated by a white (u, p) with uniform distribution (U(−0.5, 0.5), U(0.65, 0.75))


15661 [PDF p.295] superimposed on random multisines (3 sines with random phase in [0, π ] and fre-


15662 [PDF p.295] quency in [0, π /5] and with overall amplitude of 0.5 and 0.05). The reason why this

15931 [PDF p.301] 


15932 [PDF p.301] applied to derive a MIMO basis expansion, to formulate MIMO version of W-LPV


15933 [PDF p.301] and H-LPV OBF models, and to develop identification algorithms that can deliver

15936 [PDF p.301] reformulation. However, there are numerous possibilities that may be interesting for

15939 [PDF p.301] OBF and W-LPV OBF models, or using other formulations of MIMO orthonormal


15940 [PDF p.301] basis functions, like presented in Sect. 2.3.


15941 [PDF p.301]    In conclusion, it can be stated that the introduced identification approaches can


15942 [PDF p.301] directly be applied to MIMO LPV systems without the need of any modification or

15944 [PDF p.301] of model structure selection, parametrization, and estimation offers an effective and

15948 [PDF p.301] 9.6   Conclusions


15949 [PDF p.301] In this final chapter we have extended the classical prediction-error setting to the


15950 [PDF p.301] LPV framework. Using this framework and the concept of LPV series expansion


15951 [PDF p.301] we have introduced discrete-time OBF based model structures and identification


15952 [PDF p.301] methods of LPV systems. Our purpose was to establish a well understood frame-


15953 [PDF p.301] work of LPV identification and to introduce an efficient LPV system identification


15954 [PDF p.301] approach which benefits from the attractive properties of truncated expansion model


15955 [PDF p.301] structures.


15956 [PDF p.301]    Due to the absence of a transfer function type of description in the LPV case,


15957 [PDF p.301] we have seen that the behavioral theory and the series expansion representation of


15958 [PDF p.301] LPV systems were crucial ingredients in order to formulate the extension of the


15959 [PDF p.301] prediction-error framework to the LPV case. The process and noise models were


15960 [PDF p.301] formulated based on their impulse response presentation which made it possible to


15961 [PDF p.301] establish the one-step-ahead predictor in the classical sense, under the assumption


15962 [PDF p.301] that the scheduling variable is a deterministic signal.


15963 [PDF p.301]    We have shown that using truncated OBF-expansion models it is possible to ben-


15964 [PDF p.301] efit from a number of attractive properties both in terms of local and global type


15965 [PDF p.301] of LPV system identification. Beside the simple linear regression based estimation


15966 [PDF p.301] schemes it has been also shown that the introduced structures can approximate any


15967 [PDF p.301] LPV system with arbitrary accuracy if the coefficients have dynamic dependence.


15968 [PDF p.301] Furthermore, these models are not effected by changing McMillan degree of the


15969 [PDF p.301] frozen aspects of the LPV system, which represents a significant difficulty for the


15970 [PDF p.301] identification of other type of LPV model structures. We have motivated that the


15971 [PDF p.301] introduced models are effectively applicable for control as they have a direct state-


15972 [PDF p.301] space realization, however to satisfy assumptions of the control approaches, their


15973 [PDF p.301] coefficient dependencies must be restricted to be static. The introduced approaches


15974 [PDF p.301] have also been analyzed in terms of variance, bias, and consistency.


15975 [PDF p.301]    To enable the estimation of truncated expansion models with dynamic coeffi-


15976 [PDF p.301] cient dependencies, but at the same time still provide applicable models for control,


15977 [PDF p.301] 


15978 [PDF p.302] 284                                                    9 LPV Identification via OBFs


15979 [PDF p.302] 


15980 [PDF p.302] feedback-based OBF model structures have been proposed in Sect. 9.4. It has been


15981 [PDF p.302] shown, that by using static dependence, the introduced model structure is equiv-


15982 [PDF p.302] alent to OBF expansion models with dynamic coefficient dependencies. For the


15983 [PDF p.302] identification with such feedback-based model structures, the previously developed


15984 [PDF p.302] global approach is extended, formulating the parameter estimation through a sepa-


15985 [PDF p.302] rable least-squares approach. Finally, in Sect. 9.5, the extension of the introduced


15986 [PDF p.302] approaches to MIMO systems is investigated. It has been shown that for OBF mod-


15987 [PDF p.302] els, based on MIMO functions composed from scalar basis sequences, the developed


15988 [PDF p.302] approaches and results are applicable.


15989 [PDF p.302]    We can conclude that we achieved our primary objective, giving an alternative,


15990 [PDF p.302] practically applicable approach for identification of LPV systems as models of an


15991 [PDF p.302] underlying physical process. On the other hand we left many open problems in terms


15992 [PDF p.302] of the whole identification cycle in the LPV context. These provide ample food for


15993 [PDF p.302] thought and objectives of future research.
